t.bronze age settlement and cemetery of tu:
Vergina is a small village at the foot of the Pierian mountains in northern Greece, and for most of history nobody outside the region knew its name. That changed in 1977, when the archaeologist Manolis Andronikos opened a great burial mound here and found royal tombs with astonishing grave goods. The site is ancient Aigai, the first capital of the Macedonian kingdom, and one of the tombs is widely attributed to Philip II, father of Alexander the Great. The prehistoric settlement and the large cemetery of burial mounds nearby show that people had been living and burying their dead here for a very long time before the Macedonian kings.

The museum built over the royal tombs is one of the most remarkable in Greece: the tumulus has been reconstructed and you walk inside it, in near darkness, past the tomb façades and display cases holding gold, ivory and weaponry. Allow at least an hour and a half. The palace remains and the theatre where Philip was assassinated are a short distance up the hill.

The riding around Vergina is varied. The plain of the Aliakmon river below is flat and agricultural, with orchards of peaches and apples, while the mountains rise sharply behind. Véroia, about nine kilometres away, is a lively town with an old Jewish quarter and a host of small Byzantine churches; the road west from there climbs into the Vermio mountains toward the ski area at Seli and the town of Naoussa, known for its red wine. Further south, the roads into the Pieria range and around Mount Olympus are excellent, with long series of bends and big views. Greek roads vary a lot: some are freshly surfaced, others rough and potholed, and dogs and goats are part of the traffic.

Véroia is the place for fuel, a good meal and a bed. Local specialities include revani, a syrupy semolina cake that Véroia is famous for. Spring and autumn are the best seasons; summer on the plain is very hot, though the mountains stay pleasant. Go early to the museum to beat the tour groups.
t.archaeological site of dion@40.2,22.5:
Mount Olympus rises straight out of the plain behind Dion, and on a clear morning its snow-streaked summit seems close enough to touch. The ancient Macedonians built their most sacred city here, at the foot of the home of the gods, and the kings came to sacrifice to Zeus before going to war. Philip II celebrated victories here, and Alexander the Great is said to have held a great festival at Dion before setting out to conquer Persia. Walking among the ruins, you can see why they chose the place: water bubbles up everywhere, the plain is fertile, and the mountain looms like a living presence.

The archaeological park is unusually green and wet. Springs flood parts of the site, especially the sanctuary of Isis, where a statue of the goddess stands reflected in a pool among reeds, frogs and turtles. There are remains of a theatre, baths, villas with mosaics, a basilica and a city wall, and the stone-paved main street runs for hundreds of metres through the trees. The museum in the modern village holds statues and finds, including a remarkable ancient water organ. Allow at least two hours and bring mosquito repellent in summer.

The riding is the second reason to be here. From Litochoro, about nine kilometres south, a winding mountain road climbs into the Enipeas gorge toward Prionia, the trailhead for climbers heading up to the summit, with hairpins, sheer drops, pine and beech forest and constant views back down to the Aegean. Surfaces are mostly decent but watch for rockfalls, goats and cars driven by tired hikers. The road along the coast is busier and flatter, and the national motorway nearby has tolls. Olympus weather can change fast, with afternoon storms in summer and snow from late autumn.

Litochoro is the base for most visitors, with fuel, tavernas, cafés and lodging, and a lively square under the plane trees. Try local dishes like grilled meat, bean soups or fresh trout from the mountains. Dion itself has a couple of cafés, and the beaches of the Pierian coast are a short ride away if you fancy a swim after the ruins. For a classical touch, toast the gods with a glass of local wine from the nearby Rapsani vineyards.
t.temple and former convent of saint willi:
Totolapan is a small town on the northern slopes of the Sierra de Chichinautzin, in the state of Morelos, and its Augustinian convent of San Guillermo is one of the fourteen sixteenth-century monasteries on the slopes of Popocatépetl that UNESCO listed in 1994. The friars who came to Mexico after the conquest built these fortress-like complexes to convert the indigenous population, with huge walled atriums where crowds could gather for open-air masses, chapels at the corners for processions, and austere churches with thick walls. Totolapan's convent is relatively modest, but its simplicity and setting give it a special charm.

The convent was famous for a crucifix, the Cristo de Totolapan, which became an object of intense devotion in colonial times and has an eventful history of being moved and returned. The church and cloister have remains of mural paintings, and the atrium is lined with old trees. From the town, on a clear day, you can see the snow-capped cone of Popocatépetl, the active volcano that dominates the region and occasionally puffs ash into the sky.

The riding around Totolapan is very enjoyable. The town lies on the road between Tlayacapan, Atlatlahucan and the highlands toward Mexico City, and the roads wind through pine forest, cornfields and small villages, with views of the volcanoes. The altitude is high, around two thousand metres and more, so the air is cool and the engine may feel a little weaker. Weekend traffic from Mexico City can be heavy, especially on the main roads to Cuautla and Cuernavaca, and the topes, speed bumps, are everywhere. The rainy season, from June to October, brings afternoon storms, so ride in the morning.

Totolapan has small shops, a market and simple food stalls, and fuel should be available in or near town; larger towns like Cuautla and Yecapixtla have more services. Tlayacapan, a few kilometres away, is a Pueblo Mágico with another convent of the route, pottery workshops and a lively market, and is a good place for lunch. Local dishes include cecina from Yecapixtla, thin salted beef, and tlacoyos, corn cakes filled with beans. Combine several of the convents in a day, and you will have a vivid picture of colonial Mexico.
t.xochimilco 3@19.2,-99.0:
San Andrés Mixquic sits on the southeastern edge of Mexico City, in the borough of Tláhuac, and it feels like a village despite being part of one of the largest cities on earth. It is famous throughout Mexico for its Day of the Dead celebrations, when the cemetery around the church of San Andrés fills with marigolds, candles and families who keep vigil through the night of 2 November, and the whole town turns into a festival of altars, music and food. The rest of the year, Mixquic is a quiet place of canals, chinampas and vegetable fields.

Chinampas are the artificial islands of mud and vegetation, anchored by willow trees, that the Aztecs and their predecessors built in the shallow lakes of the Valley of Mexico to grow crops, and they are the reason Xochimilco and its surroundings were listed by UNESCO in 1987. The system is incredibly productive, and some of the chinampas around Mixquic are still farmed, producing lettuce, herbs, flowers and vegetables for the city's markets. The canals are home to the axolotl, the strange salamander that has become a symbol of Mexico City and of the struggle to save its wetlands.

Riding to Mixquic means riding through the dense, chaotic traffic of the southern city, with buses, microbuses and taxis competing for space, potholes and speed bumps everywhere, and drivers who treat traffic rules as suggestions. Once you leave the main avenues, the roads become calmer, running along canals and fields, with views of the volcanoes Popocatépetl and Iztaccíhuatl on clear days. Mexico City has driving restrictions based on license plates, the Hoy No Circula programme, which can affect vehicles from other states, so check the current rules before you go.

Mixquic has fuel stations on its access roads, small restaurants and street stalls selling tacos, quesadillas and tamales. A boat trip on the canals, either here or in Xochimilco itself, is a relaxing way to see the chinampas. Tláhuac and Xochimilco have more services, and the historic centre of Xochimilco, with its market and church, is a short ride away. Plan your visit for the morning, when traffic is lighter and the air is clearer.
t.ancient convent of the nativity@19.0,-99:
Tepoztlán sits at the foot of a wall of jagged volcanic cliffs in northern Morelos, and on the highest ridge above town, a small Aztec pyramid, the Tepozteco, dedicated to the god of pulque, clings to the rock. Down in the town, the Dominican convent of the Nativity, built in the mid-sixteenth century, is one of the monasteries on the slopes of Popocatépetl listed by UNESCO in 1994. Its massive church, with a facade carved with angels, the sun and the moon, and a large atrium, is impressive, and the cloister has remains of colourful mural paintings. Part of the convent houses a museum.

Tepoztlán is a Pueblo Mágico with a reputation as a mystical town, attracting spiritual seekers, artists and weekenders from Mexico City. The Sunday market is packed with stalls selling crafts, food and remedies, and the streets are lined with cafés, ice cream shops and restaurants. The climb to the pyramid is steep, taking about an hour on a rocky path, but the view over the valley is spectacular.

For riders, Tepoztlán is one of the most popular weekend destinations from Mexico City, and on Saturdays and Sundays you will see hundreds of motorcycles in town. The road from the capital, the federal highway 95D, is a toll road with long curves through pine forests as it descends from the high plateau, and the free road that runs alongside it, through Tres Marías, is twistier and slower but more interesting. Weekend traffic can be heavy, and the town's narrow cobbled streets get jammed, so arrive early. The rainy season, from June to October, brings afternoon storms; the dry season is sunny but can be hazy.

Tepoztlán has fuel at the edge of town, plenty of restaurants and hotels, and the local ice creams, in unusual flavours, are famous. Try quesadillas, tlacoyos, cecina from nearby Yecapixtla and the pulque, a fermented agave drink, which you will save for after the ride. Cuernavaca, the city of eternal spring, is about twenty kilometres away, and the roads east toward Tlayacapan and Totolapan, through hills and cornfields, lead to other convents of the route, making a great day of riding.
t.crampoia reduta tatarilor@44.3,24.8:
Out on the flat Romanian plain east of the Olt river, the village of Crâmpoia sits among endless fields of wheat, maize and sunflowers, and its name has a place in Roman history. A Roman earthen fort near the village stood on the Limes Transalutanus, the frontier line that the Romans built east of the Olt in the early third century, running from the Danube northward toward the Carpathians, a long earthen rampart with forts and watchtowers. The local name Reduta Tătarilor, the Tatars' redoubt, reflects a common habit in Romania of attributing old earthworks to the Tatars or other invaders, long after the Romans were forgotten. The site is part of the UNESCO-listed frontier of Dacia.

What survives is earthwork: banks and ditches in the fields, sometimes hard to distinguish without a map or guide. The landscape is open and the horizon wide, and on a summer evening, with the sun setting over the fields, there is a melancholy beauty to the place.

The riding is flat and straight, with long roads across the plain, linking villages of low houses with gardens and wells, and little traffic apart from farm vehicles and horse-drawn carts. Road surfaces vary, from good tarmac to potholed and patched sections, and some village roads are unpaved. Summer heat can be intense, often above thirty-five degrees, and there is little shade, so carry plenty of water. Winter is cold and windy, with snow. The Olt valley, to the west, offers some variety, with river views and willow groves.

Dobrotești, about eleven kilometres away, and the larger towns of Slatina and Caracal, further afield, have fuel, shops and restaurants. Villages like Crâmpoia have small shops and perhaps a bar, but services are limited. Local food is hearty and simple: ciorbă, sour soups, mămăligă, polenta, and grilled meats like mici, small sausages served with mustard. The Danube is about fifty kilometres to the south, and the Roman city of Sucidava, at Corabia, with the remains of Constantine's bridge across the river, is worth a visit if you are following the Roman frontier.
t.former college of san francisco javier i:
Tepotzotlán is a Pueblo Mágico just off the highway north of Mexico City, and its heart is a building that stops you in your tracks. The old Jesuit college of San Francisco Javier was a training centre for the order in New Spain, a place where novices learned theology and native languages before being sent out across the colony. When the Jesuits were expelled in 1767 the college passed to others, and today it houses the National Museum of the Viceroyalty, one of the best collections of colonial art in the country. It also forms part of the Camino Real de Tierra Adentro, the silver road that ran north from the capital towards Santa Fe, inscribed by UNESCO in 2010.

The church facade is the showstopper: a tower of carved stone in full Churrigueresque style, a riot of saints, columns and foliage, golden in the late afternoon sun. Inside, the side chapels are dripping with gilded altarpieces, and the small domed chapel known as the camarín is so dense with ornament it almost hums. Allow at least an hour if you go in.

The town around it is lively and easy to enjoy, with a big plaza, market stalls and families out on weekends. Just outside, the Arcos del Sitio, a tall colonial aqueduct striding across a ravine, make a good short side trip on a twisting country road.

Getting there means dealing with the outskirts of the metropolis. The México-Querétaro highway is a toll road, fast and busy with trucks, and you leave it at the Tepotzotlán exit. Once off it, the local roads are narrower, with topes, the vicious speed bumps that appear without warning in every Mexican town, and plenty of minibuses stopping where they please. Altitude is over two thousand metres here, so expect cool mornings, hot middays and afternoon thunderstorms in the rainy season from about June to September.

With close to forty thousand people, Tepotzotlán has fuel, banks and food everywhere. Around the plaza you will find stalls selling tamales, quesadillas and pulque, and restaurants serving mole and barbacoa on weekends. Park somewhere you can keep an eye on the bike, grab an agua fresca and sit under the trees facing that facade; it is one of the great sights of colonial Mexico.
t.yomejima and peripheral reefs@27.5,142.2:
This is the one place on the list you cannot ride to, and it is worth being clear about that from the start. Yomejima is a small, uninhabited island in the Mukojima group, the northernmost cluster of the Ogasawara Islands, roughly a thousand kilometres south of Tokyo in the open Pacific. There are no roads, no people, no landing stage for visitors, and the reefs around it are part of the protected area that UNESCO inscribed as the Ogasawara Islands World Heritage site in 2011.

Why is it protected? Because these islands have never been connected to a continent. Everything that lives here arrived by wind, wave or wing, and then evolved in isolation. The result is a natural laboratory, sometimes called the Galápagos of the Orient, with a remarkable number of plants and land snails found nowhere else on earth, along with seabird colonies and rare birds. Introduced goats, rats and plants have done real damage over the past two centuries, and much conservation work has gone into removing them from the outer islands so that the native life can recover.

The nearest place a human can actually get to is Chichijima, the main inhabited island of the chain, and even that is an adventure. There is no airport for regular flights; the passenger ship from Tokyo takes around a day each way, and sailings run only every few days. On Chichijima there is a small town, a handful of roads looping over the hills to beaches and viewpoints, and boat tours that run out to dolphin and whale-watching grounds and, weather permitting, towards the more distant islands.

So think of Yomejima as a marker on a map rather than a stop on a ride. If your route has led you here, the honest advice is to enjoy the idea of it: a speck of volcanic rock ringed by coral and deep blue water, frigate birds wheeling above, entirely without traffic. If you find yourself in Japan with time to spare and the urge to do something truly remote, the long voyage to Chichijima is one of the most memorable trips the country offers, and a rented bike or scooter on the island will get you to its lookouts.
t.gresia la biserica@44.2,24.9:
The Wallachian plain in southern Romania is about as flat as Europe gets: a vast expanse of wheat, maize and sunflower fields stretching to the horizon, broken only by lines of acacia trees, irrigation channels and villages strung along the road. Teleorman county, where Gresia lies, is in the heart of it. Two thousand years ago, this was frontier land. The Romans built a long earthwork rampart with forts and towers running north to south east of the river Olt, known as the Limes Transalutanus, to protect their province of Dacia. Gresia and the sites around it, including Roșiorii de Vede, Crâmpoia and Izbășești, lie along its line. Little survives above ground, and the remains need a trained eye or an archaeologist's map to spot, but the idea of a Roman frontier running through these fields adds depth to a landscape that can seem empty.

The plain has its own beauty. In summer, the sunflowers turn their heads towards the sun in endless fields, storks nest on electricity poles in the villages, and the sky is huge. In winter, cold winds sweep across from the east, and snow can block roads. Summers are very hot and dry, often above thirty-five degrees, so ride early and carry water.

Villages here are poor and traditional, with houses painted in bright colours, wells in the yards and elderly people sitting on benches outside their gates, watching the world go by. Many younger people have left to work abroad.

The riding is straight and simple, with long, flat roads and occasional bends. Surfaces vary widely: national roads are mostly in good condition, while county and village roads can be badly potholed. Horse carts, tractors, dogs and pedestrians are common, especially in villages, and local drivers can be aggressive when overtaking. Night riding is best avoided, as unlit carts and animals can appear suddenly.

Roșiorii de Vede, about eight kilometres away, is the nearest town, with fuel, shops and restaurants. For a taste of the region, try mici, grilled minced meat rolls served with mustard and bread, and a cold beer at a roadside terrace, or fresh watermelon bought from a stall at the side of the road in summer.
t.temple and former convent of the assumpt:
Tochimilco sits high on the southern slopes of Popocatépetl, the great volcano that towers over central Mexico, and on clear mornings the snow-capped cone seems close enough to touch. Here, in the sixteenth century, Franciscan friars built a monastery dedicated to the Assumption of the Virgin, one of the early missions established to convert the indigenous population after the Spanish conquest. Its fortress-like church, with thick walls, battlements and a large atrium where crowds once gathered for open-air mass, is part of the UNESCO site of the Earliest Sixteenth-Century Monasteries on the Slopes of Popocatepetl, listed in 1994. In the town square, an old aqueduct and fountain built by the friars still bring water from the mountain.

Popocatépetl, known affectionately as Don Goyo, is an active volcano, and it regularly puffs out plumes of steam and ash. In recent years, eruptions have scattered ash over nearby towns and occasionally closed airports. An exclusion zone surrounds the summit, and climbing it is forbidden. Check the current alert level before travelling in the area, and be prepared for ash on the roads, which can be slippery.

The area around is a landscape of fields, orchards and forests, with villages clinging to the slopes. Atlixco, a short ride away, is a Pueblo Mágico known for its flowers and nurseries, and in November it hosts a huge display of poinsettias and marigolds for the Day of the Dead. Puebla, the state capital, is one of Mexico's great colonial cities, famous for its tiles, churches and cuisine, especially mole poblano, a rich sauce of chillies, chocolate and spices, and chiles en nogada, served in late summer.

The riding is scenic but demanding. Roads climb and wind through the volcanic foothills, with views of Popocatépetl and its neighbour Iztaccíhuatl, but surfaces can be rough, with potholes and topes, the infamous speed bumps found in every village. Traffic is moderate, with trucks, buses and local drivers who can be unpredictable. The altitude, around two thousand metres, means cool mornings and warm afternoons, and the rainy season, from about June to September, brings heavy afternoon storms.

Atlixco is the natural stop for fuel, shops and restaurants. Try cemitas, large sesame-seed sandwiches filled with meat, cheese and avocado, or a bowl of mole in a local fonda.
t.domogled valea cernei domogled coronin@4:
The river Cerna runs through one of the deepest and wildest valleys of the Romanian Carpathians, a narrow gorge between limestone cliffs, before emerging at Băile Herculane, one of the oldest spa towns in Europe. The Romans bathed in its hot springs nearly two thousand years ago and named the place after Hercules. In the nineteenth century, the Habsburgs built grand bathhouses, hotels and casinos in an ornate imperial style, and Emperor Franz Joseph and Empress Sisi came to take the waters. Many of these buildings now stand empty and decaying, a haunting sight, though restoration efforts are under way. The surrounding mountains form the Domogled-Valea Cernei National Park, and parts of its old beech forests are included in the UNESCO site of Ancient and Primeval Beech Forests.

The park is a place of rare nature. The limestone slopes are covered with forests of black pine, a local variety found here, and the warm, sheltered valleys host plants more typical of the Mediterranean. The area has a large population of horned vipers, so watch where you put your hands and feet when hiking. Bears, wolves and lynx roam the forests, and eagles soar above the cliffs.

The road up the Cerna valley from Băile Herculane is a superb ride, following the river through the gorge, past waterfalls, caves and hot springs, with cliffs towering above. It continues past a reservoir towards the mountains, and in places the surface becomes rough, so check conditions before committing. South of Herculane, the Danube cuts through the Iron Gates, a series of gorges on the border with Serbia, and the road along the river is spectacular, with the giant rock carving of the Dacian king Decebalus overlooking the water. At Drobeta-Turnu Severin, the remains of Trajan's bridge, which once spanned the Danube, can be seen on the bank.

The riding is excellent, but roads can be narrow, winding and poorly surfaced, with rockfalls after storms. Summers are hot in the valleys, and winters cold, with snow at altitude. Spring and autumn are ideal.

Băile Herculane, about seven kilometres away, has fuel, shops and restaurants, and Orșova on the Danube is another option. Try fresh trout from the mountain streams, or a bowl of fish soup by the Danube, and perhaps a soothing dip in one of the hot springs.
t.temple and former convent of saint john:
In the 1530s and 1540s, Augustinian friars arrived in the valleys below Popocatépetl to convert the local population, and they built churches that look half like cathedrals and half like castles. The convent of San Juan Bautista in Yecapixtla is one of the finest: a tall, fortress-like church with crenellated walls, a striking Gothic rose window over the entrance and a vast atrium where the indigenous congregation gathered for open-air services. It is part of the UNESCO listing of the Earliest Sixteenth-Century Monasteries on the Slopes of Popocatépetl, a group of fourteen convents across Morelos and Puebla.

The town itself is famous throughout Mexico for one thing: cecina, thin slices of salted and air-dried beef, grilled and served with fresh cheese, cream, salsa and tortillas. On weekends, families drive from Mexico City and Cuernavaca to eat it at the market stalls and restaurants around the plaza, and the smell of the grills drifts through the streets.

The riding is excellent. The roads of the Ruta de los Conventos link the monasteries through the foothills of the volcano, winding through fields of corn, sugar cane and avocado, with the snow-capped cone of Popocatépetl looming over everything on clear mornings. The volcano is active, and occasionally puffs out ash clouds that can dust the region, so check the alert level before you head to higher ground. The roads are mostly paved but can be patchy, with speed bumps, known as topes, in every village, livestock and slow trucks. The rainy season from June to September brings afternoon storms; the dry months are the best time to ride.

Yecapixtla, with around seventeen thousand inhabitants, has fuel stations and basic services, and Cuautla, a larger town nearby, has more choice and a history tied to Emiliano Zapata and the Mexican Revolution. Bring cash for the market and small restaurants. After a plate of cecina, wander into the atrium of the convent in the afternoon, when the light softens and the bells ring out over the town.
t.temple and former convent of saint domin:
Hueyapan sits high on the southern flank of Popocatépetl, in the far northeast of Morelos, where pine forest and orchards climb toward the volcano and the air is noticeably thinner than in the valleys below. In the sixteenth century, Dominican friars built a convent here dedicated to Santo Domingo, with a simple church, a cloister and a walled atrium where the indigenous population gathered for worship. It is one of the fourteen sites in the UNESCO listing of the Earliest Sixteenth-Century Monasteries on the Slopes of Popocatépetl, and while it is more modest than some of its neighbours, its setting is one of the most dramatic.

The town is known for its Nahua heritage and its weaving. Women here still use backstrap looms to make woollen textiles, including shawls, ponchos and skirts dyed with natural colours, and you may find them for sale in the market or in workshops. The slopes around Hueyapan are planted with avocado, peach and plum orchards, and the views of the volcano on clear mornings, with its plume of steam, are unforgettable.

The roads up to Hueyapan are steep and winding, with sharp curves and frequent speed bumps, and they climb from the warm valleys of Morelos into the cool highlands. The surface is generally paved but can be rough, and in the rainy season from June to September, afternoon storms can make it slippery. Popocatépetl is an active volcano, and the authorities set an alert level, sometimes restricting access to the higher slopes, so check before you go. Nearby Tetela del Volcán has another of the monasteries, and the road between the two is short but rewarding.

Hueyapan, with about six and a half thousand people, has small shops and food stalls, and may have fuel at the edge of town, but for reliable services head down to Cuautla or Yecapixtla. Bring warm clothing; even in the dry season, mornings can be cold at this altitude. Try tlacoyos, thick corn cakes with beans, or a bowl of pozole, and look for fruit from the orchards, sold by the roadside in season.
t.central university city campus of the un:
The main campus of the National Autonomous University of Mexico, known as Ciudad Universitaria, is one of the great architectural achievements of the twentieth century. Built between 1949 and 1952 on a field of lava from the ancient eruption of the Xitle volcano, in the south of Mexico City, it brought together dozens of architects, engineers and artists to create a modern campus that would blend international modernism with Mexican traditions. Its most famous building is the Central Library, a tall block covered entirely in a mosaic by Juan O'Gorman, depicting the history of Mexico from pre-Hispanic times to the modern era. UNESCO listed the campus in 2007.

Around the library, the campus has more murals and sculptures, including works by David Alfaro Siqueiros on the Rectorate tower, and the Olympic Stadium, built for the university and later used for the 1968 Olympics, has a relief by Diego Rivera over its main entrance. The campus is also an ecological reserve, with an area of lava rock and native vegetation, the Pedregal, protected within its grounds. The University Cultural Centre has concert halls, theatres, cinemas and a museum of contemporary art.

Riding in Mexico City is intense. The traffic is heavy, chaotic and aggressive, with buses, microbuses, taxis and cars competing for space, and motorcycles weaving between them. The city has traffic restriction programmes that can affect when and where vehicles may circulate, so check the current rules for your plates. The altitude, around two thousand two hundred metres, affects both rider and machine. For better riding, head south out of the city to the forests of Ajusco or toward Cuernavaca, with winding roads through pine forests.

The campus area has fuel, food and services all around. Coyoacán, nearby, is a charming colonial neighbourhood with cobbled streets, plazas and the house of Frida Kahlo, now a museum, the Blue House. Try tacos al pastor, pork cooked on a vertical spit with pineapple, or a plate of chilaquiles for breakfast. The markets of Coyoacán are full of food stalls, where you can eat tostadas, quesadillas and fresh fruit.
t.mehadia praetorium zidina@44.9,22.4:
The Cerna valley in south-western Romania has been a corridor for armies and travellers since antiquity. Between the Banat mountains and the Mehedinți plateau, the valley carried the Roman road from the Danube crossing at Drobeta northwards toward Tibiscum and the heart of Dacia. At Mehadia, the Romans built a fort known as Ad Mediam, and the remains called Praetorium or Zidină, meaning ruined walls, mark the site. The stone foundations are visible in places, and the site is one of the components of the Roman frontier in Dacia proposed for World Heritage status.

Eight kilometres away, Băile Herculane is one of the oldest spa towns in Europe. The Romans dedicated its hot springs to Hercules, and in the nineteenth century the Habsburgs turned it into a fashionable resort with grand hotels, baths and promenades. Many of those buildings are now crumbling, which gives the town a haunting atmosphere, but restoration efforts are underway. The spa still functions, and you can bathe in the thermal waters.

The Domogled–Valea Cernei national park surrounds the upper valley, with limestone cliffs, beech and black pine forests, and a rich population of butterflies, snakes and birds of prey. The road up the Cerna valley from Herculane is narrow and winding, with tunnels and rock walls, and becomes rougher as it climbs toward the source of the river. South of Mehadia, the main road leads to Orșova and the Danube gorges at the Iron Gates, one of the most spectacular river landscapes in Europe.

The DN6 through the valley is a main road, with trucks and fast traffic, so take care. Băile Herculane has fuel, restaurants and accommodation, and Orșova, on the Danube, is another good base. Bring a swimsuit if you want to try the open-air thermal pools along the river. Spring and autumn are the best times, when the forests are fresh or golden and the summer crowds have gone.
The gods chose well. Mount Olympus rises almost straight out of the Aegean, from sea level near Litochoro to 2,918 metres at Mytikas, its highest summit, in barely twenty kilometres, so that from the coast road it looks less like a mountain than a wall of grey rock and dark forest with clouds snagged on top. The ancient Greeks put their twelve Olympians up there, and on a stormy afternoon with thunder rolling around the peaks you can see why.

At the foot of the mountain lies Dion, the sacred city of the Macedonians, where Philip II and Alexander the Great made sacrifices before their campaigns. The archaeological park is a lovely, half-wild place, with the ruins of sanctuaries to Zeus, Demeter and Isis lying among springs, reeds and frogs, and a good museum in the modern village. Olympus itself became Greece's first national park in 1938, protecting a range of habitats from Mediterranean scrub through beech and black pine up to bare alpine slopes, home to chamois and a rich variety of flowers, many found nowhere else.

For riders, the classic route is the road from Litochoro up to Prionia, about eighteen kilometres of climbing through pine forest with hairpins and occasional views down to the sea. It ends at around 1,100 metres, at the trailhead for the summit, where a small taverna serves hikers by a waterfall. The surface is generally decent but can be broken in places, with gravel and fallen rocks after storms, and goats on the road are normal. Summer brings heat and haze at sea level and cool air in the forest; spring and autumn are better, and the upper road can be closed by snow in winter. The Enipeas gorge below the road is a fine walk.

Litochoro, six kilometres away, is the base town, with fuel, supermarkets and many tavernas, and it has the cheerful bustle of a place full of hikers and climbers. Dion and the coastal villages have basics too. Eat grilled meat and local greens, drink a little tsipouro in the evening, and watch the last light catch the summits from the square. In the morning the mountain is often clear before clouds build, so start early if you want to see the peaks.
t.afrimesti urluieni@44.5,24.8:
Flat. That is the first impression of this part of southern Romania, in Argeș county, where the land stretches away towards the Danube in wide fields of maize and sunflowers, broken only by lines of trees and small villages. But across this plain, in the second century AD, the Romans built a frontier: the Limes Transalutanus, a line of earthworks and forts running north to south east of the Olt river, protecting the province of Dacia. At Urluieni, near the village of Afrimești, stood one of its forts.

The Limes Transalutanus was an earthen rampart with a ditch, about 235 kilometres long, with forts at intervals. The fort at Urluieni had stone walls, and excavations have found buildings, baths and finds that tell of the soldiers who lived here. Today there is little to see above ground; the site is a field with faint traces of the walls. But standing here, it is fascinating to think of the Roman frontier crossing this empty plain, so far from Rome.

The riding in this part of Romania is straightforward: long straight roads across the plain, with few bends and wide views. Traffic is light, but surfaces vary and potholes are common on minor roads. Horse carts and agricultural vehicles share the roads, and villages often have dogs that chase motorcycles. Summer is hot and dry, often above thirty-five degrees, so start early and carry water. In late summer, the sunflower fields are in bloom, turning the landscape yellow. Winters are cold, with wind sweeping across the plain.

Corbu and Hârsești are small villages with basic services, and Bârla, seven kilometres away, is a larger village with fuel. Pitești, the county capital, is further north and has all services. Romanian village food is simple and hearty: soups, grilled meat and mămăligă. If you are interested in the Roman frontier, combine this visit with others along the Limes, or ride north to the Olt valley and the mountains, where the landscape changes completely and the riding gets far more interesting.
t.cheile nerei beusnita@44.9,21.8:
The water at Ochiul Beiului, the Bey's Eye, is such an intense turquoise that it looks dyed, and the legend says it formed from the tears of a Turkish nobleman mourning a lost love. It is one of the jewels of the Cheile Nerei-Beușnița National Park, in the mountains of Banat in south-western Romania, where the Nera river has cut a deep gorge through limestone over about twenty kilometres. The park's ancient beech forests are part of the UNESCO listing of primeval beech forests of the Carpathians and other regions of Europe, and the waterfalls, caves and karst springs make it one of the most beautiful corners of the country.

The Beușnița waterfall, a series of mossy cascades over travertine terraces, is a short walk from Ochiul Beiului, and the trail through the Nera gorge itself, with its tunnels cut into the rock, is a classic hike. The forests are home to brown bears, wolves, lynx and many species of bats, and the rock faces support rare plants found nowhere else.

The roads around the park are narrow, winding and sometimes rough, with gravel sections and potholes, but they lead through beautiful villages and forests with almost no traffic. Sasca Montană, a small old mining village, is one of the main gateways, along with Șopotu Nou. To the north, the road through Anina and Oravița climbs through the mountains with tight curves and great views, and the Oravița to Anina mountain railway, one of the oldest in Romania, winds through tunnels and viaducts nearby.

Services are limited in the villages, so fill up in Oravița, about seventeen kilometres away, a small town with fuel, shops and a famous little theatre built in 1817, the oldest in Romania. Food in Banat has Hungarian, Serbian and Austrian influences: goulash, grilled meats, pastries and strong local fruit brandies. Guesthouses in the villages often serve home-cooked meals with produce from their own gardens.

May and late September are ideal for the walk into the gorge. Summer weekends can bring crowds to Ochiul Beiului. Leave the bike at the end of the road, walk into the gorge and listen to the river echoing between the limestone walls, among trees that have been growing here for centuries.
t.temple and former convent of saint micha:
Behind a crenellated wall in the middle of Huejotzingo lies one of the earliest Christian buildings in the Americas: the Franciscan convent of San Miguel Arcángel, built in the decades after the Spanish conquest on the lower slopes of the volcanoes west of Puebla. The friars arrived here within a few years of the fall of Tenochtitlan, and the church, convent and walled atrium they raised are a textbook example of how the missionaries worked, with great open courtyards where crowds of indigenous converts could gather for teaching and mass. Huejotzingo is part of the UNESCO site of the Earliest Sixteenth-Century Monasteries on the Slopes of Popocatépetl, listed in 1994.

What makes the place special are the details. In each corner of the atrium stands a small chapel, a capilla posa, carved with angels, Franciscan cords and other symbols, among the finest of their kind in Mexico. The church facade mixes late Gothic, Renaissance and native craftsmanship, and inside the convent the walls still carry faded frescoes painted by indigenous artists under the friars' direction, in tones of black, grey and ochre. The cloister is quiet and cool, a relief after the bright square outside.

The town has a lively identity of its own. It is famous for its cider, made from the apples of the surrounding orchards and sold in shops around the plaza, and for its Carnival, when hundreds of men in elaborate costumes and masks re-enact historical battles with muskets that fill the streets with smoke and noise. If you are here in the days before Lent, expect crowds and closed roads.

On a clear morning, the view west is dominated by two volcanoes: Popocatépetl, active and often smoking, and Iztaccíhuatl, the sleeping woman, with snow on her long ridge. A road climbs from the area towards the Paso de Cortés, the high saddle between them, where Cortés is said to have first seen the Valley of Mexico. Access depends on the volcano's current alert level, so check before heading up. The road is steep, with hairpins, thin air and rough surfaces near the top.

Huejotzingo has fuel, shops and plenty of food: try mole poblano or a plate of chalupas. Puebla city is half an hour away. Avoid riding after dark, and watch for topes everywhere.
t.izbasesti valea alba@44.6,24.8:
Between Pitești and Slatina, in the south of Romania, the land falls away from the Carpathian foothills towards the great Danube plain in a series of long, low ridges cut by streams. It is farming country, with fields of maize and sunflowers, orchards, vineyards and small villages strung along the valleys. Izbășești and the valley called Valea Albă, the White Valley, lie in this landscape near the small town of Stolnici, and the site recorded here is one of the many archaeological traces in the area, though there is probably little to see on the ground.

The region has a deep history. In the hills to the west, near the Olt river, lie the remains of Buridava, a Dacian settlement and later a Roman camp, and the Olt valley itself was a major route for the Roman armies crossing the Carpathians into Dacia. The rides passing through here link several of these sites, and the earthwork redoubts and fortifications scattered across the landscape tell of centuries of conflict, from the Romans to the Ottomans.

What you will notice as a rider is the rural life: horse-drawn carts, storks nesting on telegraph poles, old women sitting on benches outside their gates, and roadside stalls selling watermelons, honey and plum brandy in summer and autumn. The villages are a mix of old and new, with traditional houses alongside modern ones built with money earned abroad.

The riding is easy and pleasant. The roads are mostly flat or gently rolling, with long straights and occasional bends as they cross the ridges. Surfaces vary from good to poor, with potholes on minor roads. Traffic is light, but watch for slow tractors, carts and dogs, which often chase motorcycles. In summer, the heat on the plain can be intense, and there is little shade.

Stolnici is a small town with basic services; for reliable fuel, supermarkets and restaurants, Pitești or Slatina are better bets. Pitești is also close to the Ștefănești vineyards and to the Argeș valley, which leads north into the mountains and to the Transfăgărășan, one of the most famous roads in the world. If you have time, the ride north from here to the Carpathians is well worth it. Spring and autumn are the best seasons; winters are cold, with snow and fog on the plain.
Let us be honest from the start: you will not ride a motorcycle on Ototojima. This small, uninhabited island lies in the Ogasawara archipelago, about a thousand kilometres south of Tokyo in the western Pacific, and it has no roads, no people and strict rules about who can land. What it does have is a remarkable natural world. The Ogasawara Islands, also known as the Bonin Islands, have never been connected to a continent, and their plants and animals evolved in isolation, producing many species found nowhere else. The archipelago was listed by UNESCO in 2011, and Ototojima is one of its most precious parts.

The island is home to rare endemic land snails, dragonflies and plants, and its streams are among the few places where certain freshwater species survive. Introduced animals such as goats and rats have caused great damage across the islands, and much effort has gone into removing them and protecting the native species. Visitors to Ototojima must be accompanied by licensed guides and follow strict procedures, including cleaning shoes and equipment to avoid bringing in seeds or pests.

Getting to the Ogasawaras is an adventure in itself. There is no airport, and the only regular connection is a ferry from Tokyo, which takes around a day each way and runs roughly once a week. The voyage across the open Pacific is long, but the arrival at Chichijima, the main island, with its turquoise bays and green hills, is unforgettable. From there, boat tours visit the surrounding islands, including Ototojima, and the waters are famous for dolphins, whales and sea turtles.

On Chichijima, you can rent scooters to explore the island's small network of roads, which wind over the hills between beaches and viewpoints. It is a gentle, delightful way to get around, with little traffic and wonderful views of the sea. The island has shops, restaurants and accommodation, but everything is limited, and prices reflect the distance from the mainland.

The climate is subtropical, warm all year, with typhoons possible in summer and autumn. The best time for whale watching is in winter and spring. Plan carefully, book ahead, and be prepared for the ferry schedule to dictate your stay. It is a long way to go, but there are few places like it on earth.
t.temple and former convent of saint john:
Tetela del Volcán lives in the shadow of Popocatépetl. The town sits at about two thousand metres on the southern slope of the volcano in the state of Morelos, and the snow-capped cone, often trailing a plume of steam and ash, looms over everything. In the middle of town stands the sixteenth-century church and former convent of San Juan Bautista, founded by Dominican friars in the decades after the Spanish conquest. Its cloister has some remarkable murals, painted in muted reds and blacks, showing saints and friars of the order. It is one of the fourteen monasteries on the slopes of Popocatépetl that were added to the World Heritage list in 1994 as a group.

The early friars built these convents as centres for evangelising the indigenous population, and they share a distinctive design: large walled atriums for open-air worship, with posa chapels at the corners and open chapels where mass could be said to crowds outside. The architecture combines European models with indigenous craftsmanship, and the murals, often painted by native artists trained by the friars, blend Christian themes with local styles. Tetela's convent is smaller and quieter than some, but its setting is unbeatable.

The roads up to Tetela are a fine ride. From Cuautla or Yecapixtla, the route climbs through a landscape of orchards, avocado groves and pine forest, with sweeping views back over the Morelos valleys and up to the volcano. The road has plenty of curves and steady gradients, and the air cools noticeably as you climb. Surfaces can vary, with potholes and topes, the Mexican speed bumps, which appear without warning in every village. Popocatépetl is an active volcano, and authorities sometimes restrict access to areas closer to the crater, so keep an eye on the local news and on the volcano's alert level.

Tetela is a town of around ten thousand people with basic services, including fuel, small shops and food stalls. The local markets sell fruit from the orchards, especially peaches and avocados, and you can find tacos, tamales and atole. Leave the bike by the plaza, walk through the atrium into the cloister, and look at the murals in the quiet. Then step outside and look up at the volcano. On a clear morning, it is a sight that makes you forget the road for a moment.
t.historic centres of berat and gjirokastr:
Gjirokastër is built of stone, and it means that literally. The old houses climbing the slopes below the castle are made of grey limestone, roofed with heavy slabs of the same stone, and tall and narrow like small fortresses, with the lower floors used for storage and cisterns and the living quarters above. The town grew under Ottoman rule, and its architecture, preserved as a museum town in the communist era, earned it a place on the UNESCO list in 2005, with Berat added in 2008. The castle, one of the largest in the Balkans, holds a collection of artillery, a captured American aircraft from the Cold War, and a prison with a grim history.

Two famous names came from here. Enver Hoxha, the dictator who ruled Albania from the end of the Second World War until his death in 1985, was born in the town, and so was Ismail Kadare, the country's greatest writer, whose novel Chronicle in Stone tells of a childhood in Gjirokastër during the war. Under Hoxha, Albania became one of the most isolated countries on earth, and the hills around the town are still dotted with concrete bunkers. A Cold War tunnel built beneath the town can now be visited.

The Drino valley, below the town, is a broad green plain flanked by mountains, and the main road through it, part of the route from the Greek border at Kakavia toward Tepelenë and Vlorë, is fairly fast and in decent condition. The road over the hills toward Sarandë and the coast is better for riders, with curves, climbs and views back over the valley. Inside the old town, the streets are steep and paved with slippery cobbles, often polished smooth, and some are barely wide enough for a car. Take care, especially when wet, and consider parking below the bazaar and walking up.

Gjirokastër has fuel stations along the main road in the new town, and plenty of cafés, guesthouses and restaurants in the old quarter. The local speciality is qifqi, rice balls with herbs and egg, fried in a special pan; you will also find grilled lamb and the excellent local cheese. Walk up through the old bazaar to the castle in the late afternoon, then come back down as the lights come on in the stone houses. It is one of the most atmospheric towns in the Balkans.
t.pojejena sitarnita@44.8,21.6:
The Danube here is wide and slow, and across the water you look straight into Serbia. Pojejena is a village on the Romanian bank in the Danube gorge region known as the Clisura Dunării, and nearby Şitarniţa is the site of a Roman fort, one of the stations that guarded the river frontier. It is part of the Frontiers of the Roman Empire listing in Romania, inscribed in 2024. The Danube was the backbone of Rome's northern defences for centuries, and forts like this one lined its banks.

Just downstream the river enters the most spectacular stretch of its entire course. The Iron Gates gorges squeeze the Danube between steep cliffs, and the DN57 road on the Romanian side follows the river all the way to Orşova, with constant views of the water and the mountains. Along the way you pass the Babakai rock in the middle of the river, then the huge face of the Dacian king Decebalus carved into a cliff near Dubova in modern times, and, on the Serbian side, the Tabula Traiana, a Roman inscription commemorating Trajan's road along the gorge.

The riding on the DN57 is glorious, with curves, short tunnels and changing views, though the surface varies and traffic can be heavy in summer. Speed limits in villages are enforced, and there are often police checks. Away from the river, roads climb into the Banat mountains, where Czech villages founded by settlers in the nineteenth century, such as Sfânta Elena, keep their language and traditions.

North of Pojejena, the Nera gorge and the Beuşniţa national park offer forests, waterfalls and the turquoise lake known as Ochiul Beiului. The roads there are narrower and partly unpaved, and some sections require walking. The scenery is superb, especially in spring and autumn.

Moldova Nouă, nine kilometres away, is the place for fuel and a meal. The Danube region is famous for fish, and you can find fish soup and grilled fish in many places along the river. Summer is hot, and the river offers a chance to cool off, though currents can be strong. A late afternoon ride along the gorge, with the sun lighting up the cliffs, is unforgettable.
t.temple and former convent of the immacul:
Zacualpan de Amilpas is a small town on the lower slopes of Popocatépetl in the state of Morelos, and its centre is dominated by a sixteenth-century convent built by Augustinian friars in the first decades after the Spanish conquest. The church and former convent of the Immaculate Conception belong to the group of early monasteries on the slopes of Popocatépetl that UNESCO listed in 1994, a chain of fortified religious houses that served as the base for the evangelisation of central Mexico.

These early convents follow a pattern you begin to recognise. A large walled atrium in front of the church, where crowds of newly converted indigenous people gathered for mass in the open air; small chapels at its corners, known as posas, used in processions; an open chapel for outdoor services; and a cloister for the friars, often painted with murals. At Zacualpan, the cloister walls still carry painted decoration, and the scale of the atrium, set against the volcano behind, says a great deal about the ambitions of the friars and the labour of those who built for them.

The town has another reputation. Its Sunday market is known for keeping alive the old practice of trueque, barter, with people from the surrounding villages exchanging produce, pottery and goods without money, alongside ordinary trading. Arrive in the morning to see it at its liveliest.

The riding here is lovely. The roads that link Cuautla, Zacualpan, Temoac and the villages higher up the volcano climb steadily through fields of maize, sorghum and orchards, with Popocatépetl filling the horizon, often with a plume of steam or ash drifting from its crater. The road surfaces vary and speed bumps are everywhere, but traffic is light and the curves get better the higher you go. Popocatépetl is an active volcano, and the authorities sometimes restrict access to areas around it and publish alert levels, so check the current situation before heading up.

Temoac, a couple of kilometres away, has fuel, and Cuautla, the regional centre to the west, has everything a rider needs. In the town itself you will find small eateries and market stalls; a plate of cecina, the salted thin beef of Morelos, with fresh cream, cheese and tortillas, is a fine reason to stop. Go in the dry season, from November to May, when the volcano is most often clearly visible against the deep blue sky.
t.mares la stadion@44.8,24.8:
Pitești is the kind of city most riders pass through on the way somewhere else, and the somewhere else is usually the Transfăgărășan. The famous road over the Făgăraș mountains begins north of here, beyond Curtea de Argeș, and the hills of Argeș county around Albota and Mareș, just south-west of Pitești, are where many people start the day. The coordinates fall in this rolling farmland of orchards, vineyards and maize fields, with villages along the roads and the Carpathians a hazy blue line on the northern horizon.

The landscape has a Roman layer that few people notice. In the early third century, the Romans built a frontier line known as the Limes Transalutanus, an earth rampart with a ditch and a chain of forts running for some two hundred and thirty kilometres from the Danube north toward the mountains, east of the river Olt. Its course passed through this part of Argeș, and sites around here belong to the ensemble of Roman frontier remains in Romania. Most of it is now just a low ridge in the fields, easy to miss, but it was once the eastern edge of the empire's hold on this region.

The region has more recent fame, too. Mioveni, just east of Pitești, is home to the Dacia car factory, which has built cars here since the late 1960s and remains one of the country's largest employers. Pitești itself has a strong wine tradition: the Ștefănești vineyards nearby produce well-known wines. Curtea de Argeș, to the north, was one of the early capitals of Wallachia, and its monastery, with its intricate carved facade, is one of Romania's most beautiful churches.

From here, the Transfăgărășan, the DN7C, climbs past the Poienari fortress, the real castle of Vlad the Impaler, perched on a cliff above the Argeș gorge, and up to Lake Bâlea at over two thousand metres, through a series of hairpins and tunnels. It is usually open only from early July to the end of October, depending on snow, and is busy on summer weekends, so go early on a weekday for the best experience.

Bradu, around six kilometres away, and Pitești have plenty of fuel stations, shops and restaurants. Before heading north, eat a hearty meal of mici, grilled minced-meat rolls, with mustard and bread, washed down with a cold drink, and fill the tank: the mountain sections of the route have few fuel stations.
t.pirin national park@41.7,23.4:
Vihren, at 2,914 metres the highest peak of the Pirin mountains and the third highest in the Balkans, rises above the town of Bansko in south-western Bulgaria in a sharp, pale pyramid of marble. The Pirin National Park protects the high country around it, a landscape of granite and marble peaks, glacial cirques, more than a hundred lakes and ancient forests of pine and fir, and it was listed by UNESCO in 1983. The coordinates fall in the heart of the park, among the peaks and valleys above Bansko.

The park is a paradise for hikers, with trails leading to the high lakes and summits, and huts offering simple accommodation. The forests are home to bears, wolves, chamois and many birds, and the flora includes rare and endemic plants such as the edelweiss and the Pirin poppy. Near the Vihren hut, the Baikushev pine, a Bosnian pine said to be over 1,300 years old, is one of the oldest trees in Bulgaria.

For riders, the road from Bansko up to the Vihren hut is a great climb: a narrow road winding through the forest into the high mountains, steep in places, with views of the peaks as you emerge from the trees. The surface has been patchy over the years, so take it steadily. Parking at the top allows you to walk to the lakes or up toward Vihren. The road is closed in winter, when snow covers the mountains and Bansko becomes a busy ski resort.

Down in the valley, the Razlog basin is surrounded by the Pirin, Rila and Rhodope mountains, and the roads through it offer superb riding: south along the Mesta river toward Gotse Delchev, east over the passes into the Rhodopes, or west through the Kresna gorge, where the Struma river cuts between the Pirin and the Maleshevo mountains. Watch for livestock, potholes and occasional erratic drivers.

Bansko, a town of over nine thousand people about twelve kilometres away, has fuel, shops, restaurants and plenty of accommodation. The old town, with its stone houses and cobbled streets, has kept its character despite the growth of the ski resort, and its mehanas, traditional taverns, serve hearty food: try kapama, a slow-cooked dish of meats, sauerkraut and rice baked in a clay pot, a Bansko speciality, with a glass of local red wine from Melnik, to the south. The best time to visit is from late June to September, when the high roads and trails are open.
t.central balkan boatin reserve@42.8,24.3:
The Balkan range, the Stara Planina, runs across the middle of Bulgaria from the Serbian border to the Black Sea, and its central section is the wildest, highest and most heavily forested part. The Central Balkan National Park protects this area, and within it, the Boatin Reserve guards a stretch of ancient beech forest on the northern slopes, one of the components of the Ancient and Primeval Beech Forests of the Carpathians and Other Regions of Europe, a UNESCO site that stretches across many countries. The coordinates fall in the forests above the town of Teteven and the villages of the Vit river valley.

The beech forests here are old and undisturbed, with giant trees, fallen trunks rotting slowly on the forest floor, and a rich community of fungi, insects and birds. Higher up, the forest gives way to alpine meadows and rocky peaks, with Botev, at 2,376 metres the highest point of the Balkan range, a little to the east. Bears, wolves, chamois and red deer live in the park, and the cliffs are home to birds of prey.

For riders, the central Balkan range offers some of the best roads in Bulgaria. The Troyan pass, the Beklemeto road, climbs from Troyan over the range to Karnare and the Rose Valley, with tight bends, good views and a monument at the top. To the east, the Shipka pass, scene of fierce fighting in the Russo-Turkish war of 1877–78, crosses the range with a winding road and a huge monument on a peak. Closer to Teteven, the road through the Vit valley and over the passes to the south is quieter and narrower, with forest and steep climbs. Weather can change quickly in the mountains, with fog, rain and cold even in summer.

Teteven is an old town in the valley of the Vit, surrounded by forested mountains, with a long history of crafts and trade. Nearby, the Troyan monastery, the third largest in Bulgaria, is famous for its frescoes and the plum brandy made there. Etropole and its monastery are also worth a detour.

Teteven, a town of over ten thousand people about thirteen kilometres away, has fuel, shops and restaurants; Pirdop and Anton are smaller. Try a plate of grilled meats with shopska salad, made with tomatoes, cucumbers, peppers and white cheese, and a glass of rakia, the fruit brandy of the Balkans. The best time to ride is from late spring to early autumn, when the passes are clear and the forests are green.
t.former convent of san francisco in tepej:
Tepeji del Río is a busy town in the state of Hidalgo, on the old road north from Mexico City, and at its heart stands a sixteenth-century Franciscan convent, one of the many fortress-like monasteries built by the friars in the first decades after the Spanish conquest to evangelise the indigenous population. The church has a sober façade, a large open atrium where crowds of converts once gathered for mass, and a cloister with traces of mural paintings. The convent stands on the Camino Real de Tierra Adentro, and it is part of the UNESCO listing of that route. Like many of these early convents, it combines European Gothic and Renaissance forms with the work of indigenous craftsmen, whose hand can be seen in the carvings and paintings.

The town has grown into an industrial centre, with factories along the highway, and the historic core is small. But a short ride north lies one of the most important archaeological sites in Mexico. Tula was the capital of the Toltecs, who dominated central Mexico between the tenth and twelfth centuries, and its most famous monuments are the Atlantes, four giant stone warriors, each several metres tall, standing on top of a pyramid. They once supported the roof of a temple, and they gaze out over the valley with a stern, mysterious expression. The Toltecs were remembered by the later Aztecs as a people of great artistic and military achievement, and their legends of the god Quetzalcoatl spread across Mesoamerica.

The riding is not the main attraction here. The highway from Mexico City to Querétaro, which passes Tepeji, is one of the busiest in the country, heavily used by trucks, and it can be dangerous. The smaller roads to Tula and the surrounding towns are better, but traffic is still heavy, and the landscape is a mix of farmland, industrial zones and dry hills. Further north, the Valle del Mezquital, home to the Otomí people, has thermal springs and canyons.

Tepeji has fuel, mechanics, shops and restaurants. Try barbacoa, lamb slow-cooked in an underground pit wrapped in maguey leaves, a speciality of Hidalgo, usually eaten on weekend mornings. Check the current travel advice, ride in daylight, and use toll roads where possible.
t.slaveni la cetate auxiliary fort@44.1,24:
Slăveni is farm country, and the fort here is the sort of ruin you have to meet halfway. "La Cetate" simply means "at the fortress", the name locals gave to a rise in the fields long before anyone excavated it, and what remains of the Roman auxiliary fort is mostly a matter of banks, ditches and the shape of the ground rather than standing walls. If you expect a Hadrian's Wall photograph you will be disappointed; if you like imagining a few hundred soldiers watching a very flat horizon, you will be fine.

The setting explains the fort. This is the Oltenian plain in the south of Romania, a few dozen kilometres north of the Danube, where the Roman province of Dacia needed garrisons along its roads and river lines. Corabia, on the Danube, was the Roman town of Sucidava, and the ride's other stops hang off that old military geography. Soldiers moved up through country like this from the river toward the Olt, and the forts were placed a day's march apart, so the logic of the route is still readable on a map even when the ground is quiet.

For a rider, the interest is the approach rather than the destination. The local roads are straight and agricultural, lined with maize, sunflowers and wheat depending on the month, with the occasional horse cart and a lot of dogs that have opinions about motorcycles. Surfaces vary from decent asphalt to patched and potholed, and the verges can carry mud or straw after harvest, so keep your speed honest at the edges of villages. Summer is hot and dusty with little shade; late spring and September are kinder, and the light on the stubble fields in the evening is worth the detour.

Practicalities are simple. Slăveni and Gostavățu are small villages with a shop or two, but for fuel and a proper meal head for Drăgănești-Olt, about eleven kilometres away, which is large enough to have pumps and somewhere to sit down. Carry water in the warm months, because between the villages there is nothing at all. Take ten minutes to walk the rise, read the sign if there is one, and then get on with the day. Nobody comes here for the corners, but you will remember it as the place where the map of an empire became suddenly physical under your boots.
t.resca romula cetate@44.2,24.4:
Romula was once among the more important towns in Roman Dacia, and the ground at Reșca, in Olt county, is where it stood. The settlement grew near the river Olt on the road between the Danube frontier and the interior, and it rose to the rank of a colony in the later empire; the later name, Romula Malvensis, ties it to the province of Dacia Malvensis that was formed in the third century. Today you see fields, a few low mounds, and the faint outline of an old fortification, with finds from the site kept in nearby museums rather than at the roadside.

That makes the visit more about imagination than spectacle, which suits some riders and frustrates others. What the place does give you is context: you can see why a city grew here, on the flat open ground near a river crossing and a major road, and you can understand how a province built on military roads still had to feed, house and entertain its people. Stone from the city was reused over centuries by villagers building farms, which is one reason so little stands above ground.

The riding around Reșca is in the same spirit, flat and straightforward, with long straights between villages and the occasional bend around a farmyard. The surfaces vary widely, so ride the last kilometres with respect for potholes and tractor mud, and watch for dogs and carts. Summer is hot with little shade, and the best time is spring, when the fields are green, or early autumn, when the light turns amber over the stubble. The wind off the plain can be strong enough to push a lightly loaded bike sideways, which is worth knowing before you set off.

For practicalities, Fărcașele, about four kilometres away, is the nearest settlement of any size, and Dobrosloveni is also close, with its own shops and a small-town character; both are big enough to have a pump or a shop for a drink and a snack. If you need a wider choice, the bigger towns along the Olt valley have supermarkets and restaurants. Bring water in July and August, because a Roman ruin in a field has no café. Spend half an hour walking the ground and reading what you can, and let the quiet do the rest.
t.pchelino convent complex@42.1,23.3:
The mountains of southwestern Bulgaria are among the wildest in the Balkans, and the area between Rila and Pirin holds a string of small monasteries tucked into forested valleys. During centuries of Ottoman rule these monasteries kept the Bulgarian language, the Orthodox faith and the art of icon painting alive, and the great Rila Monastery, founded in the tenth century around the hermitage of Saint Ivan of Rila, became the national symbol. The Pchelino complex belongs to that landscape, and I will not claim more detail than the setting supports: a quiet religious site in forest and hill country, away from the busy roads.

The setting is lovely. To the north rise the granite peaks of the Rila range, the highest in the Balkans, with Musala above 2,900 metres, and to the east the Pirin, with limestone ridges and glacial lakes. Rivers such as the Struma and the Rilska run through deep valleys, and beech and pine forests cover the slopes. Sapareva Banya, a small spa town not far away, has a geyser of very hot water, reputedly the hottest in continental Europe, and the region is full of mineral springs.

Riding in the area is a pleasure. The roads climb through forest in sweeping bends, with views over valleys and ranges, and surfaces range from good to pitted, depending on the winter. Traffic is light apart from weekends and pilgrim days, when the monasteries are busy. Be ready for sudden weather changes, and watch for loose gravel on corners and animals on the road, especially at dusk. May to June, when wildflowers cover the meadows, and September to October, with golden beech forests, are the best seasons.

Monasteries expect modest dress and quiet behaviour, so cover shoulders and knees, remove helmets and sunglasses, and ask before photographing inside. Blagoevgrad, about twenty kilometres away, is a university town with several fuel stations, supermarkets and restaurants, and Sapareva Banya and Rila have smaller services. A bowl of bean soup, a plate of grilled meat with shopska salad, and a glass of local rakia complete the Bulgarian picture, though the rakia is best left until you have parked.
t.aqueduct of padre tembleque hydraulic sy:
In the sixteenth century a Franciscan friar called Francisco de Tembleque looked at the dry highlands north-east of Mexico City, where villages had trouble finding clean water, and decided to bring it from springs on the slopes of a volcano forty-five kilometres away. The result, built between 1553 and about 1571 with the labour of local Indigenous communities, is one of the longest aqueduct systems of its age in the Americas, and it still stands on a high arcade of stone arches crossing a valley. The longest arcade runs for nearly a kilometre, and the tallest arch is about forty metres high, a slender, elegant bridge on thin piers, which is why you can see it for miles across the plain.

What makes it special is a mix of European and Mesoamerican engineering, with Roman-style arches built using local techniques, mortar made with the sap of the nopal cactus, and a design that allowed for the earthquakes of the region. It was listed by UNESCO in 2015. The water ran by gravity alone for decades, and the villages of the plain, such as Otumba, depended on it.

The country around is high, windy and open, a plateau at around two and a half thousand metres, with fields of maguey, the agave that is tapped for pulque, a sour, milky drink that is the traditional tipple of the region. Apan, not far away, is the pulque capital, and you can stop for a glass, or for barbacoa, slow-cooked lamb, served on Sundays with consommé and tortillas. Santiago Tepeyahualco and San Felipe Teotitlán, the nearest villages, are small, and have shops and a church, but not much else, so fill the tank in a larger town such as Apan, Tulancingo or Pachuca.

The riding is straightforward, with long, straight highways, rolling hills and wide skies. Local roads are less predictable, with potholes, speed bumps called topes that appear without warning and slow trucks and tractors. The weather is cool at height, even in summer, with afternoon storms from June to September, and cold nights in winter, so bring layers. The dry months, from November to April, bring the clearest views and the best light on the stone, and early morning is the best time to see the arches in a clear, golden glow.
From the street, Luis Barragán's house looks like nothing. A plain facade in Tacubaya, a mixed and busy neighbourhood of Mexico City, with a wooden door and a few windows, gives no hint of the colour behind it. Barragán, the Mexican architect who won the Pritzker Prize in 1980, built the house in 1948 as his own home and studio, and he lived and worked here until his death in 1988. The UNESCO listing of 2004 recognised it as one of the key works of modern architecture, in which light, colour, silence and simple geometry do all the talking.

Inside, walls are painted in strong pink, ochre and yellow, and a window in the double-height living room is filled with a single sheet of glass divided by a cross of wood, so that the garden appears like a painting. A floating staircase of wooden planks climbs to the upper floor with no balustrade. The garden is wild and shaded, and the whole house feels like a hushed retreat from a very loud city. It is intimate, not grand, and you leave wanting to repaint your living room.

Visiting is by guided tour only, and spaces are limited, so booking ahead is essential. Photography inside is restricted, and the tours run on set days and times, so check the current rules before you go. The neighbourhood is near Chapultepec Park, with its castle and museums, and it is rich in places to eat, from market stalls to good restaurants.

Mexico City is a vast, fast and sometimes chaotic place for a bike, but motorcycles are common and drivers expect them. Fuel is everywhere, parking is the problem, so use a paid lot or leave the bike at your hotel and take the metro or a taxi. For a proper ride, leave early on a weekend and head west toward the Desierto de los Leones, a pine forest national park above the city, or take the old road toward Cuernavaca, which climbs through fir woods past La Marquesa. Air quality is better after rain, and the high altitude, about two thousand three hundred metres, takes a little power from engines and a little breath from riders.
t.decani monastery@42.5,20.3:
Visoki Dečani is a monastery that looks as if a Romanesque church from Italy had settled in the Balkan mountains. It lies in the valley of the Bistrica river, in western Kosovo, under the steep wall of the Prokletije or Accursed mountains, and its main church, built between 1327 and 1335 for the Serbian king Stefan Dečanski, is a large block of pink, grey and yellow marble, with carved portals, lions and a rose window, the work of a Franciscan master from the Adriatic coast. Inside it is a different world, with more than a thousand painted scenes covering every inch of wall and ceiling, one of the largest surviving cycles of Byzantine painting in the Balkans. It was listed by UNESCO in 2004, with other medieval monuments of Kosovo.

The monastery is still a working Serbian Orthodox community, with monks who keep bees, make wine and run a small shop selling honey, icons and brandy. It is also protected by international peacekeeping troops, who check visitors at the entrance, so bring your passport, and in some periods you need to register in advance, so check the latest rules before you travel. Dress modestly, cover shoulders and knees, and keep your voice low.

The town of Deçan, or Dečani, has about fifty thousand people in the wider area, and Lloqan is a small village nearby. Fuel and food are easy in Deçan, and Peja, a few kilometres east, is bigger. The riding in this part of Kosovo is excellent, with a road that heads south along the Bistrica toward the mountain wall, wooded valleys, a few tight bends and light traffic. Roads are in decent condition, but surfaces change quickly on mountain stretches, and animals sometimes wander across the road. The trail of the Gash river, in the ride title, leads towards Albania and the high peaks.

Kosovo is small, and its border crossings can be slow, so allow time. Carry insurance documents and check the rules on entering from Serbia, where political tensions can affect crossings. Spring and autumn are best, with snow on the peaks and warm days in the valley. Take a coffee in town, and keep an ear open for the call to prayer mixed with church bells.
t.medieval monuments in kosovo@42.7,20.3:
The Patriarchate of Peć is a cluster of four churches under one red-tinged roof, tucked at the mouth of the Rugova gorge on the edge of the town of Peja in western Kosovo. It was the seat of the Serbian Orthodox archbishops from the thirteenth century, and the heart of the church for centuries, with the frescoed churches built and extended over generations. The effect inside is intimate, with low arches, dim light and walls covered in saints, and the nuns who live there today run a small shop with candles and icons. The place is part of the UNESCO listing of medieval monuments in Kosovo, from 2004, along with Dečani, Gračanica and the church of Our Lady of Ljeviš in Prizren.

Peja, with nearly fifty thousand people, is the town to base yourself in. It has a lively bazaar with Ottoman-era stone buildings, a clock tower, a mosque and a reputation for its beer, brewed locally since the 1930s, and for a relaxed cafe culture that spills onto the pavements. Fuel and services are easy, and hotels range from simple to comfortable.

Behind the town the Rugova gorge cuts into the Prokletije mountains, a road of tunnels and high rock walls, with a river at the bottom and via ferrata routes on the cliffs. It is a good ride, with smooth bends, cool air and light traffic, though rockfall is a hazard and the road narrows in places. Further up, the road continues toward the Montenegrin border and the high pastures, and you should check which crossings are open to foreigners, since rules change. Insurance for the car or bike is needed, and the green card may not be accepted, so buy local cover at the border if required.

Strellc i Epërm, a village of about six thousand in the Istog area, lies to the east, and Dlaboka Reka, from the ride title, is across the border in Albania. The valley is green, with maize fields and orchards, and the mountains rise like a wall in the south. In summer it is hot in town and cool in the gorge, and snow closes the high roads in winter. Come in May or September, and ask permission to enter the Patriarchate, because the monastery has its own rules and a guard at the gate.
t.dlaboka reka@41.8,20.6:
Few borderlands in the Balkans feel as folded and unhurried as the country around Peshkopi, in the Dibra mountains of north-eastern Albania. Across the frontier the same people are Macedonia's Dlaboka Reka, the Deep River, and the double name tells you the story: a Slavic and Albanian valley land cut through by a political line that locals still cross for weddings and markets. The Black Drin runs through the region, the great peaks of the Korab range stand along the border, and Mount Korab itself, at 2,764 metres, is the highest in both Albania and North Macedonia.
