Peshkopi is the capital of Dibra county and the only real town for miles, a compact place of about fifteen thousand people with fuel, banks, cafes and a famous set of sulphur springs on the hillside nearby, where Albanians have taken the waters for generations. If you are crossing from the Macedonian side towards Mavrovo and Rostusa, treat Peshkopi as the last big refill; the villages beyond are small and the petrol stations scarce. Fill the tank when you can, and carry cash in lek or denars, since cards are a gamble in the hamlets.

The riding is the sort you remember. The roads wind along gorges and over ridgelines, with long climbs through beech and oak and open pasture above, and the surface varies from freshly laid asphalt to broken patches where a spring washout has been patched with gravel. Livestock use the road without apology, and a herd of goats can appear around any bend. Corners are generally medium and open, but tighten as the road drops into valleys. Spring brings snowmelt streams over the road, and winter makes the high passes difficult or impossible, so the months from May to October are the sensible window.

Culturally this is a conservative and hospitable part of the world. Wherever you stop, you will probably be offered coffee, or raki, or a plate of byrek. The old churches and mosques stand close together, a reminder that the valley has long been mixed in faith as well as language. Take your time, ask the way, and accept that the route may take longer than the map says.
t.xochimilco federal district xochimilco 1:
Mexico City is built on a lake, or rather it was, and Xochimilco is the part of that old water world that survived. Before the Spanish, the Aztecs and their neighbours built chinampas, narrow artificial islands of mud and reeds held in place by willow trees, and farmed them intensively to feed Tenochtitlan. Canals ran between the plots, and the whole system was a remarkably productive kind of garden. A part of it still works, and it earned a place on UNESCO's World Heritage list in 1987. The name is Nahuatl and means roughly the place of flowers, which suits the nurseries that fill the district.

For most visitors the main attraction is a ride on a trajinera, a long, flat, brightly painted boat poled slowly along the canals, with mariachi bands, taco boats and flower sellers alongside. It is touristy and tremendous fun, particularly on a Sunday when local families pile in with huge picnics. Farther out, the canals are quieter, and on the deeper channels you can find the axolotl, the strange salamander that never grows up and is a symbol of the city. A famous and slightly eerie corner is the Island of the Dolls, where hundreds of weathered dolls hang from trees.

On a motorbike, this is Mexico City at its most demanding and its most rewarding. Traffic can be thick, speed bumps called topes appear without warning, and the ring roads are huge and fast. Motorcycles weave between lanes, and you need to keep your mirrors and your wits about you. The reward is that the south of the city, around Xochimilco and the Cuemanco canoeing track, is full of green and open spaces. Weekend mornings are the best times, before the crowds arrive.

Fuel is everywhere, and the market has superb food, from tamales to esquites, and the garden centres at Madre Selva are a joy even if you have nowhere to put a plant. At 2,240 metres, the city is high enough to make engines run a little lean, and the afternoon rain in summer arrives like clockwork.
t.drobeta turnu severin drobeta@44.6,22.7:
The Danube at Drobeta is a river that has just come out of a gorge and is not yet sure what to do with its freedom. Upstream, it squeezes through the Iron Gates, the great rock gorge between the Carpathians and the Balkans, and the water here has the heavy, slow look of something that has been pent up. Drobeta-Turnu Severin lies just below the dams, a city of about a hundred thousand, and on its riverbank are the stones of a very old story.

In the early second century AD, the Roman emperor Trajan wanted to invade Dacia, the kingdom on the north bank. His engineer, Apollodorus of Damascus, built a bridge of timber on stone piers across the Danube here, over a kilometre long, and for more than a thousand years it was the longest bridge in the world. Only the foundations of its piers can now be seen at low water, and a few ruins on the Romanian bank, but the memory is powerful. The Roman fort and baths of Drobeta stand beside the museum, and the Tabula Traiana, a carved Roman inscription, was moved when the dams were built. Farther west, a huge face of the Dacian king Decebalus has been carved in the rock above the river at Dubova, an astonishing sight from the road.

The road along the Danube gorge, past Orsova and through the Cazane defile, is among the most dramatic in Romania. It twists along the cliff, with the river and the Serbian bank across the water, and tunnels and viaducts add variety. Surfaces vary, traffic can be heavy with trucks, and in summer the roads fill with tourists. Early morning is peaceful and the light is lovely. Stay alert on the blind corners.

Drobeta-Turnu Severin has fuel, hotels and good restaurants, and Simian, just to the south, is a handy little town. Fish from the Danube, grilled or in soup, is a regional speciality, and a dry white wine from Mehedinti is the right companion. Spring and autumn are comfortable, and summer can be hot and still.
t.corabia sucidava celei@43.8,24.5:
At Celei, a few kilometres from Corabia on the Danube, the Romans built a bridge. It is a thing worth pausing over, because the bridge was built in AD 328, in the time of Constantine the Great, and it linked the Roman fortress of Sucidava on the northern bank with the province on the other side. The bridge was nearly two and a half kilometres long, one of the grandest engineering projects of the late empire, and it gave Rome a way to project power across the river long after the rest of the frontier had begun to crumble. A later emperor, Justinian, rebuilt Sucidava in the sixth century, and the fortress was in use for a very long time.

Today, you see low walls, foundations and a few towers on a field beside the river, with a small museum in Corabia that holds the finds. Like many Roman sites on the Danube, it is more evocative than spectacular: you have to bring your imagination, and the wind off the water helps. Sunsets here are wide and slow, and the river is broad, brown and busy with barges. On the opposite bank, in Bulgaria, you can see the low hills and the town of Somovit.

Corabia is a port town of about twenty thousand people, with a long promenade, a grain port and a modest, rather melancholy charm. It has fuel, cafes and a few restaurants, and Orlea, next door, has a market. The roads in the area are straight, flat and sometimes cracked, with potholes after winter, and the traffic is mostly trucks, farm machinery and the occasional horse cart. The best riding is on small roads along the river, where you can stop at a fisherman's shack for fried fish and a cold beer.

The Danube here is a source of life: carp, catfish and the occasional sturgeon, and in spring the floodplain is full of birds. Summers are hot and can be dusty, so the best months for riding are May, June and September.
t.lumi i gashit@42.5,20.1:
Here the borders of Montenegro, Kosovo and Albania meet in the Prokletije, the Accursed Mountains, a rugged range of limestone peaks that rises above two thousand metres and is among the wildest country in the Balkans. The label uses the Albanian name for a stream, Lumi i Gashit, the river of Gashi, and the nearest places on the Montenegrin side are Plav and Gusinje, where Albanians and Bosniaks make up a large share of the population. Plav sits on a glacial lake, a cold, clear body of water ringed by high peaks, with a small mosque, an old Ottoman tower house and a quiet lakeshore promenade.

The mountains here have a reputation for being harsh. The name Prokletije may come from a Slavic word for accursed, or from the Albanian bjeshket e nemuna, the mountains of the damned, and both reflect how difficult the terrain was for travellers. Blood feuds, clan law and the Kanun of Lek Dukagjini shaped life in these mountains for centuries, and traces of that old order remain in the stone towers, the hospitality and the sense of honour. The valleys, however, are green and open, with orchards, meadows and clear streams, and the villages of Vusanje and Grebaje are gateways to some of the best hiking in the Balkans.

The riding is fine, if rough in places. Roads wind along valleys and over passes, with tight bends, patchy asphalt and unmarked drops. The route east towards Pec, in Kosovo, climbs over a high pass, and the border crossing requires proper documents and insurance, so check the requirements beforehand. Snow lingers on the upper slopes until June, and thunderstorms in the afternoon can be fierce. Autumn, with the beech forests turning gold, is the best season.

Plav, eighteen kilometres away, has fuel, shops and cafes, and larger services are in Pec and Decan across the border. Expect coffee, strong and served with a glass of water, and in the villages, fresh bread, cheese and honey. Visitors who show respect and patience are warmly welcomed, and a few words of the local language go a long way.
t.patriarchate of pec monastery@42.7,20.3:
The Serbian Orthodox Church has had its seat at Pec since the thirteenth century, and the Patriarchate stands where the Rugova gorge opens onto the plain, with the walls of the mountains rising straight behind it. Three churches, joined by a shared porch, make up the complex, and inside them the walls are covered in frescoes that range from the thirteenth to the seventeenth centuries. The oldest, the Church of the Holy Apostles, was built under Archbishop Arsenije and has a serene, early painting style, while the later churches added by his successors show the growing wealth and ambition of the medieval Serbian state. UNESCO lists it together with Visoki Decani and other monasteries as the Medieval Monuments in Kosovo.

The setting is easy to enjoy, with a small garden, a stream, and the sound of the nuns who live there going about their work. Visitors can buy candles, icons and jam, and the monastic community welcomes quiet and respectful guests. The monastery lies in a politically sensitive region and is protected by security forces, so you will normally be asked to show your passport at the gate. Dress modestly, with shoulders and knees covered, and ask before taking photographs inside the churches. Check the local situation and opening hours before you travel, as they can vary.

For riders, the real prize is the Rugova canyon, which begins just outside the town and cuts into the mountains in a deep, narrow gorge with sheer limestone walls. The road threads through tunnels and past waterfalls, and climbs eventually toward the Montenegrin border, with views of rock faces and the high peaks beyond. Surfaces vary, and landslides and rockfalls can be a problem after rain or in spring. The Bistrica river runs through Pec, and the little cafes along it are good for coffee in the sun.

Pec, or Peja, is a lively town of nearly fifty thousand people, with fuel stations, bakeries and restaurants. The local beer, Birra Peja, is a good companion to grilled meat and flija, the layered pancake dish of the region. A few kilometres to the south, the monastery of Visoki Decani is the other great sight of the area, with a magnificent stone church. The best seasons are late spring and autumn, when the weather is mild and the crowds thin.
t.boyana church@42.6,23.3:
Boyana is a village on the southern edge of Sofia, tucked against the lower slopes of Mount Vitosha, and it holds a small church that changed the history of European painting, or at least its footnotes. The church is made of three parts built over several centuries, but the middle part, a tiny two-storey chapel, was decorated in 1259 for Sebastokrator Kaloyan, a local ruler, and his wife Desislava, who are painted in the narthex as donors. The frescoes show eighty-nine scenes with more than two hundred and forty human figures, and they are astonishing for their realism. The faces have individual expressions, the saints look like real people, and they predate the Italian Renaissance by generations.

Because of the fragility of the paintings, the number of visitors is limited, and the time you can spend inside is short, with groups admitted for a few minutes at a time. Book ahead if you can, and expect to wait, because the rules are enforced. Photography is not usually allowed inside. The reward is the sense of looking at the medieval Bulgarian world, with its pride and sophistication, painted on a wall the size of a modest room. UNESCO listed the church in 1979.

Getting here is a short ride from the centre of Sofia, on city roads that wind through the suburb of Boyana, past villas and embassies and onward to the mountain. Vitosha rises to 2,290 metres at Cherni Vrah, and the road up to the Aleko ski area is a great climb, with a series of bends through beech and spruce forest, with views across the city. It can be crowded on weekends, with hikers and day-trippers, and in winter, snow and ice make it a task for studded tyres. In summer, the cooler air on the mountain is a relief.

Sofia has fuel stations everywhere, and a very good range of cafes, bakeries and restaurants. Try banitsa, the cheese pastry, and shopska salad, and in autumn, the local wines. Bulgaria requires an electronic vignette for roads outside towns, so buy one for your motorbike before you leave the city. The best seasons are late spring and early autumn, when the weather is warm and the hills are green or golden.
Ivan of Rila was a hermit who, in the tenth century, withdrew into the forests of the Rila mountains to live in a cave and a hollow tree, and the monastery that grew up around his grave became the spiritual heart of Bulgaria. Rila Monastery sits in a valley at about 1,150 metres, surrounded by steep forested slopes, and the Rilska river runs beside it. The buildings you see today date mostly from the nineteenth century, after a great fire in 1833 destroyed the older ones, but within the courtyard stands a medieval tower, Hrelyo's Tower, from 1335, and the main church is covered in vivid murals.

The monastery was a centre of Bulgarian language and culture during the long centuries of Ottoman rule, when the monks kept the written language alive, copied manuscripts and taught children to read. This is why Bulgarians treat it with such reverence. The courtyard, with its striped arcades and wooden galleries, is a beautiful sight, and the church's exterior frescoes depict devils, saints and the Last Judgement in vigorous detail. Pilgrims light candles and kiss icons, and visitors should dress modestly. Leave the bike in the car park and walk in.

The ride up from the Struma valley is the highlight. The road runs through gorges and forests, with plenty of bends and an assortment of rough patches, and it climbs steadily to the monastery. Further on, the high Rila mountains offer the glacial lakes and the peak of Musala, at 2,925 metres the highest in the Balkans. Near Sapareva Banya, a spa town on the way, a geyser of steaming water, the hottest in Europe, shoots from the ground. In summer, the monastery car park fills with coaches, and early morning is the best time to come.

Fuel can be bought at Rila village, a few kilometres away, and Dupnitsa, a bigger town to the north, has everything. Near the monastery, bakers sell mekitsi, fried dough with honey or jam, and the fresh trout from the river is excellent. Roads are open year-round, though snow can close the higher parts in winter, so check conditions. Late spring and September are quieter, and the autumn colours on the slopes are glorious.
t.historic centre of the city of mexico@19:
Under the paving of the Zocalo there is a lake bed, and under that, the island city of Tenochtitlan. The Aztecs founded it in the fourteenth century on a swampy island in Lake Texcoco, linked it to the shore with causeways and filled the lake with floating gardens, and when Hernan Cortes arrived in 1519 he found a city larger and cleaner than any in Spain. After the conquest in 1521 the Spaniards drained the lake, built their cathedral on the ruins and began a new capital, and the result is the layered centre we see today. The Metropolitan Cathedral, a huge, ponderous baroque pile that took nearly three centuries to finish, leans noticeably, because the ground beneath it is soft clay, and engineers have spent decades trying to stop it sinking unevenly.

The great square itself, one of the largest in the world, is flanked by the National Palace, where Diego Rivera's murals sweep across the stairwell with a rich account of Mexican history, and by the offices of the old city. Just behind the cathedral, the excavated foundations of the Templo Mayor, the main temple of the Aztecs, lie exposed, a rough grey stack of stone with serpent heads. The area is a World Heritage site along with Xochimilco, together recording how the capital grew from a lake city into a colonial centre.

For a rider, the centre of Mexico City is a stress test, and the honest answer is not to take the bike in. Traffic is dense, the roads are cobbled in places, potholes and speed bumps appear without warning, and the city sits at 2,240 metres, so engines run thin and cars crawl. There are restrictions on older vehicles on certain days under a programme called Hoy No Circula, and parking in the centre is scarce. Leave the bike somewhere secure on the edge, or use the metro, which is cheap, fast and busy.

Outside the city, the ride changes completely. The roads east to Puebla pass between the volcanoes Popocatepetl and Iztaccihuatl, and the climb to Paso de Cortes, at about 3,600 metres, is a classic, cold and misty. Fuel is easy everywhere in the metropolis. Eat tacos al pastor, tamales and a bowl of pozole, and take your time. In the early morning, before the crowds, the Zocalo has a hushed scale that is worth seeing.
t.historic centre of mexico city and xochi:
In February 1978, electricity workers digging a trench near the Zocalo struck a huge carved stone disc, and the city found out what lay under its feet. The stone showed the dismembered goddess Coyolxauhqui, and it marked the base of the Templo Mayor, the double temple at the heart of Tenochtitlan. That accident changed Mexico City's idea of itself, and the colonial streets around the cathedral have since been opened up to reveal the Aztec capital below. The historic centre and the canals of Xochimilco, to the south, were inscribed together on the World Heritage list in 1987, because between them they tell how a lake civilisation became a colonial city.

Xochimilco is the survivor of the lake. Its canals and chinampas, narrow artificial islands built up from mud and reeds and planted with maize, flowers and vegetables, were the farms that fed Tenochtitlan, and some of them are still cultivated. Today colourful flat-bottomed boats called trajineras glide along the waterways, bearing families, birthday parties and mariachi bands. The canals are also the last natural home of the axolotl, the strange salamander that keeps its gills for life and can regrow lost limbs, which is now critically endangered.

The ride from the centre to Xochimilco is a slog through the south of one of the largest cities on Earth. The roads are busy and rough, the lights are many, and traffic can slow to a crawl. Use the ring road, the Periferico, where possible, and avoid rush hours, when the traffic is brutal. Many riders weave between lanes, and cars expect it, but newcomers should be careful, especially in the rain, when painted lines and metal covers get slippery. A weekday morning is calmer than a Sunday, when families flood the canals.

Fuel is no problem anywhere in the metropolitan area, and secure parking at the embarcaderos is available for a small fee. The boat ride is slow and sociable, with vendors selling food, drinks and flowers from other boats, and the pace of it is a good counterpoint to the city. In the cool season, the canals are quiet and misty in the early light, and the willows along the banks are lovely. Look out for herons and egrets, and for the narrow strips of chinampa that still push out between the waterways.
t.drobeta turnu severin podul lui traian@4:
When the emperor Trajan wanted to invade Dacia for the second time, he told his engineer to build a bridge across the Danube, and the engineer, Apollodorus of Damascus, made it happen. The bridge at Drobeta, completed in 105 AD, was a marvel, with twenty stone piers carrying timber arches over a river that is more than a kilometre wide at this point, and for a thousand years it was the longest arch bridge in the world. It was built to move the legions across the river in one season, and it did its job. The wars that followed ended with the conquest of Dacia in 106 and the creation of a new Roman province.

Today you can see the remains on both banks, a stump of brick and stone at the Romanian end near the old fort, and a few piers that stick out of the water in dry summers. Trajan's Column in Rome shows the bridge in a carved relief, a long string of arches. The Iron Gates Region Museum, in Drobeta-Turnu Severin, houses a model of the bridge, as well as Roman finds, a ground plan of the fortress, and an exhibition on the Danube gorge.

The Danube is the real character of the place. Just upstream, the river squeezes into the gorge of the Iron Gates, which cuts through the Carpathians for about a hundred kilometres between Romania and Serbia, and the river runs deep and swift between steep, forested cliffs. The road along the northern bank, DN57 and DN6, is one of the best rides in the country, with views of the water, rock tunnels, and the colossal rock-carved face of Decebalus near Orsova, which is the tallest rock sculpture in Europe, completed in 2004. Traffic can be heavy on the main road with lorries, but the shoreline stretch is a joy on a clear morning. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, with soft light on the water, and the summer can be hot and busy.

With over a hundred thousand people, Drobeta-Turnu Severin has fuel, restaurants and hotels in plenty, and Simian, a few kilometres away, is a suburban town. Try a plate of grilled Danube fish, and a glass of local red wine, and take time to wander the park around the ruins at dusk, when the river turns pink.
t.central balkan severen dzhendem reserve@:
Bulgaria's Balkan range gave the whole peninsula its name, and the central stretch is where it looks most like a proper mountain wall. The Severen Dzhendem reserve lies in the Central Balkan National Park, the high ridge that runs east to west above the Rose Valley. To the south the land drops towards Kalofer and Karlovo, and to the north it falls away into the foothills and the towns around Apriltsi and Troyan. The tallest peak in the range, Botev, rises to a little over 2,300 metres not far from here, and the high ground is grassy ridge, cliff and old beech and fir forest.

A strict nature reserve is a place to look at from outside, and the reserve itself is closed to casual visitors. What you can enjoy are the roads around it. Karlovo, with about 20,000 people some 17 km away, is the larger town for fuel, food and a bed. Kalofer, the small town on the Tundzha river, is the birthplace of Hristo Botev, the poet and revolutionary who died fighting the Ottomans in 1876 and whose name the peak now carries. The town has a quiet museum dedicated to him, and the old stone houses on its streets are worth a short stroll.

The riding in this part of Bulgaria is rewarding. Roads climb out of the valleys in long, rhythmic bends, sometimes with patched asphalt and the odd pothole, then cross passes in the range at around 1,500 metres or so. Snow can linger late into spring, and fog pours over the crest in the afternoon, so ride early in the day if you want clear views. Summer is lovely, with the hay meadows in flower and shepherd dogs patrolling the hillsides, so slow down for flocks on the road.

Wildlife in the reserve is the sort that thrives where people stay out: brown bear, wolf, chamois and eagles over the ridges. You are very unlikely to see any of them, but you may well see a lot of butterflies in summer. This is also the edge of the Valley of the Roses, and if you come in late May or early June the rose-picking harvest is on and the air near Kazanlak smells of attar. Try the local banitsa, a flaky cheese pastry, with a glass of yoghurt drink called ayran, and you will be properly fed.
t.earliest 16th century monasteries on the:
Popocatépetl is one of the highest volcanoes in North America, at about 5,400 metres, and it still smokes. From Mexico City on a clear winter day you can see the plume, and on the south side, in the state of Morelos, the foothills are dotted with the monasteries that the first Spanish friars built in the sixteenth century. They arrived in waves, Franciscans in 1524, Dominicans in 1526 and Augustinians in 1533, and in a few decades they converted and taught the people of the valleys, building fortress-like convents with open-air chapels, huge atria for crowds, and cloisters decorated with painted scenes. Eleven of them became a World Heritage group in 1994.

Atlatlahucan, an Augustinian foundation of the 1570s, is one of the best. The church is solid and plain from outside, with a stout facade and a belfry, but inside the cloister there are murals in black and white, executed by indigenous artists in a technique known as grisaille, showing saints and symbols in vivid detail. Nearby Tlayacapan, Yecapixtla and Oaxtepec have their own monasteries, and the region is known for its carnival with the chinelos, masked dancers in feathered hats and velvet robes who leap and spin.

The roads here are among the most enjoyable in central Mexico. From Cuernavaca or Cuautla they run through hills of maize fields, orchards and rocky outcrops, with views of the volcano on a clear morning. Roads between the villages are narrow, with sharp curves, and topes appear in every village. Rain in summer can bring landslides and flooding. The volcano has an exclusion zone, and eruptions have occasionally closed roads and dusted the villages with ash, so check the status before heading to the higher slopes.

Atlatlahucan is a town of about eight thousand with fuel and food, and the region is known for its mole, its tamales and its fruit, especially the sweet ones from Oaxtepec. Visitors are welcome in the churches but should respect services and dress modestly. The best months are November to April, when the skies are clear and the air is dry, and early morning is a good time to see the volcano.
t.ogasawara islands@27.7,142.1:
About a thousand kilometres south of Tokyo, in the Pacific, a scatter of small volcanic islands sits on the road to nowhere. These are the Ogasawara Islands, also called the Bonin Islands, and they have never been joined to any continent. That isolation is the whole point. Snails, plants and insects have evolved here in ways found nowhere else, which is why UNESCO listed the islands in 2011 and why some people call them the Galapagos of the East.

The coordinates here fall among the smaller northern outliers, near the Mukojima and Nakodojima groups, which are uninhabited and largely closed to casual visitors. The main inhabited islands are Chichijima and Hahajima, reached by a ferry from Tokyo that takes about a day each way and runs only every few days. If you are on a motorbike, you will need to understand that the ride is a short one: a few narrow roads on Chichijima, a few more on Hahajima, with the sea always close.

History is unusual too. Western and Pacific Islander settlers arrived in the 1830s, a mix of sailors and adventurers, and the islands later fell under Japanese control. Commodore Perry stopped here in 1853 before sailing on to Japan. During the Second World War the islands were fought over, and Iwo Jima is not far south. The US administered Ogasawara until 1968, and some residents still carry names that reflect that mixed past.

The sea is the real attraction. Humpback whales pass between roughly January and April, dolphins can be seen year round, and green turtles nest on the beaches. The water is clear and warm, and the forests contain endemic trees, including the Bonin palm, and a flying fox found nowhere else. Weather is subtropical, with typhoons in late summer and autumn, so check the ferry schedule. Fuel and food are limited to the village on Chichijima, so plan the day with some care, and treat the islands as a place to slow down.
t.rila monastery@42.1,23.3:
The road to Rila Monastery climbs a long valley through forests of beech and spruce, and when the monastery appears the effect is theatrical. Its walls enclose a courtyard of striped arcades in black, white and red, with a church in the middle covered in frescoes, and behind it the green flanks of the Rila mountains rise towards peaks of more than two and a half thousand metres. It is the largest and most important monastery in Bulgaria, and UNESCO listed it in 1983.

The monastery was founded in the tenth century by Ivan of Rila, a hermit who lived in a cave nearby and became the patron saint of Bulgaria. Pilgrims followed, and the community grew. Through the long centuries of Ottoman rule it kept Bulgarian language and culture alive, which gave it a symbolic place in the national story. A fire destroyed most of the buildings in 1833, and the monastery was rebuilt over the following decades in the form you see now. The tall tower of Hrelyo, from the fourteenth century, is the one medieval structure that survived.

The church of the Nativity, in the courtyard, is covered in murals painted by some of the best Bulgarian artists of the Revival period, including Zahari Zograf. Visitors are asked to keep their voices low and dress modestly, and photography inside the church is restricted. The monastery bakery is known for its fresh bread, and the little shops sell honey and icons. Trout from the Rila river often features on the menu in the restaurants nearby.

The ride up the valley is a real pleasure, with a decent surface, gentle bends and forest on both sides. The road climbs steadily, and it can be cool and damp even in summer. Rila, the nearest small town, has fuel, and Sapareva Banya, famous for its hot springs, is not far away. Go early in the day to avoid coach parties, and stay for the evening if you can, because once the day visitors leave, the place is calm. Autumn colours are glorious, and winter brings snow.
t.orlitsa convent complex@42.1,23.2:
The town of Rila is a small place at the foot of the mountains that bear its name, and the Orlitsa convent stands just a short way outside it, in the valley of the Rila river. It is a quiet complex, a working community of nuns, with a small church and gardens, and it gets a tiny fraction of the visitors that go to the great monastery further up the valley. For that reason alone it is worth a stop, since you can sit in the courtyard and hear the river instead of a crowd.

Bulgarian convents often have a particular character. They are modest, tidy and built around a garden, with flowers in the beds and vines on the walls, and the nuns do much of the work themselves, from baking and weaving to growing vegetables. Many were founded in the Middle Ages and survived centuries of Ottoman rule, and some were closed under communism and later revived. I do not know the founding date of Orlitsa, so I will not give one, but the setting is easy to describe: a green valley, a clear stream and wooded hills.

The area around Rila is a good one for riding. The road up to the monastery, about seventeen kilometres away, climbs through beech and conifer forest with long, easy bends, and the Rila mountains rise on every side. Lower down, the valley is farmland with orchards and fields of potatoes and beans. Kocherinovo, to the north, is a bigger village, and Sapareva Banya, a bit further, is a spa town with hot springs. The mountains are a hiker's paradise, with glacial lakes and high peaks, and the Pirin range lies to the south.

Fuel is available at Rila town, but the stations in the villages are few, so fill up when you can. Weather in the mountains changes quickly, with fog and rain in the afternoon, and cold nights even in summer. The best seasons are late spring and early autumn, and the quiet light of early morning is a pleasure. Be respectful of the nuns, dress modestly, and speak softly. A cup of herbal tea, and a bench in the shade, are all you need.
t.latomou monastery@40.7,23.0:
Latomou is a modest-looking place with a remarkable secret. Tucked in the upper part of Thessaloniki, the monastery is also known as Osios David, after a hermit who is said to have lived in a tree nearby, and its small church holds a mosaic of the fifth or sixth century that ranks among the oldest and loveliest in the city. The apse shows Christ in a vision of the prophet Ezekiel, seated on a rainbow, beardless and youthful in a landscape of rivers and trees, with the four living creatures around him and two prophets in the corners. The style is closer to ancient Roman painting than to the stern icons of later Byzantium, and the colours are still fresh.

The mosaic was hidden for centuries. After the Ottoman conquest of 1430 the church became a mosque, and the mosaic was covered with plaster, and only in the early twentieth century was it uncovered, almost by chance, while the building was being repaired. This is the Thessaloniki story in a nutshell: a city that was Roman, Byzantine, Ottoman and Greek, and has layers of each, concealed and revealed by fires, earthquakes and politics. The monuments of early Christian and Byzantine Thessaloniki are collectively listed by UNESCO, and Latomou is among them.

The ride into the upper town is a steep and complicated business. Narrow one-way lanes climb the hill, some of them cobbled, and parking is scarce, with cars crammed against every wall. A motorcycle is far better than a car here, but the gradients and surface can be tricky after rain. Ágios Pávlos and Sykiés are the districts around, both busy, residential and full of small bakeries, and you should expect to ask for directions, since street names are often confusing. The views over the Thermaic Gulf from the hillside are fine, particularly at dusk.

Fuel and food are easy to find in Thessaloniki, a large city with every supply. For a snack, try a bougatsa, the creamy or cheese pastry, or a koulouri, the sesame bread ring that locals eat for breakfast. Visit in spring or autumn, as summer heat in the city can be overwhelming, and check the opening hours of the church, which are limited. The upper town cafes offer cold drinks and good views for a rest.
t.church of prophet elijah@40.6,23.0:
Thessaloniki has so many Byzantine churches that the city seems to be built on top of them, and the Church of the Prophet Elijah is one of the later ones, dating from the early fourteenth century when the city was still a great centre of art under the Palaiologan emperors. It stands in the upper part of the old town, near Sykiés, a church with a broad central dome on a high drum and alternating courses of stone and brick, the decoration typical of the period. Some of the elements are tall and elegant, giving the building a lightness that surprises in so solid a material.

Like many churches in the city it changed religion more than once. After the Ottoman conquest of 1430 it was turned into a mosque, and it remained so until the Greek army took the city in 1912. The interior has traces of old paintings, though much has been lost. Elijah's was the church of the Palaiologan period, when Thessaloniki was the second city of the empire, and the generation of artists working here influenced the painting of Mount Athos and the Balkans. Today the church is used for services and occasional visits, so check the opening times with the local office.

The trip to the church is a ride through residential Thessaloniki, with pedestrian lanes and short steep climbs. Sykiés is a dense suburb of nearly forty-five thousand people, with a busy main road, shops and cafes, and the neighbouring Ágios Pávlos is smaller. The roads are narrow and parked cars make them tighter, so ride slowly and watch for doors opening. On the hillside above the old city walls, the upper town has little streets of old wooden houses with overhanging upper floors, and some of them have been lovingly restored.

For fuel and food, use the main roads, where stations and grocery shops are plentiful. Greek hospitality can be generous, and a small cafe may offer you a glass of water and a sweet spoon preserve with your coffee, if you ask. The weather is hot in summer and cool, damp and occasionally snowy in winter, so spring and early autumn are the best times for a visit. After the church, walk up to the Byzantine walls, where you can see the whole city and the gulf spread out below.
t.church of st catherine@40.7,23.0:
In the upper town of Thessaloniki, just above the busy streets of Sykiés, stands the Church of Saint Catherine, a late Byzantine building of the thirteenth or fourteenth century, with brick and stone patterns in its walls and a cluster of domes and apses that give it a lively outline. It is dedicated to Saint Catherine of Alexandria, who was said to have been tortured on a wheel for her faith, and the cult was strong in the eastern Mediterranean. The church was originally larger and had a covered walkway, and like its neighbours it spent centuries as a mosque after the Ottoman conquest. Today it is a church again, a quiet place among the houses.

The building is typical of what archaeologists call the cross-in-square type, but with an ambulatory around three sides, which is unusual, and some people link it to monastic patterns elsewhere in the empire. Its walls have the decoration of brick set in zigzag and herringbone, the feature the Thessaloniki builders of that age loved. Inside, the frescoes are mostly faded, but the proportions are fine, with a sense of space greater than you expect from the outside.

Riding to it is an urban affair. The streets are narrow, hilly and often one-way, with a mixture of old and new houses and small gardens. Cars park on both sides, so a motorbike is easier, but you need patience for the maze, and a paper map is no less useful than a phone in the shadow of tall buildings. In summer the heat can bounce off the stone, and in winter the streets can be wet and slippery. Early morning and evening are the pleasantest times to visit, with fewer people and softer light.

Sykiés and Ágios Pávlos have fuel stations along the main roads, and plenty of grocery shops, bakeries and little restaurants where you can get a decent grilled meat dish for lunch. The ones off the tourist routes are often best, with handwritten menus and big portions. Greek coffee is served in a small cup with the grounds at the bottom, so do not drink to the last sip. The old walls of the upper town are a short climb above the church, with views over the red roofs and the sea to the south.
t.church of st demetrios@40.6,23.0:
Saint Demetrios is the patron saint of Thessaloniki, a Roman soldier martyred in the early fourth century, and his church is the heart of the city's religious life. The basilica stands on the hill above the old Roman forum, on the site where Demetrios is said to have been imprisoned and killed, and over the centuries it was rebuilt several times after fires. The present church, a great five-aisled basilica of the seventh century, was devastated by the fire of 1917, which destroyed much of the city, and was rebuilt in the following decades. A few of the early mosaics survived, set in pillars and walls, showing the saint with children and officials, and they are among the most moving works of the period.

Beneath the church there is a crypt, a series of vaulted chambers in the ruins of a Roman bath, where tradition places the saint's prison. It is cool, dim and quiet, and a small museum holds fragments of sculpture and tombs. Demetrios is also the protector of the city in battle and plague, and in the stories he turned up on the walls to repel attackers, including the Slavs in the seventh century. The feast day in late October is celebrated with processions and a fair, and the church fills with candles.

Thessaloniki's roads are a challenge, since it is the second city of Greece, with roughly a million people in the metropolitan area. The traffic is dense, drivers are impatient and scooters weave through every gap. The streets around the church are one-way, and parking is scarce, though motorbikes are usually tolerated on the pavement edges, and the district is a short walk from Aristotelous Square and the sea front. Tram tracks are not an issue here, but the surface can be slippery with polished stone and wet leaves. Go on a weekday morning to avoid the worst of the traffic.

Fuel is plentiful on the ring roads and avenues, and food is excellent: a plate of grilled sardines, a sweet trigona pastry filled with custard, or a bowl of hearty bean soup will cure fatigue. The nearby streets are full of cafes where the old men play backgammon, and the market quarters offer cheap and cheerful snacks. Visit in spring or autumn and give yourself time inside the crypt. Dress modestly for the church and do not photograph the faithful while they pray.
t.byzantine bath@40.6,23.0:
Among the more unusual monuments on the Thessaloniki list is the Byzantine bath, one of the few surviving examples of the public bathing establishments that the empire inherited from Rome. The building dates from the thirteenth or fourteenth century, and it stands in the upper part of the old town, a low, vaulted structure of stone and brick with a cluster of small domes that let in light. Inside there are the traces of a series of chambers, a changing room, a warm room and a hot one, with the remains of the hypocaust, the system of channels under the floor that carried hot air from a furnace. Bathing was not purely a matter of hygiene in the Byzantine world, but also social life, gossip and business.

The bath changed hands as the city did. After 1430 the Ottomans kept the hamam tradition alive in Thessaloniki, with their own domed bathhouses, and the Byzantine building was in use for a time in that way. The city's later fires and building have hidden many such structures, and it is easy to walk past without noticing. Look for the little domes, which stand a bit above the rooftops, with glass lights in them like small eyes.

Riding in this part of the city is slow going. The streets around the bath are narrow and steep, with traffic lights at the bigger junctions and buses on the main roads. Motorbikes are everywhere, and you will fit in if you keep a steady pace and watch the car doors. The surface is a mix of asphalt and old paving, with manhole covers and wet leaves for hazards. If it is hot, take the shade of the plane trees on the squares and drink plenty of water, which is on sale at every kiosk.

Ágios Pávlos has about seven thousand people, and Sykiés about forty-five thousand, with fuel on the main roads and groceries on every corner. For a meal, try a souvlaki wrapped in pita or a plate of mezedes with a glass of tsipouro, the local grape spirit that Thessalonians are proud of. A coffee at a hillside cafe will show you the whole bay, with Mount Olympus faint in the distance on a clear day. The bath is small, so a visit takes only a short time, but it is a good reminder that the city's history was ordinary as well as grand.
t.church of the holy apostles@40.7,22.9:
Ask a Thessalonian for the prettiest church in town and a fair number will name the Holy Apostles, a small building from about 1310 to 1314 near the old Roman and Byzantine heart of the city, a few steps from the Egnatia Street axis. It was built, according to tradition, by the patriarch Niphon, and it is a showpiece of the Palaiologan style: five domes, a ring of arches, and walls where bricks have been laid in bands, zigzags and little crosses until the whole surface looks embroidered. On the outside, the pattern is the thing. Inside, mosaics from the same decade have survived in the domes, showing the Pantokrator and groups of apostles in tiny cubes of glass.

The church was also a mosque for a long period, and the Ottomans left a washing fountain in the courtyard. Restoration in the twentieth century removed later additions and revealed the beauty of the brickwork. A courtyard garden around the church is cool and green, and the sound of traffic fades in it, so it is a good place to sit for a few minutes. Because the building is small, with a low door, you have to stoop slightly to enter, which adds to the feeling of stepping into another world.

The location is right at the boundary of Sykiés and Neapoli, two dense districts with a combined population well beyond seventy thousand. Streets here are flat compared with the upper town, but they are crowded with parked cars, delivery vans and a continuous stream of scooters. Treat junctions with care, because drivers tend to assume priority and buses stop without warning. Early morning or Sunday is the quiet time, when you can roll up to the courtyard and park alongside the wall.

You will not struggle for fuel, since stations stand along the avenues, and grocery shops, bakeries and tavernas cluster in every block. A bakery that has a tray of freshly baked tiropita, the cheese pie, will make a decent lunch for a couple of euros. Greek summers are hot, and I would plan a visit for April, May or October, when the stone is warm and the air light. When you leave, ride down towards the sea and look back at the hill, where the old walls line the skyline and the domes rise above the red roofs.
t.church of st sophia@40.6,23.0:
Hagia Sophia in Thessaloniki is the church the city's people call simply Agia Sofia, and it sits on a paved square in the middle of the old town, with cafes and plane trees all around. It is much older than it looks, because parts of it date to the seventh or eighth century, and the central dome is modelled loosely on the great church of the same name in Constantinople. The big mosaic in the dome is the star: Christ ascending in a ring of light, with the Virgin and the apostles below, set against a gold ground. Experts date it to the ninth century, a rare survival from the period after the Iconoclast controversy, when images were banned and destroyed.

Look at the apse mosaic too. The Virgin is enthroned in the half dome, with a stern, graceful look, and the lettering round it is early. The church was a mosque for five hundred years after the Ottoman conquest, and the gaps in the interior show where the Muslim prayer niche stood. Fires and earthquakes damaged it, and the large 1978 earthquake shook the city. Today it is a UNESCO site and a working church, with services on feast days.

The riding is not the point of this one, because the square sits in a zone of dense traffic and one-way streets. Aim for the pedestrian edge and walk the last couple of hundred metres, locking your helmet to the bike if you can. At rush hour the central avenues clog, and the best way to approach is from the seafront road, which is often quicker. Kasandrou Street and its parallels climb up to the hill, and from a bike they can look a little forbidding. In winter the stone in the square is slippery.

Practical matters are easy. Thessaloniki is a major city, with stations on every ring road and supermarkets in every district. The square around Hagia Sophia has lots of seating, and a pastry shop sells bougatsa, the local cream pie, while nearby tavernas serve food at lunchtime. In the evening the area fills with students and musicians. For a more peaceful moment, come at 8 a.m. before the sun gets high, when the dome mosaic gets its first light through the windows and the bells begin.
t.blatades monastery@40.7,23.0:
Vlatadon, or Blatades, is the monastery to see if you want to understand why Thessaloniki's upper town is the city's loveliest part. It sits against the old Byzantine walls, near the Eptapyrgion fortress, and it was founded in the 1360s by two brothers named Vlatas, with a church that mixes the brick and stone of the Palaiologan style. The monastery has been a centre of church learning for centuries and still houses the Patriarchal Foundation for Patristic Studies, so you may find priests and students crossing the courtyard with books. It is a place where life continues.

The history is a good one. The monastery was founded when Thessaloniki was in decline and under pressure, and the Ottomans took the city in 1430, yet the monks kept the building through most of the occupation. A tradition says Paul preached to the Thessalonians on this very hillside, and the monastery was built on that spot. Its walls and the garden at the front frame one of the best views in the city: the Thermaic Gulf stretching out below, the port, the white tower, and on clear days the huge shape of Mount Olympus floating on the horizon.

To get there, the old town hill is the challenge. Roads climb past Tsimiski and Kassandrou in steep, narrow turns, and the last stretches are quite tight, with cobbles and sudden gradients. A motorbike has the advantage of squeezing into small spaces, but remember that the road surface can be rough and that buses squeeze by with inches to spare. Avoid hot afternoons, when the stone reflects heat. Walking the last two hundred metres may be wiser than riding, and the shaded lane has a wonderful scent of pine and jasmine in spring.

Fuel is found along the avenues at the bottom of the hill, and any number of small shops will supply bottled water. The monastery's visitor hours are limited, and it is not a place for loud conversation or shorts, so cover your shoulders. A cafe near the walls offers an excellent view over the roofs, and the owners will not mind if you linger over a frappe. Come in the late afternoon if you can, when the evening light hits the white walls and the gulf turns copper, and wait for the sunset.
t.city walls@40.6,23.0:
Thessaloniki's walls are the great monument that holds the whole city together. They run in a long triangle from the sea up the hill and back down, and in places they stand ten metres high, with square and round towers, brick bands and later repairs patched in like scars. The first walls were built in the late fourth century and again in the fifth, when the city was a vital Roman port on the Via Egnatia, the road that linked the Adriatic with Constantinople. Later emperors repaired them over and over, and the Ottomans too, and the pattern of stone, brick and rubble tells the story to anyone who looks closely.

At the top of the hill stands the Eptapyrgion, the Fortress of Seven Towers, which the Ottomans used as a prison and which held prisoners until 1989. The Trigonion Tower, a three-sided bastion at the corner, is the most famous point, and from its platform you look over the whole city. The south walls, along the harbour, were pulled down in the nineteenth century to let the city grow, so the sea front is open now. Today a walk along the surviving sections offers fine views and an atmosphere of wild flowers and broken stone.

For a rider, the road that follows the line of the walls is the best bit of tarmac in town. It climbs from the lower suburbs through the old quarter, with twisting streets and hairpin bends that feel almost Alpine in miniature, and the best views of the gulf. Some lanes are very narrow and steep, so a small bike is better than a tourer. After rain the cobbles are treacherous. Go early on a clear morning, or an hour before sunset, to enjoy light and fewer cars.

Ágios Pávlos is the nearest district and has fuel and shops on its main roads, with the larger Sykiés beyond. Take water with you, and wear a hat in summer, because the walls offer little shade. The tavernas near the Trigonion serve grilled meat and salads, and the owners are used to walkers and cyclists. There is a legend that the city was saved from attack by a vision of Saint Demetrios on the walls, which gives you something to think about as you stand on the stones at dusk and watch the lights come on below.
t.church of acheiropoietos@40.6,23.0:
The name of this church means not made by hands, and it refers to an icon of the Virgin that was believed to have appeared miraculously. The building itself is an early Christian basilica from about the middle of the fifth century, one of the oldest surviving churches in Thessaloniki and one of the best examples of its type in the Mediterranean. Inside you find a long nave with a double row of green and red marble columns, topped by carved capitals, and above them a gallery where the women sat. Light falls through the arched windows in a bright, even way, and the proportions are easy and noble. A few fragments of mosaic, with plants and birds, survive on the arches.

When the Ottomans took the city in 1430 they turned it into a mosque, named after the conqueror's commander, and added a minaret that was later taken down. The Greek army reclaimed the building in 1912. It stands at a busy spot on Agiou Dimitriou Street, among shops and cafes, so you could easily pass it without noticing. The simple brick exterior gives few hints of the grandeur within.

Parking near the church is difficult, but a motorcycle can usually find a slot at the pavement edge. The streets are all one-way and filled with traffic, the junctions full of impatient drivers and delivery scooters. Weekends are quieter, particularly early on Sundays, when you can ride through the old centre almost unmolested. There are streets with polished marble paving that become slick in the rain, and in summer the city heat builds up between the buildings. Visit in the morning, and take a few minutes to listen to the quiet inside.

Fuel stations are on the avenues further out, and in the middle of the city you will find shops of every kind. Try the local sweet shops, where syrupy pastries and spoon sweets are sold by weight. There is a long tradition of coffee drinking in Thessaloniki, and the cafes near the church are packed with people from morning until late. If you want to walk further, the Roman Forum and the Arch of Galerius are within a short stroll, and they show how much of the ancient city remains buried below the shops.
t.church of st nicholas orphanos@40.6,23.0:
Saint Nicholas Orphanos is a small church tucked away in the upper town of Thessaloniki, near the old walls and the Vlatadon monastery, and it is a place that rewards the traveller who likes quiet corners. It was built in the early fourteenth century, in the last great period of Byzantine painting, and its modest size hides an extraordinary set of frescoes. The paintings cover the walls and domes with scenes from the life of Christ and the saints, in vivid blues, reds and ochres, drawn with a grace and movement that was new in the art of the time. The name Orphanos, which means orphan, is a puzzle, and historians still argue over its origin.

The church was founded by a high official of the court, and its frescoes seem to be the work of artists from the capital, so they link Thessaloniki with the artistic life of Constantinople. In the nineteenth and twentieth centuries the building was partly neglected, used as a stable at one stage, and then restored. The people of the neighbourhood have kept it alive, and today you can step into a space that looks more like a jewel box than a church. A caretaker usually opens it at set hours, so check ahead and be prepared for a short wait.

The lanes around it are an old Greek hillside quarter, with white-washed houses, tiled roofs and blue shutters, and the sound of a radio from an open window. The streets are very steep and narrow, with tight bends and short ramps that make a loaded touring bike a handful. Park at the bottom and walk, particularly in summer, when the afternoon sun is strong and the stones are slippery with dust. Dogs and cats wander the lanes, and in spring the gardens are full of roses and lemon trees.

Fuel and food are a short ride downhill, with stations on the main roads in Ágios Pávlos and Sykiés. A little taverna in the upper town may serve you a plate of stuffed vine leaves, a bowl of lentils or grilled octopus with lemon, and you will probably be offered a glass of wine from the owner's barrel. Go in the late afternoon, when the church is often open and the light turns golden on the walls, and stay for the sunset over the bay from the nearby ramparts.
t.church of christ saviour@40.6,23.0:
The Church of Christ the Saviour, Soter in Greek, is one of the smaller Byzantine churches in Thessaloniki, built in the early fourteenth century in the same flowering of art that gave the city its Holy Apostles and Saint Nicholas Orphanos. It stands in the upper part of the old town, a compact building with a central dome and a perimeter walkway on three sides, covered with brick patterns that catch the light. Inside there are fragments of mosaics and frescoes, with delicate faces and soft colours that show the refinement of the Palaiologan court. Many of the paintings were lost when the building was used as a mosque and then as a storeroom.

The building has been altered over the centuries, with a new roof and a restored dome, and the surrounding houses press against it so tightly that you almost miss it. This is the quality that makes the old town of Thessaloniki so appealing: monuments not set apart in parks, but folded into daily life, with washing lines and flowerpots at their feet. The church takes on a different feeling in the evening, when the bells ring and old women gather at the door for the service.

The streets around are steep, narrow and one-way, with surface patches that change from asphalt to paving without warning. A motorbike is a good choice, but be patient with the maze of lanes and do not rely on GPS, which can be misled by the high walls. In winter rain makes the road slick, and in summer the heat can be intense. If you can, walk the last part, as the lanes are shaded by walnut trees and fig trees and the neighbours may say hello.

Fuel and cafes are down the hill in the busier districts of Ágios Pávlos and Sykiés, with all the usual services. If you are hungry, look for a baker selling spinach pie or a vendor with warm sesame rings, and settle on a bench with a view of the gulf. Greek hospitality shows itself in small gestures, a glass of water brought unasked, a sweet offered to a stranger. Spring is the best season, with the scent of orange blossom, and you can then ride down to the harbour for a walk along the promenade at dusk.
t.church of st panteleimon@40.6,23.0:
Saint Panteleimon was a physician and martyr, a healer who treated the poor without charge, and churches in his name were built across the Greek world to ask for his protection from illness. The one in Thessaloniki is a small fourteenth-century church in the old quarter, with a single dome and the careful brickwork of the Palaiologan builders. It is easy to miss, because it sits in a street of ordinary houses, and has none of the grandeur of the great basilicas. That, though, is the reason to look for it. A building like this shows you what a neighbourhood church was like when the city was crowded with them, and each guild or quarter had its own.

The church has a long and rather typical history. It was built, rebuilt after fire, converted into a mosque in the Ottoman period and returned to Christian use after 1912. Within, a few traces of old paint remain on the walls, and the modest interior has the feel of a place where people have been praying for six hundred years. A caretaker keeps the key, and a note on the door may tell you the opening times. Do not be surprised if it is closed when you come, which happens often with the smaller monuments.

The riding in this area is a matter of patience. The lanes are narrow, with parked cars on both sides and unexpected one-way turns, and a motorbike is the only vehicle that really fits. Keep the speed low, because children play in the streets and dogs doze in the road. The surface is patched and can be greasy with oil or leaves, and the slopes make starting from a stop tricky when the road is wet. Evening is the best time, when the heat has gone and the lanes are full of people sitting on their doorsteps.

Fuel is within a kilometre or two on the larger roads of Ágios Pávlos and Sykiés, and you can get all you need in the little shops. Try a coffee in a cafe where the old men sit and argue about football, or buy a bag of pistachios from a street seller. A few steps uphill the walls begin, and from them you can look down over the whole sprawling city, with the cranes of the port and the glitter of the gulf.
t.church of panagia chalkeon@40.6,23.0:
The Panagia Chalkeon, Our Lady of the Coppersmiths, is one of the oldest dated churches in Thessaloniki, and it can be dated to 1028 because of an inscription naming the founder, a Byzantine official called Christophoros. It stands on Egnatia Street, right on the old Roman road, in what was the metalworkers' quarter, and the name recalls the trade that filled the streets with the noise of hammering. The church is built of brick in the cross-in-square plan, with a central dome and three apses, and the outside is decorated with tall blind arches and patterns of brick that give the walls a handsome rhythm. In its day it was a showpiece of the new Byzantine style that developed after the Iconoclast period.

It has been a mosque, a storehouse and a ruin, but in the twentieth century it was cleaned and restored, and its frescoes were uncovered. Inside you can see parts of an eleventh-century painting, with the Virgin and Child in the apse, and the interior has a small, intimate scale. The church sits a little below the level of the modern street, because the city has risen around it over a thousand years, and a few steps lead down to the door. That detail makes a good point to ponder about the layers of a city.

Egnatia Street itself is a wide, noisy, fast-moving avenue, so it is not a pleasant place to ride. Heavy traffic, long buses and double-parked delivery vans make it a test of nerves, and you should plan to park on a side street and walk. The surface is good asphalt, but the junctions are chaotic, and pedestrian crossings are treated as a suggestion. The best hours are early on Sunday morning, when the city is almost empty.

You are in the centre of a large city, so everything is at hand. Fuel stations cluster on the avenues, and the surrounding blocks are packed with cafes, pharmacies and grocery stores. Try the nearby Modiano market, with its stalls of olives, fish, spices and cheese, or the Bezesteni covered market, built by the Ottomans in the fifteenth century. In the summer heat the shade of the arcades is welcome, and the smell of roasting coffee drifts out of doorways. Visit in spring or autumn and make time for the neighbouring Roman Forum.
t.rotunda@40.6,23.0:
The Rotunda is a huge round building of brick, with walls six metres thick and a dome spanning about twenty-four metres, and it has been standing since the early fourth century. It was probably built for the Roman emperor Galerius, who made Thessaloniki one of his capitals and who may have intended it as his mausoleum, though in the end he was buried elsewhere. Around AD 400 it was turned into a church, with a ring of mosaics added to the dome and the walls, and a tall apse added on the east side. The mosaics, of saints in prayer before gold and colour backgrounds, survive only in part, but the few that remain are among the finest in the Christian world.

In 1590 the building became a mosque, with a minaret that still stands in the courtyard, the only one left in the city that has survived from the Ottoman period, and the Greek state later used the building as a church and then as a museum. It has withstood earthquakes for seventeen centuries, which is remarkable, and the restoration work continues. It is a rare monument that shows Roman, early Christian and Ottoman layers in a single structure, and it has become a symbol of the city. The Arch of Galerius stands a few hundred metres south on the same axis, carved with scenes of the emperor's victories over the Persians.

Be prepared for the traffic. The Rotunda sits at the edge of a busy road junction near the Egnatia axis, with heavy flows of cars, motorbikes and buses, and parking is difficult. Choose a side street and stroll. The pavements around the monument are wide and open, with trees and benches, and they are popular with students and locals in the evening. In winter, a cold north wind called the vardaris can blow down from the Balkans, which is a reminder that the city is not as Mediterranean as it seems.

Fuel is easy to find on the main avenues, and the nearby streets are filled with cafes and restaurants. Take the chance to try a koulouri, a sesame ring, from one of the street vendors, or a cup of salep, a hot milky drink, in winter. The best time to see the interior is in the morning, when the light from the high windows brings out the colours, and the dome seems to float above you. Check the opening hours, which vary, and remember that you can walk around the outside at any time.
Vergina is a quiet farming village on the lower slopes of the Pieria mountains, in the plain of Imathia, and for most of its history nobody thought much about it. Then in 1977 the archaeologist Manolis Andronikos opened a tumulus and found an untouched royal tomb, with a gold chest, a gold wreath of oak leaves and the cremated bones of a middle-aged man, and the question was whose. The widely accepted answer is Philip II of Macedon, father of Alexander the Great, who was murdered in the theatre of Aegae in 336 BC, and the find confirmed that Vergina is the old Macedonian capital Aegae, where kings were crowned and buried.

The site today is a remarkable piece of museum design. The Great Tumulus, a mound over a hundred metres across, has been left in place and a modern museum built inside it, so that you walk down in the dark and the tombs appear in front of you, one behind another, with their painted facades. The finds are astonishing: gold larnakes, silver vessels, ivory heads, armour and a small gold quiver. A painted frieze on Tomb II shows a lion hunt. Outside, the foundations of a palace with a huge courtyard stand on a terrace above the village, and the theatre where Philip died is nearby.

The country around is gentle and green. From Véroia, about eleven kilometres away, the road runs south through orchards of peach and cherry, and the Vermio mountains stand behind, often still white with snow in April. Roads here are good and not busy, with long, flat stretches across the plain and a few curves where they enter the foothills. Spring and early summer are lovely, with poppies and the smell of cut grass, while late summer is hot. Farm vehicles and the occasional dog are the only hazards.

Véroia, with over forty thousand people, has fuel, shops and a pleasant old quarter with Byzantine churches and a Jewish quarter along a river gorge, while Vergina itself has a few cafes and a bakery. Imathia is known for its peaches, and in season roadside stalls sell them by the crate. Do book some time inside the museum, because the lighting is dim and the displays reward patience. Check opening hours, as they change between summer and winter, and bring a light layer, since the tomb chambers are cool.
t.meijima and peripheral reefs@26.6,142.2:
Meijima is one of those names that sounds like a joke until you learn the story: the small islands of the Ogasawara chain were given family names, a sort of island clan strung out across the Pacific. Meijima, roughly translated, is the niece. It lies far south of Tokyo, around a thousand kilometres out in the open Pacific, and there is no road to it, no bridge, and nothing resembling a petrol station.

What makes the place important is isolation. These islands rose from the sea floor and have never been joined to a continent, so everything living here arrived by wind, wave or wing. The result is an evolutionary workshop, sometimes called the Galápagos of the East, with land snails that have split into dozens of species and plants found nowhere else. The reefs around the islands are full of coral, reef fish and green turtles, and in winter humpback whales come to breed. UNESCO recognised the Ogasawara Islands as a natural world heritage site in 2011.

For a rider, this is a place you see from the sea, or rather from the deck of a boat or the window of the ferry that makes the long trip from Tokyo. The journey to the main inhabited island takes about a day and the ferry sails only every few days, which means your stay is measured in days rather than hours. Once there, small roads and excursion boats do the rest, and the tour operators know the rules for landing on protected ground. Most of the small islands are off limits to casual visitors.

Do bring a bike if you must, but plan to rent a scooter on the main island, because the island roads are short and winding. Fuel and food are available on the inhabited islands, in a small harbour town with a handful of cafes serving fresh fish, island lemon and passionfruit sweets. Weather can turn quickly with typhoons from July to October, and the calm months of spring and early summer are the friendliest.
t.hirajima and peripheral reefs@26.6,142.2:
Hirajima belongs to the same far-flung Ogasawara chain as its neighbours, a scatter of small islands and reefs in the Pacific about a thousand kilometres south of Tokyo. Its name simply means flat island, which suits something low and unassuming compared with the sharp, forested peaks of the bigger islands nearby. There are no roads on it in any real sense, and there is no way to ride to it, so this is a sea-level look at a protected place.

The story of the chain is a tangle of nations. Polynesian and Micronesian travellers may have passed this way long ago, and Spanish and Dutch sailors marked the islands on their charts. The first permanent settlers in the 1830s were a mixed group from the Pacific and the West, led by a man called Nathaniel Savory, and their descendants lived here when Commodore Perry's ships called in 1853. Japan claimed the islands in the 1870s, and after the Second World War the United States ran them until they were handed back in 1968. That history still shows in the family names and the English words in the local dialect.

Offshore, the water is clear and the colours range from deep navy to a startling pale turquoise over the reefs. Divers and snorkellers will find coral gardens and sharks, and the chance of seeing dolphins on the boat trip is high. Birds nest on cliffs and ledges, and some species breed nowhere else.

To get anywhere near it you need to take the ferry from Tokyo to the main island of Chichijima, a journey of roughly twenty-four hours, then arrange a boat. Chichijima has a small port town with fuel for the scooters and cars that serve the islanders, along with simple restaurants and guesthouses. Book ahead, because rooms are limited, and expect sea conditions to decide your schedule.
Imotojima, the younger sister, is a name that gives the Ogasawara islands a family feel, and the islands really do read like a family spread across the sea: Mukojima, Yomejima, Anijima, Imotojima and the rest.

The beauty is in the colour of the sea and the details of the reef. Around the islets, corals grow in shallow shelves, with parrotfish, butterflyfish and the occasional reef shark. Green turtles feed on the seagrass, and from about January to March humpback whales arrive to calve, sometimes surfacing right beside tour boats. Above water there are seabirds, with some species nesting on cliffs and boulders, and the vegetation includes endemic palms and shrubs adapted to wind and salt.

Getting to the chain is an expedition of its own. The ferry from Tokyo takes roughly a day, and the schedule is limited, so a visit requires several nights. People who come do so for the sea and for quiet, not for fast riding or sightseeing in the usual sense. On the main island of Chichijima there is a small town with fuel and food, and rented scooters or cars let you tour the short coastal roads, which wind between headlands and sandy coves.

Plan around the weather. Typhoons from late summer into autumn can cancel boats, and the sun is strong all year, so bring sun protection. Respect the rules, too: landing on protected islets generally requires permits and a registered guide, which keeps the ecosystem intact. That gentle restraint is part of why the place has stayed so pure.
t.higashijima and peripheral reefs@27.1,14:
Higashijima means eastern island, and like its relatives in the Ogasawara chain it sits in the middle of the Pacific, around a thousand kilometres south of Tokyo and at the end of one of the longest regular ferry runs in Japan. No road leads to it, and nobody rides there. What it offers is a glimpse of one of the world's most isolated natural laboratories, seen from a boat on a good day.

The reefs that surround these islands are the reason for the heritage listing. Corals grow here at the northern limit of their range, nourished by warm currents, and the water is clear enough that snorkellers can see the bottom from the surface. Hawksbill and green turtles come to nest on certain beaches, and the sea is alive with reef fish, rays and the occasional shark. Winter brings humpback whales that pass close enough to the boats for you to hear their breath.

On land, the story is one of endemic species. Snails, beetles and trees evolved here separately from anywhere else, and invasive animals brought by settlers, such as goats, cats and rats, have taken a heavy toll. Much recent conservation effort has gone into removing those pests and protecting what remains. The Bonin flying fox and the Bonin honeyeater, once found on these islands, are examples of how fragile the balance can be.

The main port of the inhabited area is Futami on Chichijima, and you reach it after a ferry trip of about twenty-four hours from Tokyo. The ferry sails only a few times a month, so visitors usually stay for several days. There is fuel on the main island for rented scooters, plus small restaurants and guesthouses. Book early, bring motion sickness tablets, and treat the schedule as a suggestion because weather decides everything.
t.some parts of chichijima and peripheral:
Chichijima and Hahajima are the two inhabited islands of the Ogasawara chain, and the only ones where a visitor can really spend time. Chichijima, the father island, has the port village of Futami, a handful of beaches, quiet roads and a small museum that tells the settlers' story. Hahajima, the mother island, lies about fifty kilometres further south, a long green ridge with a tiny village and trails that climb through forest.

You get here by boat from Tokyo, a day of open ocean each way, and there is no airport. That alone has protected the place, and when UNESCO listed it in 2011 it noted the unusual speciation of land snails and the many plants found nowhere else. Bonin flying foxes, a fruit bat with a wingspan of more than a metre, hang in the trees, and marine life ranges from dolphins to sharks. Whale watching in winter and spring is a highlight.

History here has odd chapters. A small group of settlers from the Pacific and the West, including an American called Nathaniel Savory, made their home in the 1830s, and the descendants are still around. Commodore Perry visited in 1853 before steaming on to Japan. During the Second World War, Chichijima was a fortified Japanese base, and rusting guns and tunnels survive in the hills. After the war the US controlled the islands until 1968, which explains certain English-sounding names and foods.

Chichijima has a few short roads that you can ride or drive on rented scooters, winding past bays and headlands with lovely sea views, and a lookout on the hill is a favourite spot for sunsets. There is a petrol station for local vehicles, restaurants serving fresh fish and sashimi, and small guesthouses. Hahajima is quieter and has fewer facilities. Check ferry schedules before committing, since they can be limited, and typhoon season can interrupt services.
t.museum city of gjirokastra@40.1,20.1:
Gjirokastër is a city of stone, and it makes you look up. Houses with thick walls and slate roofs, many built as tower-like fortified homes called kulla, climb the steep hillside under a huge castle, and the cobbled lanes that link them are so slanted that you will think twice about riding up them. The old town was recognised by UNESCO in 2005 as a rare surviving example of an Ottoman town with its character intact, and it has a dignified, slightly melancholy air.

The castle, one of the largest in the Balkans, has seen Byzantine, Ottoman, Italian and Communist occupants, and the display inside includes captured aircraft and a tunnel network built during the Cold War. Gjirokastër is also known as the birthplace of two very different men: Enver Hoxha, who ruled Albania as a communist dictator for four decades, and Ismail Kadare, the novelist who wrote about the city in his memoir Chronicle in Stone. The city's mixed history of Greek, Albanian and Ottoman residents is part of its fabric.

The Drino valley is a wide, green corridor, with the Mali i Gjerë mountains to the east, and the approach from the south or from Saranda takes you through olive groves and small villages. Roads in southern Albania have improved, but you should still watch for potholes, livestock and drivers who overtake in unlikely places. Summers are hot, so ride in the morning, and winter brings rain and cold winds, with snow in the surrounding mountains. The ride to Saranda and the ferry to Corfu goes through lovely coastal scenery.

Gjirokastër has fuel stations on the main road, plenty of guesthouses in old stone houses, and cafes in the bazaar, which climbs steeply from the main square. Try qifqi, rice balls flavoured with herbs and fried, and byrek, flaky pastry filled with cheese or spinach. Keep your bike somewhere secure, preferably in a courtyard, and expect to walk, because the old lanes are better suited to feet and donkeys.
t.anijima and peripheral reefs@27.1,142.2:
Anijima, whose name means elder brother island, lies a short boat ride off Chichijima in the Ogasawara or Bonin Islands, a chain of volcanic specks roughly a thousand kilometres south of Tokyo. Nobody gets here by accident. The only link to the mainland is the ferry that makes the journey of around twenty-four hours, running about once a week, and the whole group has never been joined to any continent. That isolation is why UNESCO listed it as a natural World Heritage Site in 2011, calling it an oceanic Galápagos.

You will not ride on Anijima itself, which has no real road network, but the water around it is the reason for the point. The reefs and clear channels are home to green turtles, which nest on the islands, and reef fish in an extraordinary range of colours. From roughly January to April, humpback whales come to the area to breed, and boat trips from Chichijima can bring you astonishingly close to mothers and calves. Dolphins are around most of the year.
