Boats and small guided groups are the only practical way to see it, and local operators follow rules that keep their distance from the animals.

On land the story is of plants and snails. Evolution on these islands produced endemic trees and a collection of land snails found nowhere else, and the arrival of rats, goats and feral cats did serious damage. Years of work to remove invasive animals from the smaller islets have helped native species recover. The Bonin flying fox, a large fruit bat, is one of the few native land mammals.

For practical purposes the base is Chichijima's port town. It has a modest selection of guesthouses, small restaurants and a petrol station, and rental scooters and bicycles are available for the island's short roads. The weather is subtropical, with the typhoon season from about August to October, and it is worth building flexibility into any plan, since a ferry can be delayed by weather. The islands also have a layered human history, from early settlers who arrived in 1830 to the wartime years and American administration until 1968, giving the place an unusual blend of Japanese and Western names and customs.
The Ogasawara islands name each other like a family, and Nishijima is among the younger members of the group, a modest uninhabited island west of Chichijima, the father island. Chichijima, Anijima and Ototojima, the elder and younger brothers, and Hahajima, the mother island, make up the main cast. The names are Japanese, and yet the main harbour town on Chichijima is called Ōmura, and the bay on its northern side Futami, and the older Western names like Peel Island and Port Lloyd still turn up on charts. That patchwork tells you how the island chain was settled.

Whalers and sailors used these anchorages in the early nineteenth century, and in 1830 a small party of settlers, a mixture of Europeans, Americans and Pacific Islanders, landed at what became Port Lloyd and stayed. Commodore Perry stopped here in 1853 on his way to Japan, and Japan formally claimed the islands in the 1870s. The war brought a heavy garrison, and Iwo Jima, to the south, saw one of the great battles of the Pacific. After the war the islands came under American control until their return to Japan in 1968. Descendants of the early settlers still live on Chichijima, and some of their family names appear on mailboxes.

The reefs around Nishijima are part of the same World Heritage Site, listed in 2011 for its unique evolution. Underwater, there is hard coral, a lot of small reef fish and the green turtles that feed on the seagrass beds. Above, seabirds nest on the cliffs. The best way to see all of this is by a small tour boat from Chichijima's port, since landing on the smaller islets is restricted to protect them.

The ferry that links the islands to Tokyo takes around a day and sails only about once a week, so anyone planning a visit should allow several days, with spare time in case of weather. Chichijima has shops, a few places to eat and fuel for the island's short roads. Winter is the whale season, and summer is better for swimming and diving, though typhoons can arrive from late summer.
South of Chichijima the Bonin chain thins out, and then Hahajima, the mother island, rises out of the Pacific with its own scatter of small satellites around it. Mukōjima, the island that gives this point its name, is one of those satellites, a low spit of land in the Hahajima group that you look across a channel to see. Its name simply means the island on the other side, which is the sort of down-to-earth naming the islanders have given to everything in sight. Nearby are Anejima, Imōtojima and Meijima, elder sister, younger sister and niece.

Hahajima is the only inhabited island in this group, home to a few hundred people in two small villages, Okimura and Kitamura. The ferry that serves it from Chichijima takes about two hours, and most visitors make it a day or overnight trip by small boat after the long ferry from Tokyo. A narrow island road runs along the coast and up toward the hills, with views of the sea on both sides, and it is quiet, with little traffic, short climbs and the smell of salt and warm vegetation. The highest point, Chibusa-yama, wears cloud around its top much of the year.

The islands have been protected as part of the Ogasawara World Heritage Site since 2011, and the point of interest is the unusually isolated ecology. Species of plant, land snail and insect have developed here that exist nowhere else, and the area around Hahajima holds some of the best surviving native forest. The sea around the islet is bright blue, and divers and snorkellers on guided boats can find coral gardens and reef fish. In winter humpback whales pass the coast, and from some of the headlands you can watch them from land.

Landing on tiny islets such as this is restricted to protect nesting birds and fragile vegetation, so the sensible way to see it is on a boat tour from Hahajima's port. Fuel and basic supplies are available in the village, but nothing is plentiful, and everything arrives by ship. Typhoons in late summer and autumn can disrupt crossings, so give yourself spare days at either end and keep the plan loose.
t.mukojima and peripheral reefs@27.7,142.1:
Three little islands sit alone in the Pacific more than a hundred kilometres north of Chichijima, and the Japanese gave them a joke that has lasted. Mukōjima is the bridegroom, Nakōdojima the matchmaker and Yomejima the bride, and together they form the Mukojima group, sometimes called the Parry Islands after a British naval officer. Nobody lives here now. The islands are volcanic remnants, treeless in places and grazed down in the past by goats, and they receive almost no visitors.

That emptiness is the reason the group matters. It lies inside the Ogasawara World Heritage area, and its steep slopes and ledges are nesting ground for seabirds, including albatrosses, which spend most of their lives on the wing over the open ocean and come ashore only to breed. Conservationists have worked here to protect those colonies and even tried to establish a new breeding site for the rare short-tailed albatross, a bird that was once hunted almost to extinction for its feathers. The sea around the islands is deep blue and rich with fish, and whales pass through in winter.

For a rider, honesty is the best policy. There are no roads, no harbours and no shops, and landing is not permitted without special authorisation, because the vegetation and nesting birds are so fragile. The point exists as a marker on the map for anyone following the whole chain of the Ogasawara Islands, and you will see it, if at all, from a boat. The long ferry from Tokyo to Chichijima takes about a day, and tours that go as far as the Mukojima group are rare, weather-dependent and usually arranged through guides on Chichijima.

If you do make it, expect a cold wind even in summer, swells that rise quickly when a storm is passing, and a sense of scale that makes a motorcycle seem a very distant idea. Typhoons come through from late summer, and the winter months are rougher but offer whale watching on the way. Bring seasickness tablets, because the crossing can be long and lively.
t.sofia@42.7,23.3:
Sofia sits under a mountain, and that is the first thing to understand about it. Vitosha rises right behind the southern suburbs, a broad, dome-shaped massif topping out at Cherni Vrah, around 2,290 metres, and on a clear morning the snow is visible from the boulevards. People ski there in winter and hike in summer, and the city's residents treat it like a back garden. The capital of Bulgaria is a plain, solid place of about one and a quarter million, with Soviet-era blocks, Ottoman remnants and an unexpected number of small parks.

The layers of history show in the centre. The city's name comes from the church of Saint Sophia, which gave the city its modern name, and the older Roman Serdica is visible in excavations under the metro. The little brick Rotunda of Saint George, from the fourth century, hides inside a courtyard behind government buildings. The golden domes of the Alexander Nevsky Cathedral, completed in the early twentieth century to honour the Russian soldiers who died in the war that freed Bulgaria from Ottoman rule in 1877 and 1878, dominate the skyline. In the suburb of Boyana, a small medieval church holds frescoes that predate the Italian Renaissance and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Riding in and out of Sofia needs patience. The ring road and main arteries are heavy at rush hour, and drivers have their own ideas about lanes. Once you clear the city, the A3 and the older roads south reach the Rila mountains by way of Dupnitsa and Blagoevgrad, a journey of a couple of hours that leads to Rila Monastery in its forested valley. Surfaces are acceptable, though potholes appear after winter, and mountain weather can change quickly. Bulgaria sells vignettes for motorways, so buy one for the bike before using them.

The city has fuel at every turn, plus workshops and shops. For food, try shopska salad with white cheese, banitsa pastries for breakfast, and rakia, the fruit brandy that appears as the generous opener at many meals. Late spring and early autumn are lovely times to ride.
t.puebla@19.0,-98.2:
Puebla looks like an old Spanish painting that someone left in the sun. The colonial city, founded in 1531 on a plateau in central Mexico, has a historic centre of more than two thousand buildings covered in glazed tiles, baroque carving and bright paint, and UNESCO listed it in 1987. The street plan is a tidy grid around a large main square, the Zócalo, with a cathedral whose towers are among the tallest in the country. The ceramics called Talavera, white and blue earthenware painted with flowers, decorate churches, kitchens and fountains, and workshops in the city still make them by hand.

Two volcanoes tower over the town, and when the air is clear, you can see them from the streets. Popocatépetl, which is active and sometimes sends up a plume of ash, and Iztaccíhuatl, whose long ridge is said to resemble a sleeping woman, form the horizon to the west. The great pyramid at Cholula, a short drive away, is the largest in the world by volume, though from outside it looks like a grassy hill with a small church on top. The Spanish built the church deliberately over the sacred site.

Puebla has a distinct place in Mexican history and cuisine. On 5 May 1862, a smaller Mexican force defeated the French army outside the city, the battle celebrated as Cinco de Mayo. In the kitchen, the city claims mole poblano, a dark sauce of chilli, spices and chocolate, and chiles en nogada, stuffed green chillies in a walnut cream sauce topped with pomegranate seeds, the colours of the Mexican flag. The convent of Santa Mónica and its sweets, and the Biblioteca Palafoxiana, one of the oldest libraries in the Americas, are well worth the visit.

For riders, the roads leading out of Puebla include fast toll highways, called cuotas, and slower free roads, called libres, which wind through villages. Toll roads are quicker and better maintained, but they cost money, and the free roads have topes, speed bumps, that appear without warning. Fuel is easy to find in the city. The rainy season, from June to September, brings afternoon storms. Keep an eye out for ash, which can make the road slippery.
t.rila monastery complex@42.1,23.3:
Rila Monastery sits at around eleven hundred metres in a forested valley of the Rila mountains, the highest range in the Balkans, where Musala at nearly three thousand metres stands above all the peaks of south-eastern Europe. The monastery lies at the end of a long road that follows the Rilska river upstream through beech and spruce, and the approach feels like going back in time. Mist hangs in the trees, the air smells of resin, and the river noise grows louder as you climb.

The founder was Ivan of Rila, a hermit who lived in a cave in the tenth century and was revered for his holiness, and after his death a community grew around his memory. Through centuries of Ottoman rule, the monastery kept alive Bulgarian language, writing and faith, and it is often described as the spiritual heart of the nation. A fire in 1833 destroyed most of the old buildings, and the present monastery was built in the following decades, with the great church and its richly painted porches covered in frescoes of saints, demons and angels by the painter Zahari Zograf and others. Only a stout stone tower from the fourteenth century survived the fire, and it still stands in the courtyard.

The courtyard is the thing. Four wings of arcaded galleries in black and white striped stone enclose the central church, with wooden balconies on several levels and a hundred or so small monastic cells. UNESCO recognised it in 1983. Visit early or late if you can, because the coach parties arrive in mid-morning and the place changes with the crowds. Sample the mekitsi, warm fried dough sold at stalls near the entrance, preferably with jam or white cheese.

The ride to and from the monastery is a pleasure, with a smooth, curving road through the forest, tight enough to require attention without being difficult. Fog and wet leaves can make it slippery, and in winter snow closes the upper sections occasionally. Rila town, about seventeen kilometres away, offers basic supplies, and Dupnitsa, twenty-four kilometres off, has a larger choice of fuel stations and shops. The monastery has simple rooms for visitors if you want to stay the night, which is the best way to hear the bells in the morning mist.
t.paimio sanatorium@60.5,22.7:
In the early 1930s, Finland needed a hospital for tuberculosis, and the architect Alvar Aalto won the competition to design it. The Paimio Sanatorium, finished in 1933, is one of the landmarks of modern architecture, a white, functionalist building set among pines on a ridge, in which every detail was designed to help the patient recover. Rooms faced south to catch the sun, windows were large, floors were coloured to calm the eye, and basins were shaped to make noise as little as possible so that the person in the next bed would not be disturbed. Aalto thought of the building as a medical instrument.

He also designed the furniture, and the Paimio chair, a lounge chair of bent birch plywood, was made for patients, whose breathing, it was thought, would be helped by the angle of the seat. It became a classic of twentieth-century design and is still produced. The sanatorium stopped treating tuberculosis when drugs made it curable, and now serves as a hospital, but parts of it are open for tours. A visit shows the stairwell with its yellow floor, the long sunbathing terraces and the dining room, and the whole building feels strikingly fresh for its age.

The ride goes on to Villa Mairea, another Aalto building, a private house in Noormarkku built a few years later, with a mix of wood, stone and white plaster that points toward his later style. The road from Paimio runs through southwestern Finland, a landscape of fields, spruce forest and lakes, with red wooden farmhouses and very little traffic. Surfaces are smooth, speed limits are strictly enforced, and elk and deer are a real hazard, particularly at dusk and dawn. In high summer, the light lasts almost all night, and in winter, you should not be on a bike at all.

Paimio has just over ten thousand people, with fuel and supermarkets, and the larger city of Turku lies about thirty kilometres to the south-west, with a medieval castle and a cathedral. Local food includes salmon soup, rye bread and cinnamon buns, and a coffee break is a national institution, called kahvitauko. The best months are June to August, with warm days and long evenings, and September has crisp, clear air. Check the rules for tyres in winter, and carry a warm layer even in summer, because the weather can turn cool.
t.oaxaca@17.1,-96.7:
Oaxaca sits in a high valley in southern Mexico, at about 1,500 metres, with mountains on every side and an old city at its centre that feels more like a village in its pace. The Zapotec and Mixtec peoples have lived in this region for thousands of years, and their influence is still strong, with a number of indigenous languages spoken and local crafts such as woven rugs, black clay pottery and carved wooden animals sold in the markets. The Spanish added churches and convents, and the cathedral and Santo Domingo, with its gilded interior, are among the finest in the country.

Food is the great draw. Oaxaca is known as the land of seven moles, rich sauces made with chilli, chocolate, nuts and spices, and of tlayudas, huge crisp tortillas piled with beans, cheese and meat. Chapulines, roasted grasshoppers seasoned with lime and chilli, are a snack you will see in every market. Mezcal, the smoky agave spirit, is made in the villages around the valley, and tasting rooms in town let you sample the different kinds.

For riders, the city is a base for day trips into the valleys. The ride east toward Yagul and Mitla follows the highway through farming country, with agave fields, small towns and stalls selling mezcal and cheese. Mitla is known for its stone mosaic fretwork, and Yagul, on a hilltop, has a ball court and a view across the valley. Nearby there are caves with some of the oldest evidence of agriculture in the Americas. The roads are mostly paved and in decent shape, but potholes, speed bumps and livestock are common, and it is wise to avoid riding after dark.

Oaxaca city has fuel and every sort of service, and the villages along the main roads have stations too. In the mountains beyond, the road to the coast is long and twisting, with limited services, so fill the tank and check conditions before setting out.

The best season is the dry months, from roughly October to May. During the rainy season, afternoons bring storms and the roads can be slick. Early evening in the zócalo, with music, balloons and a table at an open cafe, is a good way to end a day.
t.plovdiv@42.1,24.8:
Plovdiv has been lived in for about six thousand years, which makes it one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in Europe, and it wears the age lightly. The city sits on the plain of the Maritsa river in the middle of southern Bulgaria, built around a cluster of rocky hills that rise out of the flat ground like islands. Locals talk about the seven hills, though one was quarried away long ago. Philip of Macedon took it in the fourth century BC and gave it the name Philippopolis, and the Romans later made it an important city on the road from Belgrade to Constantinople.

The Roman theatre, built under Trajan in the second century AD, is still used for concerts, and it faces out over the plain through a gap between hills. Above it the Old Town climbs in a jumble of cobbled lanes, Ottoman-era houses with overhanging upper floors, painted in strong colours, and tiny galleries. Down in the flat centre, a long pedestrian street leads past the remains of the Roman stadium, which lies partly beneath the shopping street. The Kapana district, a tangle of narrow streets that was rebuilt from a run-down craft quarter, is full of cafes, bars and small workshops. Plovdiv was European Capital of Culture in 2019.

For a motorcyclist, Plovdiv is a useful, easy city. About three hundred and forty thousand people live here, so there is fuel on every approach road, plenty of garages, and wide boulevards. The ride begins when you leave. To the south, the Rhodope Mountains rise quickly above Asenovgrad, with the ruined fortress of Asen in a gorge and lovely, twisting roads through beech forest. To the north, the Rose Valley and the Stara Planina ranges open up towards the Central Balkan, a longer ride with more mountain.

For dinner, order a shopska salad of tomato, cucumber and white cheese, grilled kebapche, a plate of banitsa, and a small glass of rakia to start. Prices are modest by western standards. Summer is hot, with temperatures often in the mid thirties, so start early and be off the plain by midday. Late spring, when the roses bloom, and early autumn offer the best mix of light and cool air. Drivers can be impatient and overtake in interesting places, so keep your eyes on the mirrors.
t.bansko@41.8,23.5:
Bansko lies at the foot of the Pirin Mountains in south-west Bulgaria, at the northern end of the Razlog valley, and the first sight of it is the wall behind: Pirin's jagged limestone peaks, climbing to Vihren at 2,914 metres, the second-highest mountain in the country after Musala. The range is a national park and a UNESCO site, and its high lakes, dwarf pine and rare Bosnian pine hold some of the most unspoiled alpine country in the Balkans. Winter brings snow from December well into spring, and Bansko is one of the busiest ski resorts in Bulgaria, with a gondola that runs from the edge of town.

The old town is surprisingly pretty for a place that has grown so fast. Behind the new hotels, the narrow cobbled lanes still hold stone houses with heavy wooden doors, high walls and slate roofs built in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, when Bansko was a prosperous trading and craft town. Traditional taverns known as mehanas have low beams, open fires and walls hung with rugs, and the poet Nikola Vaptsarov was born in the town in 1909. The Holy Trinity church, with its thick walls and sunken floor, was built low so as not to offend Ottoman rulers who banned tall Christian buildings.

For a rider, Bansko makes a good base. Razlog, the larger neighbour, has fuel and supermarkets, and there are stations on the road in and out of Bansko itself. The road south over the Predel pass, at roughly 1,100 metres, leads to Gotse Delchev and the Rhodopes, with good curves and views over the Pirin. In summer, the air is cool at altitude, but thunderstorms build over the peaks in the afternoon, so aim to be down by then. Watch for potholes, tractors, and the occasional horse cart.

Eat in a mehana: kapama, a slow-cooked stew of meats and cabbage; banitsa with cheese; and the local cured sausage the town is known for, washed down with red wine from the Struma valley. Summer and early autumn are best, when the days are long, the meadows are green and the air smells of pine and woodsmoke. Come in winter only if you plan to ski, since the passes can be icy and the best roads close.
t.clinton oklahoma@35.5,-99.0:
Clinton sits in western Oklahoma on the old road that Americans called the Mother Road, and the town has leaned into that fact. The Oklahoma Route 66 Museum is here, laid out decade by decade from the road's birth in 1926 through the Dust Bowl, the migration west that John Steinbeck wrote about, and the postwar boom of motels and neon. For someone about to ride the same alignment, it works as a good briefing before the miles start. The Washita River runs just to the south, and the land around is red soil, wheat, cattle and wind.

The riding on this stretch is a lesson in patience. The old road runs flat and often straight, sometimes beside the interstate and sometimes drifting off into wheat fields, with concrete slabs patched in a dozen eras and the occasional faded sign for a long-gone diner. What you get is space: big skies, long horizons, grain elevators rising from the plain like cathedrals, and in spring the threat of storms that can be seen from fifty kilometres away. Crosswinds are often strong, so brace for them on the open sections, and avoid the tornado-prone afternoons of May if you can.

Clinton has nearly ten thousand people, which means fuel, motels and diners are all easy. Weatherford, a little over twenty kilometres to the east, is another option, and farther west Elk City carries on the Route 66 theme with its own museum. Mornings are cool even in summer, but by midday the heat on the plains can be fierce, so carry water and keep an eye on the gauges between towns. The distances between services are not wild, but the landscape makes them feel longer.

Stop for a burger and a milkshake, because the road demands it. The sort of place that survives on this highway tends to be family-run and unhurried, and the people behind the counter will often ask where you are headed before you have sat down. Westward lie the Texas Panhandle and the New Mexican mesas, and the road keeps changing as it goes.
t.umea@63.8,20.3:
Umeå is the kind of city you do not expect at sixty-four degrees north: young, bookish and full of bicycles. About eighty thousand people live here on the Ume river, a number swelled by a big university and a hospital, and the average age is low enough that cafés and bars stay busy long after you think a northern town should have gone to bed. In summer the sun barely drops and the evenings feel endless; in midwinter it is the reverse, and the whole place leans on candles, saunas and coffee.

The city was devastated by fire in 1888, and the wide boulevards lined with birch trees are the result. Planners made the streets broad to act as firebreaks and planted rows of birches along them, which is why Umeå calls itself the City of Birches. It was a European Capital of Culture in 2014, and the Sami heritage of the region got far more attention than before, with exhibitions and events on the indigenous people of the north. The Västerbotten Museum and the nearby open-air museum are the places to learn more.

For riders the surroundings are gentle. The Blue Highway runs from here toward the Norwegian coast, following the river inland through forest, farmland and the occasional lake, a long, steady road with few real corners and a lot of space. In the other direction the coast leads to the Kvarken Archipelago, shared with Finland and recognised by UNESCO for its remarkable geology. The land here is still rising from the sea after the last ice age, at nearly a centimetre a year, and the shoreline slowly changes shape, creating shallow bays, boulder fields and new islands. You can see it on the maps and, with luck, in the reeds.

Practicalities are easy. Umeå has fuel at every size of station, supermarkets, repair shops and a good variety of restaurants, including the local speciality of reindeer, usually served as a rich stew or thinly sliced with potatoes and lingonberries. Cinnamon buns are a Swedish institution, and the coffee break known as fika is something to take seriously.

Ride here in the long light between late May and August, or in September when the forest turns yellow and the air smells of mushrooms. Reindeer and elk wander onto roads, especially at dusk, so stay alert and keep speeds sensible after dark.
t.tulsa@36.2,-96.0:
Tulsa grew rich on oil, and it still carries the confidence of a city that once called itself the Oil Capital of the World. In the 1920s the fields around it produced fortunes, and the money went into buildings, so that the downtown skyline is one of the best collections of Art Deco architecture in the United States, with ornate towers and a church, Boston Avenue Methodist, that looks like a cathedral from the future. A seventy-six-foot statue of an oil driller, built for an exposition and known as the Golden Driller, stands on the fairgrounds with one hand on a derrick, and the locals love him.

Route 66 runs through the middle of the city, and Tulsa has a fair claim to be one of its capitals. Cyrus Avery, a local businessman, helped create the highway in the 1920s and is called the Father of Route 66, and a memorial bridge named after him spans the Arkansas River on the west side of town. Old motels, neon signs and diners are scattered along 11th Street, among them the Meadow Gold sign, a restored glowing relic. To the east, in Catoosa, the Blue Whale, a smiling concrete whale with a pond, was built in the 1970s by a man as a gift for his wife and has become one of the road's best-loved oddities.

There is a darker chapter, too. In 1921 a white mob attacked the Greenwood district, a prosperous Black neighbourhood known as Black Wall Street, killing many people and burning more than a thousand homes and businesses in what is now recognised as the Tulsa Race Massacre. Greenwood Rising, a history centre opened in 2021, tells the story, and a visit is a sobering but necessary part of understanding the city.

As a rider, you will find Tulsa an easy city to cross, with wide streets, good surfaces and plenty of fuel at every junction. The old road leaves on the east side and heads toward Catoosa, Claremore and the rolling green hills of Oklahoma. Summer is hot and stormy, with tornado warnings in spring, so keep an eye on the weather. Eat barbecue or a chicken-fried steak, and enjoy the slower pace. The Gilcrease and Philbrook museums are among the best in the region, and both are worth an hour if a rest day arrives.
t.vikos gorge@40.0,20.7:
Vikos is a gorge that people struggle to describe without numbers. It runs for about twelve kilometres through the limestone of the Zagori in Epirus, in north-west Greece, with walls that in places drop nearly a thousand metres from rim to river, and it has been listed in the Guinness book as the deepest gorge in the world in proportion to its width. A road cannot take you into it, but the viewpoints on the rim, near Monodendri and Vikos village, do the job well, with the stone walls falling away into a green shadow.

The best-known viewpoint is the one called Oxya, just outside Monodendri, where a short path leads to a rocky platform over the abyss. The view runs down the length of the canyon, with the pale cliffs, the dark forest on the floor and the high peaks of the Tymfi range beyond. A little further on, the Beloi viewpoint looks out over the gorge from the other side. Both are best early, when the light is soft and the clouds are low, and the mist in the canyon can be dramatic after rain. Stay behind the barriers, as the drops are sheer.

The villages around the gorge are the other attraction. Zagori has forty-odd stone villages, with slate roofs, cobbled lanes and arched stone bridges built by local masons in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, when the region was wealthy from trade. The bridges, such as the three-arched Kokkori bridge, are beautiful and many are still in use. Monodendri has a handsome monastery perched on the rim, from which a path descends to the bottom of the gorge.

The roads here are twisty, narrow and often rough, with steep climbs and tight corners, and fog or rain can arrive quickly, so ride carefully. Fuel is not available in the small villages, so fill up in Ioannina, the large lakeside city about thirty kilometres away, or in Konitsa to the north. Cafés and tavernas in Monodendri and Vikos serve grilled meat, local pies and cheese. Summer is dry and warm, but the nights are cool, and autumn colours are superb.
t.papingo@40.0,20.7:
Papingo is two villages, really, the big one and the little one, climbing the foot of the Tymfi massif in the Zagori, where the stone houses and slate roofs seem to grow out of the mountain. Above them, a wall of grey limestone rises to Astraka and the ridge that reaches nearly two and a half thousand metres, and the cliffs catch the last light in the evening in a way that makes people stop in the street. It is a very quiet place, with a few guesthouses and tavernas, and the sound of water running somewhere.

That water is a feature. Below the village, a stream called the Rogovo runs through a series of clear rock pools, cold enough to take your breath away, and in summer people walk down from the village to swim. The pools are small and shallow, and the water is snowmelt, so a dip is more of a shock than a swim, but it is wonderful after a hot ride. The area is part of the Vikos-Aoos National Park, which is home to brown bears, wolves, chamois and many birds of prey, though you are unlikely to see them from the road.

The road up to Papingo is a good one for riders, with a long winding climb through oak and plane woods, tight bends and a few hairpins, and a surface that is mostly decent but narrow. The traffic is light, apart from the odd local car and the animals, but the road is steep and there are drops, so keep to the right. The last stretch into the village is cobbled in places, which can be slippery after rain, so park at the edge and walk in.

Fuel is not available in the village, so fill up in Konitsa, about ten kilometres away, or in Ioannina, thirty-odd kilometres further. The tavernas serve local food, with pies, grilled lamb, wild greens and sheep cheese, and the guesthouses are warm and simple. Mountain weather changes fast, so bring a waterproof, and in spring and autumn pack a warm layer, as the nights can be cold, even in a stone-walled room.
t.golubac@44.7,21.6:
Golubac fortress looks like something drawn by a child who loved castles: nine towers of different heights, tumbling down a rock to the water's edge, with a harbour wall and a great arched gate in front. It stands where the Danube, having crossed the wide Pannonian plain, narrows suddenly into the gorges of the Iron Gates, and for centuries whoever held it controlled river traffic. Hungarians, Serbs and Ottomans fought over it repeatedly in the fourteenth and fifteenth centuries, and it changed hands more than once. After a long restoration it reopened to visitors in the 2010s, and you can now walk the ramparts and climb the towers.

The village itself is tiny, perhaps sixteen hundred people, and the nearest large town is across the river in Romania. On the Serbian side, Veliko Gradište is the sensible place for fuel and supplies, so fill the tank there before you start along the river road. A local legend explains the swarms of tiny black flies that sometimes plague this stretch in early summer: the Golubac fly is said to have been born from the blood of a dragon killed by Saint George in a nearby cave. Whatever the origin, the flies are real, so carry a visor wipe in late spring.

The ride along the Danube from here is one of the best in the Balkans. The road hugs the river, tunnelling through limestone in places, with the Romanian bank rising steeply on the other side and the water sliding past wide and green. Curves are gentle and fast, the surface is generally good, and the traffic is light outside the summer weekends. The Djerdap National Park protects the gorge, with its griffon vultures, lynx, and oak and beech forests, and the air feels cleaner here than in the plain.

Weather matters. In winter the river fog is thick and the road can be icy, and in summer the afternoon sun beats on the cliffs. Autumn is probably the best season, with golden light and few other visitors. The view of the fortress from the road, as you come round the bend with the river below, is worth stopping for, so pull over safely. Cafes near the entrance serve strong coffee, grilled fish from the Danube, and rakija, the plum brandy that Serbs drink with ceremony.
t.donji milanovac@44.5,22.2:
Donji Milanovac is a young town in an ancient place. The old village of the same name, along with several others, was drowned in 1972 when the Iron Gates dam raised the Danube by many metres, and a new town was built on the high ground a few years earlier to take the displaced people. It is a tidy, planned place of about two and a half thousand, laid out around a wide bay, with a promenade, a small port and a clutch of cafes where fishermen and tourists sit side by side. Majdanpek, the nearest larger town, is up in the hills, and across the river lie the Romanian villages of the Banat.

The area is a treasure house for anyone interested in the deep past. A short way upstream lies Lepenski Vir, a prehistoric settlement dating back some eight thousand years, where the people who lived here carved heavy boulders into the likeness of fish-headed figures, among the oldest monumental sculpture in Europe. A museum now protects the site, and it was moved to higher ground to save it from the flood. Downriver, cut into the cliff above the water, runs a Roman road, and there you can still see a stone tablet, the Tabula Traiana, which commemorates the emperor Trajan's engineering of the passage around the year 100.

On the Romanian bank, a few kilometres downstream, an enormous face has been carved into the rock, depicting Decebalus, the last king of the Dacians, who resisted Trajan. It was finished in the early 2000s and can be seen clearly from the Serbian road or from a boat. The Danube at the Iron Gates is a place where ancient emperors and modern engineers have both left their marks.

The road from here to Golubac, and eastward toward Kladovo, is some of the finest riding in the region. It is mostly smooth, with wide curves and tunnels, and it runs close to the river for long stretches. In midsummer it is hot and quiet. In spring and autumn the hills are green or gold. Fuel is available in town, but do not rely on stations in the villages. Grilled river fish, fresh bread and local wine are the order of the day, and the sunset over the gorge is a fine way to end it.
t.kladovo@44.6,22.6:
The Danube here is squeezed through a gorge between the Carpathians and the Balkans, and the result is one of the great river landscapes of Europe. The Iron Gates, called Porțile de Fier in Romanian and Đerdap in Serbian, run for about a hundred kilometres, with cliffs rising steeply on both sides and the water flowing wide and slow. The coordinates here are on the Romanian bank, near Drobeta-Turnu Severin, and Kladovo is the Serbian town opposite, just across the river.

The history is old and dramatic. In AD 105 the Roman emperor Trajan ordered a bridge to be built across the Danube here, designed by the architect Apollodorus of Damascus, a wooden-decked structure on stone piers that was the longest bridge in the world for a thousand years. Its stone piers can still be seen at low water, and the ruins of the Roman fort at Drobeta are in the town. Nearby, on the Serbian side, a rock plaque, the Tabula Traiana, commemorates the building of the road along the gorge. On the Romanian side, a gigantic face of the Dacian king Decebalus, about forty metres high, is carved into the rock, finished in 2004, a modern monument to an ancient enemy.

In 1972, a huge hydroelectric dam, built jointly by Romania and Yugoslavia, closed the gorge and raised the water, drowning rapids, villages and the island of Ada Kaleh, a small Turkish community. The dam carries a road across the river, with a border crossing, so you can cross between the two countries on the wall itself, and passport checks are required.

Riding along the Danube on either side is a pleasure. The Romanian road, the DN57, hugs the cliffs with bends, tunnels and views of the water, and the surface is generally good, though rockfall and slow trucks are common. On the Serbian side, the road is also winding, with similar views. In summer, the heat is strong, and fog can lie over the river in the mornings. Expect border queues at the dam in high season.

Fuel is easy in Drobeta-Turnu Severin, with several stations and plenty of places to eat, and it is a good place to fill up before the gorge, since villages along the road are small. Try the fresh Danube fish, grilled or in a soup.

Go in the morning, when mist lies on the water and the cliffs emerge slowly into the light.
t.oklahoma city@35.5,-97.5:
Oklahoma City was born in a single afternoon. On the twenty-second of April 1889, at noon, thousands of settlers lined up on the edge of the Unassigned Lands and, at the sound of a gunshot, raced in on horses, wagons and on foot to stake claims, and by nightfall a tent city of ten thousand people had grown on the prairie where the city now stands. The Land Run, as it is called, left a legacy of improvisation and optimism that the place has never lost. Today it is a sprawling state capital of more than six hundred thousand people, with a lively downtown, a canal in the old Bricktown warehouse district and an energy that surprises visitors who expect a quiet prairie town.

Oil is part of the story, and the state capitol is the only one in the country, I believe, with a working oil well on its grounds, a nod to the wealth that poured out of the earth in the early twentieth century. The Stockyards City district, with its cowboy boot shops, saddlers and steakhouses, is the heart of the cattle trade, and the livestock auction on Mondays and Tuesdays is still a real working event. A different kind of memory is held at the national memorial to the 1995 bombing, where an empty chair for each of the victims stands on a quiet lawn beside a reflecting pool, and it is a place of silence and respect.

Route 66 runs through the city, along streets that were once the main road west, and a good number of the old motels, diners and neon signs survive. A short ride north-east takes you to the Round Barn at Arcadia, a handsome red barn built in 1898 and now a museum, and the towns beyond have their share of vintage gas stations and soda fountains. The ride across the plains from here is wide and open, with big skies and long views.

Fuel and food are everywhere, and the city has a thriving food scene, from barbecue and chicken-fried steak to Vietnamese soup. Wind is a constant, often strong and gusty, and summer heat can be fierce, so start early. Spring brings thunderstorms and, now and then, tornadoes, so check the forecast. Be sure to allow time for the memorial, and for a long, slow dinner.
t.velingrad@42.0,24.0:
Velingrad lies in a wide basin in the western Rhodope, with wooded ridges rising on every side and the high Rila range just across the valley to the north. It is a young town by Balkan standards: it was formed in 1948 by joining three older settlements, Chepino, Lade and Kamenitsa, and it takes its name from Vela Blagoeva, a teacher and socialist activist. What really defines it is water. Dozens of mineral springs bubble up here, hot and cool, and Velingrad styles itself the spa capital of the Balkans.

Hotels with outdoor pools and spa treatments line the streets, and the town park has fountains and a small lake where Bulgarians come to rest for a week at a time. There is little to see in the way of ancient monuments; the pleasure is in the pace. Hot mineral baths, a plate of grilled meat and a glass of local wine make a restorative way to end a hard day on the road.

For riders, the area around Velingrad is a delight. Roads climb into the Rhodope through beech and spruce forest, winding past reservoirs and little villages with stone-roofed houses. The famous routes lead south to Dospat and the Trigrad Gorge, and west towards Batak, with a rolling character: not extreme, but with beautiful, flowing bends and wide views. Surfaces vary from smooth to broken, and cows and shepherds may share the road, so keep an eye on the blind corners.

Fuel is easy in a town of twenty-four thousand, and Rakitovo, a few kilometres away, is another option. In the mountain villages stations are rare, so fill up before leaving. Summers are warm and fresh at altitude; spring and autumn offer colour and cooler air. Winter snow arrives early on the higher passes.

Try local specialities like banitsa, the flaky cheese pastry, and kavarma, a slow-cooked stew of meat and vegetables in a clay pot.
t.vidin@44.0,22.9:
Vidin sits on the south bank of the Danube in the far north-west corner of Bulgaria, where the river forms the border with Romania and the plain stretches flat to the horizon. The city of fifty-odd thousand is quiet and a little worn, but its position on the river made it a significant stronghold for centuries, and the proof is Baba Vida, a squat medieval fortress with thick walls and round towers that stands right at the water's edge. It dates from the Middle Ages, was strengthened under Bulgarian tsars and Ottoman rulers, and is among the best-preserved castles in the country. Legend says it is named for a princess who defended it, though the story is surely tidier than the truth.

The Ottoman centuries left other traces: a mosque and a library with a lovely courtyard, and a handsome synagogue that testifies to the Jewish community which once thrived here. In the late eighteenth century a rebellious local pasha, Osman Pazvantoğlu, defied the sultan from Vidin for years and made the city his private capital.

For the rider, Vidin is mostly about the Danube and the open country, rather than technical corners. The roads across the plain are straight and sometimes rough, particularly in the countryside, and you should watch for potholes and farm vehicles. But the mountains of the Stara Planina rise to the south, and the approach roads that climb into them offer winding bends, empty tarmac and the pleasure of forest silence.

The Danube Bridge 2, opened in 2013, connects Vidin with Calafat in Romania, making this a handy crossing between countries. Fuel stations are plentiful in town and on the approach roads, and along the river promenade you can find cafes serving grilled fish, shopska salad and the local rakia.

Come in late spring or early autumn. Midsummer is hot, and winter brings fog and cold winds off the river.
t.korce@40.6,20.8:
Korçë stands on a high plain in south-eastern Albania, about eight hundred and fifty metres above the sea, with bare mountains on every side. The air is cooler and drier here than on the coast, the winters are hard, and the town has a different feel from the rest of the country: tree-lined boulevards, old two-storey houses with iron balconies, and a sense of refinement that older Albanians still call the Paris of Albania, only partly joking. It was an important commercial and cultural centre in the late Ottoman period, and merchants who grew rich abroad built handsome homes here.

The town's cultural weight is real. In 1887 the first Albanian-language school was opened in Korçë, at a time when teaching in Albanian was forbidden, and the building is now a museum of education. The big Orthodox cathedral, rebuilt in the 1990s after being destroyed in the communist period, dominates the centre, and the old bazaar, with its low shops and cobbled lanes, still operates. The serenades that once echoed in the evening streets are part of local memory, and the town is known for good food, beer and a love of music.

Korçë's beer, brewed here since the 1920s, is the national favourite, and you can sample it at the terraces that fill the main boulevards in the evening. Grilled meatballs called qofte, local sausages, and stuffed vegetables are common on menus.

For riders, the area is a good base. The road to the lake at Pogradec crosses a pass and offers views over Lake Ohrid, while the mountain roads south toward Ersekë and the Greek border pass through high pastures and villages with stone houses. Surfaces vary a lot, and you should expect potholes, livestock and the occasional slow truck. Traffic in the city is chaotic, with plenty of horn-blowing, so approach with patience.

Fuel is easy, since Korçë is a town of nearly sixty thousand with several stations. In winter, snow and ice make mountain passes challenging, so aim for May to October.
t.pogradec@40.9,20.7:
Pogradec lies at the south-western corner of Lake Ohrid, with mountains rising steeply behind and the water stretching away toward North Macedonia. Ohrid is one of the oldest lakes in Europe, deep and very clear, and it holds fish found nowhere else, including a famous species of trout. The lake is shared between Albania and North Macedonia, and the border runs through the middle of the water, so from the Pogradec promenade you can see the opposite shore on a clear day, with its lights twinkling after dark.

The town itself was a sleepy lakeside spot, and now has a long boulevard lined with cafes, a pebble beach, and hotels that fill up in July and August when Albanians and Kosovars come to cool off. There is not a lot of formal history to see, though a short ride to the Lin peninsula brings you to the remains of an early Christian church with mosaic floors, built in the sixth century, and the village there has a lovely, quiet setting among olive trees.

For a rider, the pleasure is in the setting and the road around the lake. A route along the shore toward Tushemisht passes springs bubbling out of the rock, then climbs into the hills with views across the water, and the road toward Korçë climbs through oak woods and farmland with some smooth, curving stretches. Surfaces vary, and cars can be unpredictable, so keep a margin on blind corners. Much of the traffic is light outside the high summer.

Pogradec has all the fuel and food you need, with stations around the edge of town and plenty of cafes serving grilled fish. A cold beer and a plate of fresh fish on the waterfront is a fine ending to the day.

The best months are May, June and September, when the water is warm, the air is clear and the crowds are smaller.
t.konitsa@40.0,20.8:
A single stone arch, about forty metres wide, crosses the Aoos river just outside Konitsa, and it is one of the finest bridges in the Balkans. It dates from 1823, in the last Ottoman decades of Epirus, and for two centuries it has stood over a green river with high mountains beyond. The bridge looks fragile, but it has survived floods, wars and earthquakes, and in the summer, local youths dive from its parapet into the cool water, a tradition more frightening to watch than to do.

The town stands at the junction of the Aoos and Voidomatis valleys, a few kilometres from the Albanian border, in a green basin ringed by mountains. Above it rises Smolikas, at 2,637 metres the second-highest mountain in Greece after Olympus, and one of the least visited. Its slopes are covered in beech and fir, with an alpine lake, Drakolimni, or Dragon Lake, near the summit, home to a rare species of alpine newt. A second ridge, Gamila, stands to the north-east, with its jagged limestone peaks. This is a landscape of dramatic scale and sharp light.

Konitsa itself is a working town, with a main square, a few cafés and tavernas, and small hotels that cater to rafters, hikers and the occasional motorcyclist. The Aoos is a popular river for rafting and canoeing in spring, when snowmelt swells the flow. Local cuisine features lamb, goat, trout and cheeses, and the pies of Epirus, thin pastry layered with greens, leeks or cheese, are a highlight.

Riding to Konitsa from Ioannina takes you along the Aoos valley, with a good surface and long, flowing curves, and the views of the mountains grow with every kilometre. The road is quiet, though trucks from the border may slow progress. Beyond the town, a narrow road climbs toward the mountain villages of Smolikas, such as Pades and Palaioseli, where the asphalt can be rough and the bends tight. Weather in the Pindus can be unpredictable, with sudden thunderstorms in summer and heavy snow in winter, so check conditions before you set out. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, and the autumn colours are particularly fine.

Konitsa has fuel stations, supermarkets, banks and pharmacies, and is the best place for services before heading into the mountains. Ioannina, about forty kilometres to the south, is the nearest large city. A coffee in the square and a walk to the bridge in the evening, when the stone glows in the last light, is a pleasant way to finish the day.
t.skopje@42.0,21.4:
Skopje lies in the valley of the Vardar river, ringed by mountains, and it is a city that was knocked down and rebuilt in living memory. In July 1963, a powerful earthquake destroyed most of it, killing over a thousand people, and the international response was large; Kenzo Tange, the Japanese architect, drew up a reconstruction plan. The result is a strange mix of Ottoman old town, brutalist concrete and, in recent years, an expensive programme of neoclassical buildings and statues in the centre. Nearly half a million people live in the city, so fuel and services are plentiful.

The Old Bazaar is the best part, one of the largest surviving Ottoman bazaars in the Balkans, with narrow lanes, copper workers, tea houses and mosques. The stone bridge over the Vardar dates from the fifteenth century, though it has been repaired, and the Kale fortress above the river has a long view. Mother Teresa was born in Skopje in 1910, and there is a memorial house to her. Macedonian food is rich and tasty: tavče gravče, baked beans in a clay pot, shopska salad with sheep's cheese, and grilled kebapi with flatbread.

For a ride, Skopje is a good starting point for the mountains to the west. The road leads toward Tetovo, then climbs into the Mavrovo National Park, with the huge Mavrovo reservoir and the peaks of the Šar and Korab ranges. The surface is variable, with good main roads and rougher secondary ones, and drivers are fast and imaginative. Traffic in the city is heavy, so leave early. The air in winter can be badly polluted, as in many Balkan cities, so the best seasons for riding are spring and autumn.

North Macedonia has a long history of settlement; the lakes and mountains are among the oldest in Europe, and the region has many Byzantine churches with remarkable frescoes. Galičnik, a mountain village on the route, is famous for its traditional wedding festival held each July. Fill the tank in Skopje and bring water and snacks, as the roads into the mountains are quiet. The route is a lovely contrast to the busy capital.
t.mavrovo@41.7,20.7:
Mavrovo is the name of a lake, a village, and a very large national park, and the three overlap in a way that confuses everybody for the first ten minutes. The park is the biggest in North Macedonia, a block of high ranges along the Albanian border including Korab, the country's top peak, and the Radika river collects most of its water. The reservoir was built in the 1950s to feed a hydropower scheme, and it covered a church. The bell tower of St Nikola still stands in the lake when the water is low, a little stone drowned thing that has become the emblem of the place, and it is the picture you will see on every postcard in the region.

The approach from the east climbs out of the Polog valley through gorges and beech woods, and the road is easy riding: good surface, long bends, a few switchbacks, and traffic that thins out the higher you go. Weather is the main thing to respect. The valley can be hot and still and the lake shore can be cool, with a wind that comes straight off the water. In winter the village turns into a ski resort, and chains and snow tyres are the norm from late autumn. In summer it empties out to a few walkers and fishermen.

The park shelters brown bear and wolf, and the Balkan lynx, a rare animal and a point of real national pride, lives in these mountains in small numbers. You will not see one. What you might see are shepherds and their big white dogs, and it is wise to give those dogs a wide, calm berth if the flock is near the road. The beech forests in October burn orange and gold, and that is when I would ride it if I could pick.

For practical purposes, Rostuša and Gostivar are the bigger centres for fuel and shopping, and the village itself has a few small hotels, cafés and a restaurant or two near the shore. Order trout or lamb, the bread is baked fresh, and the sheep cheese is salty and good. The side road towards Galičnik leaves close by, and it deserves its detour.
t.galicnik@41.6,20.7:
Galičnik hangs on a mountain shoulder at around 1,400 metres, high above the Radika valley, and the road up to it is a winding, narrow affair that keeps you honest. The surface is tarmac but not always smooth, there are tight bends where two cars have to negotiate, and in places the drop is serious. Rostuša, in the valley below, is the nearest town to speak of, and once you commit to the climb there is no turning back for coffee. Most of the village is stone houses with wooden balconies and slate or stone roofs, cut into the steep slope and facing out over a big, wild view.

Few villages in the Balkans have as much to say as this one. It was famous for its stonemasons and builders, the Mijaks, men who left their homes for much of the year to work across the Balkans, building churches and houses in other people's towns, and sending money back to the families they had left. Most of Galičnik's year-round population is gone now, and many of the old houses are used as summer homes. Once a year in July the village fills up again for the Galičnik Wedding, a traditional festival in which a couple are married in the old village costume with music and dancing, and the whole place turns into a slow, happy crowd. It is worth planning around if you can.

The village also gives its name to a white sheep's cheese, brined and firm, which you can find in small shops and on restaurant tables across the country. Eat some with bread and a green pepper, and drink something cold with it. Cafés open and close with the tourist season, and that goes for the little restaurants too, so do not count on a hot meal in the shoulder months.

Fuel is not available in the village. Rostuša is five kilometres below, and Debar, the bigger town on the way to the Albanian border, is thirteen kilometres away. The road is a dead end, so you ride back down the way you came, which is no hardship: the descent shows you the valley in a way the climb never lets you look.
t.vanino@49.1,140.3:
Vanino is where the Baikal-Amur Mainline meets the sea. The railway, built across thousands of kilometres of permafrost, swamp and mountain, finishes here on the Tatar Strait, and the port town of around eighteen thousand people is arranged around the idea of loading things onto ships: coal, timber, containers, and at the quay a railway ferry that links Vanino to Kholmsk on Sakhalin. The ferry has been the island's lifeline since the 1970s and it gives the dock district a restless, working feel.

The name also carries a darker memory. In the 1930s to 1950s, Vanino was one of the transit points through which prisoners were shipped to the camps of Kolyma, and a song about the Vanino port, sung in prison and then everywhere, is still known to many Russians. You will not find much by way of memorial in the harbour, but if you know the history you feel it in the long, wind-scoured quays and the steel-grey water.

For a rider, the road from Komsomolsk-on-Amur is the real draw, a long push east across the Sikhote-Alin mountains. It has been improved over the years, but conditions differ along the way, with good asphalt in some sections and rough, broken or gravel patches in others, and heavy trucks that make the dust and mud worse. Check recent reports before setting out. Summer brings rain and fog, autumn gives clear air and good colour, and winter closes the high ground with snow. The coast itself can be blustery, with a damp, salty wind off the strait.

Vanino has the services you would expect of a port: petrol stations, shops, cafes and simple hotels, with the neighbouring settlements of Zavety Ilyicha and Mayskiy only a few kilometres away. Sovetskaya Gavan, the larger town, lies just across the bay if you need more choice. Take the chance to eat well, because the road you came on has few places for it. The sea smells of salt, creosote and fish, the hills are covered with larch and fir, and there is a real satisfaction in arriving where the road, and the continent, simply stop.
t.sovetskaya gavan@49.0,140.3:
Sovetskaya Gavan has one of the best natural harbours on the Pacific coast of Russia, which is why it has been fought over, fortified and renamed. It sits on a deep bay on the Tatar Strait, reached through a narrow entrance, and in the 1850s the explorer Gennady Nevelskoy's party gave it the name Imperial Harbour. The Soviet authorities changed it in the 1920s, and today about thirty thousand people live here, a mix of dockworkers, sailors, fishermen and the families of naval personnel, since the Pacific Fleet maintains a presence in the area.

The ride in is a long one, either down from Komsomolsk across the mountains or along the coast from Vanino. The road crosses ridges covered in larch and spruce and drops to the sea through wet, mossy valleys, and conditions are unpredictable. Expect some asphalt, some gravel and a lot of trucks, and keep the weather in mind, because rain and fog are frequent and winter closes some sections. Autumn, when the air is clear and cold, is the best time to see the bay at its sharpest.

Services are good by local standards. There are fuel stations, supermarkets, banks, restaurants and a couple of hotels, and the nearby settlements of Lososina and Mayskiy fill in the gaps. For anything serious you would go back toward Vanino or Komsomolsk. Take a walk along the waterfront: the old harbour buildings, the naval vessels in the distance and the boats unloading fish give a very good picture of what life here is about. Seafood is the best bet at lunch, particularly salmon, crab and fish soup, which is usually warm, generous and cheap.

This end of Khabarovsk Krai feels like a different country from the Amur valley. The climate is damp and cool, shaped by the cold sea, and fog rolls in on summer mornings. The forest comes right to the water, and in autumn the hillsides blaze with maple and birch among dark conifers. It is also an area of bears and tigers, though both are rare to see. Be careful on the wet bends, enjoy the sense of being at the extreme eastern end of mainland Russia, and take an hour with the harbour before turning around.
t.kholmsk@47.0,142.1:
Kholmsk looks like a town built on a staircase. It climbs the steep hills on the western shore of Sakhalin, facing the Tatar Strait, and its ferry terminal and port are the island's main link to the mainland. Before 1945 this part of Sakhalin belonged to Japan, and the town was known as Maoka. Traces of that era remain in odd places, from old stonework to a few preserved buildings, and the name change is part of why the place feels layered, with older bones beneath Soviet concrete.

The road that brings you here from Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk is one of the island's best rides. It crosses the Western Sakhalin Mountains, climbing through forests of fir, spruce and dense, head-high dwarf bamboo, and then drops to the sea in a series of bends. The asphalt is generally good, though frost damage and landslips can interrupt it, and the gradients are steady rather than savage. Fog is the main hazard, rolling in off the strait and cutting visibility, particularly in early summer. September is a lovely month, with clear air and the first colour in the leaves, while winters bring heavy snow that can close the pass for short periods.

With about thirty-two thousand residents, Kholmsk has everything you will need: petrol stations, supermarkets, cafes serving fresh seafood and a handful of hotels. It is also a place to stock up before moving on, since distances on Sakhalin can be long and services thin. The ferry port is worth a look even if you are not travelling, with its trains and trucks lined up to board, and the sight of a railway ferry loading is a small spectacle in itself.

The sea smells of salt and fish, and the sky often turns pink and gold over the water in the evening. Sakhalin is known for its salmon, crab and sea urchin, and the markets sell them fresh and dried, along with the salty seaweed salad found throughout the Far East. Wander down to the front and eat something from the water, then take the road back over the mountains with the sun behind you. It is a short ride, but one that gives a lot for the effort.
t.korsakov@46.6,142.8:
Korsakov is the southern gateway of Sakhalin, a port town of about thirty-five thousand people on the shore of Aniva Bay, where the island narrows toward its southern tip. It began in the 1860s as a Russian military post named after a governor, and after the Russo-Japanese War in 1905 it passed to Japan, who called it Odomari and held it until the end of the Second World War. The old stone and wooden buildings of that period have mostly vanished, but the harbour layout and the terraced streets above it still have an unmistakable Japanese-era shape.

The writer Anton Chekhov crossed Sakhalin in 1890 and wrote a famous book about its penal colony, and he left the island by ship from this bay. If you like to place a story in a landscape, the harbour at Korsakov is a good spot to do so. The water is grey and cold, ferries and fishing boats move in and out, and the hills behind the town are covered with spruce and bamboo. It is not a pretty place in the postcard sense, but it is full of atmosphere, particularly in the long light of an autumn afternoon.

The road along Aniva Bay is gentle riding, with easy curves, light traffic and views over the water to distant headlands. The surface varies from good to patchy, and the weather can change fast, with fog common in summer and strong winds in autumn. Winters are snowy and the road can ice up in shaded corners, so late spring to early autumn is the best period. Beware of potholes after the thaw.

Services in the town are comprehensive: petrol stations, shops, cafes, a market and hotels, and Aniva, about twenty kilometres away, is the next place to turn to for supplies. Fresh fish and crab are the local speciality, and the market stalls are the best place to try them. Walk along the shore before you move on, when the horn of a ship carries over the bay and the smell of salt and seaweed fills the air. It is an end-of-the-road town with a story much bigger than its size.
t.aniva@46.7,142.5:
Aniva is a quiet town of nearly eight thousand people at the head of the bay that bears its name, on the southern end of Sakhalin. Like much of the south of the island it was Japanese until 1945, and the area still hints at that past in odd corners of its older streets and in the names that lingered for years. The bay in front of it is broad and shallow, ringed by low hills, and the climate is a little milder than the north of the island, with long autumns and plenty of fog in early summer.

For a motorcyclist, Aniva is a practical and pleasant stop on the coastal road between Korsakov and the small villages to the east. The road is usually good asphalt, with light traffic, wide bends and long views over the water, and the surface suffers mostly from frost heave and the occasional pothole. The gradients are mild, and the whole route can be ridden in a relaxed afternoon. Autumn gives the best light, with the hills turning copper and gold, and the sea turning a deep, cold blue.

Being a town of this size, Aniva has fuel, shops, cafes and simple accommodation, and Korsakov, a little over twenty kilometres away, offers a wider choice. Troitskoye, a village of about three thousand people some twenty-five kilometres off, has less. Eat fish while you are here, as the bay is rich in salmon, herring and crab, and the market sells smoked and salted varieties. Do not be surprised if the portions are enormous and the tea comes with a spoonful of jam.

The headland that closes the bay to the south ends at Cape Aniva, where a lighthouse stands on a rock above the sea. The structure, built by the Japanese in the 1930s, is one of the island's best-known landmarks, a squat concrete tower with a light that has guided ships around a dangerous corner for decades. Reaching it takes more time and a rougher road than the main route, so check conditions and give yourself daylight. Even if you only look at it on the map, it tells you something about how important this tiny corner of Russia has been to people who sail.
t.poronaysk@49.2,143.1:
Poronaysk is the main town of the middle part of Sakhalin's east coast, with nearly seventeen thousand people spread along the Poronay River where it meets the wide, shallow Terpeniya Bay on the Sea of Okhotsk. Like the south of the island it was Japanese territory until 1945, when it was called Shisuka, and a paper mill built in that period shaped the town for years. Today it is a modest, windy place, but it is the best-equipped stop for a long way in either direction, which is what counts on this coast.

The road that brings you here along the east coast has a rough, unfinished feel that many riders enjoy. It runs through flat country of larch, spruce and bog, with long straights, occasional river crossings and wide views over the sea. The surface varies from reasonable asphalt to patched or gravel sections, and traffic is mostly local, with lorries and the odd fishing truck. Fog is frequent in early summer, and winter brings heavy snow and wind. The best period is July to September, when the grass is green and the sea is calm.

You can count on fuel, shops, cafes and a few places to sleep in Poronaysk, which makes it a natural place to restock before heading further. The villages of Gastello and Leonidovo, with a thousand people or so each, are smaller and less reliable, so fill up here. Salmon and other fish are the food of the region, often smoked or salted, and in summer the markets overflow with them.

Nature is the reason to look beyond the town. The Poronaysky Nature Reserve, on the shores of the bay, protects wetlands, forests and coastline that are crucial for migratory birds, from swans and geese to sandpipers and gulls, and in autumn the sky can be full of them. Brown bears are common on Sakhalin, and while you will rarely see one, they leave their marks along the rivers when the salmon run. The bay has an open, lonely beauty, with low light and a huge sky, and an hour on the shore here can feel like a quiet reward for the long road.
t.tikhaya bay@48.1,142.5:
Tikhaya Bay means quiet bay, and the name is a promise that a good many sheltered coves along the Russian Far East try to keep. This one lies in the middle of Sakhalin, an island about nine hundred kilometres long, where long mountain ridges run from north to south and the coast is a mixture of cliffs, boulder beaches and river mouths. There is no town recorded nearby, and the nearest sizeable places are a long way off, so what follows is a picture of the country around it rather than of a particular building or jetty.

The riding in this part of Sakhalin is wild and often rough. Roads leave the main highway on tracks of gravel and mud, crossing streams and climbing short steep rises, and a few kilometres can take much longer than you expect. Conditions vary with the weather: rain turns clay to grease, fog drifts in without warning, and the wind off the sea is cool even in July. A light bike, spare fuel and a decent repair kit are sensible, and so is telling somebody where you are going. Late July to early September is the most reliable period.

You will not find fuel, a shop or a cafe at the bay, so everything comes from a town before the turn-off. Water is available from the streams, but treat it before drinking. Plan the whole day around that, because there is nowhere to buy anything once you leave the highway.

The nature is the reward. Sakhalin's forests are dense with Sakhalin fir and Ezo spruce, and the undergrowth is thick with dwarf bamboo that can grow taller than a man. Brown bears are common and fish well when the salmon run in late summer and autumn, so keep noise up in the woods and food well stored. The coast is rich in birds, and offshore, seals and sometimes whales can be spotted in calm weather. In the evening, the sea turns silver, the cliffs go dark and the only sound is the surf, which is exactly what the name promises.
t.central balkan stara reka reserve@42.7,2:
Just above Karlovo, the Stara Reka tumbles out of the Balkan mountains through a steep gorge of beech and rock, and climbing alongside it you leave the town's lowland heat behind within minutes. The reserve that bears the river's name protects the upper part of that valley and forms part of the Central Balkan National Park, one of the largest protected areas in this part of Europe. Its ancient beech forests are included in the UNESCO listing that ties together primeval beech woods across the continent.

Up here the forest is the main event: tall grey trunks, deep leaf litter, mossy boulders and a cool green light even at midday. Above the treeline lie open ridges grazed by sheep in summer, with cliffs where wallcreepers and golden eagles nest, and the forests shelter brown bears, wolves and chamois. Access inside the reserve itself is on foot by marked trails and is strictly regulated, so the motorcycle stays at the edge and you continue on your own legs for a while.

Below, history is close. Karlovo is the birthplace of Vasil Levski, the revolutionary who is something like Bulgaria's national saint, and his house is a museum. A few kilometres east, Kalofer gave the country its great poet and rebel Hristo Botev. Both towns lie in the Valley of Roses, where the Damask rose is grown for rose oil; in late May and early June the harvest fills the air with scent at dawn, when the petals are picked before the sun gets strong. The whole valley sits between the Balkan range to the north and the gentler Sredna Gora to the south.

For riding, the valley road between Karlovo and Kazanlak is fast and pleasant, and the crossings of the Balkan range to the north are what you came for, notably the Troyan pass with long climbs, open views and surfaces that vary from smooth to patched. Snow can close the high roads in winter. Karlovo, with around twenty thousand people, has fuel, cafés and grilled kebapche, and the mountain springs by the trailheads run cold and clear on the hottest days.
t.minamijima and peripheral reefs@27.0,142:
A thousand kilometres south of Tokyo, in the Pacific Ocean, the Ogasawara Islands rise from the sea, a scattered chain of volcanic islands that have never been connected to a continent. Minamijima, a small uninhabited island just off Chichijima, is one of their jewels: a ring of jagged limestone around a sheltered cove, the Ogiura, with white sand, turquoise water and a sinkhole beach that looks like something from a dream. The island and its reefs are part of the Ogasawara Islands World Heritage site, listed by UNESCO in 2011.

The islands are known as the Galápagos of the Orient, because their isolation has allowed many unique species to evolve, including land snails, plants, insects and birds found nowhere else. Minamijima has strict rules to protect its fragile ecosystem: visitors must be accompanied by a licensed guide, the number of visitors per day is limited, and the island is closed for part of the year. On the beach, you may see the shells of extinct land snails, a reminder of the island's long evolutionary history. Around the islands, the sea is home to dolphins, whales and sea turtles, and the reefs are rich in fish and coral.

There is no motorcycle riding on Minamijima itself, as it is uninhabited and accessible only by boat. On Chichijima, the main inhabited island, you can rent scooters to explore the island's roads, which wind along the coast and over the hills, with viewpoints over the sea and the reefs. Traffic is light, and the roads are narrow and twisty. Getting to the islands requires a ferry journey of around twenty-four hours from Tokyo, as there is no airport.

Chichijima has a small town with shops, restaurants and accommodation, as well as fuel for scooter rentals. Local specialities include seafood, such as turtle stew, a traditional dish, and tropical fruits like passion fruit. Book boat tours to Minamijima in advance, as places are limited, and respect the rules to protect this unique environment. Bring sun protection, water and a sense of wonder.
t.xochimilco 2@19.3,-99.1:
Before the Spanish arrived, the Valley of Mexico was a land of lakes, and the people who lived around them developed an ingenious way to farm the water. They built chinampas, artificial islands of mud and vegetation anchored by willow trees, separated by canals, and grew maize, beans, squash and flowers on them. In Xochimilco, in the south of Mexico City, a remnant of that world survives, with a network of canals and chinampas that is still farmed and navigated today. It is part of the UNESCO listing of the Historic Centre of Mexico City and Xochimilco, and the most famous image of the area is the trajinera, a brightly painted flat-bottomed boat that carries visitors along the canals, often accompanied by mariachi bands and floating food stalls.

Xochimilco is also home to the axolotl, a strange salamander that never fully grows up, keeping its feathery gills throughout its life. It is critically endangered in the wild, and efforts are being made to protect it in the canals. The chinampas themselves are threatened by pollution, urban growth and falling water levels, and some farmers are working to keep the traditional methods alive.

Riding in Mexico City is a challenge. The traffic is heavy, chaotic and unpredictable, and the air quality can be poor. The city has a programme that restricts vehicle use on certain days according to licence plate numbers, and visitors should check how it applies to them. The roads can be potholed, and speed bumps, topes, appear without warning. Still, riding through the city is an experience, and the south of the city offers an escape: the road up to the Ajusco volcano climbs through pine forests to more than three thousand metres, with views over the valley, and it is a popular ride for local motorcyclists.

Xochimilco has plenty of fuel stations, shops and restaurants, and the markets are full of food, flowers and crafts. The best time to visit the canals is on a weekday morning, when they are quieter. The weather is mild all year round, but the rainy season, from June to September, brings heavy afternoon storms, so plan your rides for the morning.
t.temple and former convent of saint andre:
Calpan is a small town on the lower slopes of Popocatépetl, and in its centre stands a sixteenth-century Franciscan convent that is one of the masterpieces of early colonial art in Mexico. Built soon after the Spanish conquest, when friars were racing to convert the Indigenous population, the church is set within a huge walled atrium where crowds could gather for open-air Mass. In each corner of the atrium stands a posa, a small chapel used for processions, and the four posas at Calpan are covered in astonishing carved reliefs: the Last Judgment, the Annunciation, saints and symbols, carved by Indigenous craftsmen who mixed European designs with their own style.

The convent is one of the group of early sixteenth-century monasteries on the slopes of Popocatépetl listed together by UNESCO, and it shows the blend of cultures that defined colonial Mexico. Calpan is also known for chiles en nogada, the elaborate dish of stuffed poblano chillies covered in walnut sauce and pomegranate seeds, whose colours echo the Mexican flag, and the town makes much of its claim to the dish during the late summer season when walnuts and pomegranates are ripe.

The ride here is defined by the volcanoes. Popocatépetl and Iztaccíhuatl rise to the west, snow-capped and huge, and Popocatépetl often puffs smoke and ash. The roads from Puebla and Cholula cross farmland and small towns, with plenty of topes, speed bumps, some of them large enough to unsettle a bike, as well as buses, trucks and the occasional animal. The road from Cholula towards the Paso de Cortés, between the two volcanoes, is a spectacular climb. The dry season from November to April gives the clearest views.

Fuel is easy to find in Calpan and in the surrounding towns, and Cholula, with its enormous pyramid crowned by a church, and Puebla, with its tiled colonial centre, are both close and full of food. Keep an eye on the volcano's activity, as ash falls occasionally affect the region, and be aware of local advice on road safety and security.
t.central balkan steneto reserve@42.7,24.7:
