Steneto is a deep, wild valley on the northern slopes of the Balkan range in central Bulgaria, enclosed by cliffs and covered in ancient beech forest, and it is one of the strict reserves of Central Balkan National Park, part of the Primeval Beech Forests World Heritage listing. Access is restricted, and nature is left to itself: old trees fall and rot, and the forest is home to bears, wolves, wild boar and a rich variety of birds, including several species of woodpecker and owl. The Cherni Osam river flows through the valley, and its clear waters are home to trout.

The nearest town on the northern side, Troyan, is famous for its monastery, the third largest in Bulgaria, with frescoes by Zahari Zograf, and for its ceramics, with their distinctive dripped and swirled glazes, and its plum brandy, Troyanska slivova. On the southern side of the range, Karlovo is the birthplace of Vasil Levski, the hero of the Bulgarian struggle for independence from the Ottomans, and the town sits at the western end of the Rose Valley, where roses are grown for their oil, used in perfumes around the world.

The road over the Troyan pass, linking Troyan and Karlovo across the Balkan range, is one of the best rides in Bulgaria, with long climbs, hairpins and views over the mountains, and at the top the Arch of Freedom monument stands on a ridge. The surface is variable, sometimes good, sometimes rough, and cloud can drop onto the pass in minutes, bringing fog and cold rain. The pass is usually closed in winter. The beech forests are an electric green in May and burnished gold by mid-October, either of which justifies the trip.

Troyan and Karlovo, at either end of the pass, both have fuel, shops and mehanas, the traditional Bulgarian taverns, so plan your fill-ups around them. Troyan monastery, with Zahari Zograf's colourful frescoes, deserves an hour, and the ceramics workshops in town sell the trademark swirled pottery. Shopska salad, banitsa pastry with white cheese and grilled meats are on every menu, and the local plum brandy, Troyanska slivova, is the obvious nightcap. The reserve itself is closed to visitors, so enjoy the forest from the marked trails of the park around it.
The Zócalo, the vast main square of Mexico City, is one of the largest public squares in the world, and standing in it you are at the centre of over seven hundred years of history. This was the heart of Tenochtitlan, the Aztec capital, built on an island in Lake Texcoco and home to perhaps two hundred thousand people when the Spanish arrived in 1519. After the conquest, Hernán Cortés's men built their new city directly on top of the ruins, using the stones of the temples to construct churches and palaces. The historic centre, together with the canals of Xochimilco to the south, was listed by UNESCO in 1987.

On the north side of the square stands the Metropolitan Cathedral, the largest in the Americas, built over almost three centuries and leaning slightly as it sinks into the soft lakebed soil. On the east is the National Palace, where Diego Rivera's murals tell the story of Mexico across a vast staircase. Just off the corner of the square, the excavated remains of the Templo Mayor, the main Aztec pyramid, were uncovered after electricity workers found a huge carved stone of the moon goddess Coyolxauhqui in 1978. Walking among its layers, built one over the other, is one of the great experiences of the city.

The historic centre around the Zócalo is a dense grid of colonial palaces, churches, markets and street vendors, at once grand and chaotic. Sinking, earthquakes and pollution have left their marks, but restoration in recent decades has brought much of it back to life. The city sits at about 2,240 metres above sea level, and the thin air can leave newcomers breathless.

Riding here is an extreme sport. The traffic is dense, unpredictable and aggressive, and the roads are pitted with potholes and topes. Mexico City also has a driving restriction programme, Hoy No Circula, which bars vehicles from circulating on certain days depending on their plates and emissions; check the current rules before you ride in. Fuel is easy to find, but parking a bike safely needs planning. Better to leave the bike at your hotel and explore on foot. Food is the reason to stay: tacos al pastor, tamales, churros with chocolate, and countless markets.
t.central balkan kozya stena reserve@42.8,:
High on the main ridge of the Balkan range, the Stara Planina, that runs across Bulgaria from west to east, the Kozya Stena reserve protects a wild landscape of limestone cliffs, beech forests and alpine meadows. Its name means goat wall, after the chamois that live on its crags. The reserve is part of Central Balkan National Park, one of the largest protected areas in Europe, and since 2017 its oldest beech stands have been inscribed alongside the primeval beech forests of the Carpathians and the rest of Europe. Wolves, bears and wild boar roam the forests, golden eagles soar over the ridges, and the meadows burst with wildflowers in early summer.

To the north lies Troyan, a town known for its plum brandy, Troyanska slivova, and its distinctive pottery with dripped glazes in green, brown and yellow. Troyan Monastery, a few kilometres east in the village of Oreshak, is the third largest in Bulgaria, with beautiful frescoes by Zahari Zograf, and it played an important role in the struggle against Ottoman rule; Vasil Levski, the national hero, used it as a base. To the south, across the mountains, the Rose Valley around Kazanlak and Karlovo is where most of the world's rose oil is produced, from roses harvested in May and June.

The Troyan Pass road, linking Troyan to the Rose Valley at Karnare, is one of the best riding roads in Bulgaria. It climbs through forests and meadows to the pass at about fifteen hundred metres, where a large monument called the Arch of Freedom stands on a summit near the road, with views over the whole range. The road is mostly well surfaced, with tight curves, hairpins and steep sections; the southern side is particularly dramatic. Weather changes quickly at the top, with fog, rain, wind and even snow out of season. In winter, the pass may be closed or require chains.

Troyan, nineteen kilometres away, is the obvious place for fuel, shops and restaurants; Klisura and Anton are small villages on the southern side with limited services. Try banitsa, cheese pastry, and kavarma, a meat stew, with a glass of local rakia in the evening. Mountain huts in the national park, reached on foot, offer simple food and beds for walkers. Bring warm clothes even in summer; at the top of the pass the temperature can be twenty degrees colder than in the valley.
t.archaeological monuments zone of xochica:
Xochicalco sits on a terraced hilltop south-west of Cuernavaca, and from the top you understand immediately why someone built a city here: the view runs over the valleys of Morelos in every direction, to the lakes, the hills and, on a clear day, the snowy shoulders of Popocatépetl far to the east. The city rose after the fall of Teotihuacan, flourishing roughly between AD 650 and 900, a time of upheaval when fortified hilltop centres grew strong by controlling trade. It was protected by moats, walls and ramparts, and its people mixed influences from the Maya, the Gulf Coast and central Mexico in a way that makes it unique.

The most famous building is the Temple of the Feathered Serpent, its lower walls carved with great undulating serpents, seated figures and glyphs that some scholars read as a record of a meeting of astronomers correcting the calendar. There are ball courts, palaces and a remarkable observatory: a cave with a vertical shaft cut through the rock, through which the sun shines straight down at its zenith in spring and summer, lighting up the floor. A good site museum at the entrance explains it all, and the site is a World Heritage site in its own right.

The riding around here is a good mix. From Mexico City, the highway south climbs over the mountains past the lakes of Zempoala before dropping into the warmer valley of Cuernavaca, the city of eternal spring. From there, smaller roads lead to Xochicalco and on to the lakes and the town of Taxco, famous for its silver and its steep cobbled streets, along a road that twists through dry hills. East of Cuernavaca, a route leads to the sixteenth-century monasteries on the slopes of Popocatépetl, also a World Heritage site. Watch out for topes, the speed bumps that guard every village, and avoid riding at night.

The site is open in the daytime and the heat in the afternoon can be intense, so arrive early with water and a hat. The nearest villages have basic shops, and Alpuyeca, on the highway, has fuel, as do the towns along the road to Cuernavaca. Try cecina from Yecapixtla, salted thin beef, a speciality of Morelos, and the fresh fruit sold at the roadside stalls.
t.historic centre of puebla@19.0,-98.2:
Puebla was founded in 1531 as a Spanish city from the start, laid out on a grid between the volcanoes and the road from Veracruz to Mexico City, and it grew into one of the richest towns of New Spain. Its historic centre is a World Heritage site, and walking through it you see why: dozens of churches, palaces and mansions, many covered in the hand-painted Talavera tiles for which the city is still famous. The cathedral, with its two tall towers, dominates the main square, and a few blocks away the Rosary Chapel of the church of Santo Domingo is a dazzling space of gilded stucco and carved angels that has to be seen to be believed.

Puebla is also a city with a place in history beyond Mexico. On 5 May 1862, the Mexican army defeated invading French troops here, a victory that is celebrated as Cinco de Mayo, much more in the United States than in Mexico itself, where the celebrations are mainly local. The forts of Loreto and Guadalupe on the hill above the city, where the battle was fought, now hold museums.

Food is a reason to come in its own right. Mole poblano, a dark, complex sauce of chilies, spices and chocolate, was born here according to legend in a convent kitchen, and chiles en nogada, stuffed poblano peppers with a white walnut sauce and pomegranate seeds, are a seasonal speciality in late summer, their colours matching the Mexican flag. Calle de los Dulces, the street of sweets, is lined with shops selling traditional candies.

Riding in Puebla is city riding, with heavy traffic, buses and taxis, and the topes are everywhere. Better to park and walk in the centre. But the surroundings are spectacular. On a clear morning Popocatépetl and Iztaccíhuatl stand to the west, and the roads up to the sixteenth-century Franciscan monasteries on the slopes of Popocatépetl, such as Huejotzingo and Calpan, make a beautiful day trip. Cholula, next door, has the largest pyramid in the world by volume, now a grassy hill topped by a church. Fuel, accommodation and mechanics are everywhere. The altitude, over two thousand metres, makes the evenings cool, so bring a jacket.
t.rosiorii de vede valea urlui@44.1,24.9:
Southern Romania is as flat as a table, and the Teleorman plain, through which the river Vedea flows towards the Danube, is wheat and sunflower country as far as the eye can see. The Romans pushed their frontier across this plain in the second century, building a long earthen rampart known as the Limes Transalutanus, east of the Olt river, with a ditch and a line of forts and towers behind it. Near Roșiorii de Vede, at Valea Urlui, one of these sites is part of the Roman frontier of Dacia listed by UNESCO. The rampart can still be traced in places as a low bank running through the fields, and on the ground you need a good eye, or a guide, to spot it. From the air it is much clearer.

Roșiorii de Vede is an ordinary market town, an important railway junction, with a few old houses, churches and a busy central square. The region is poor and agricultural, and the villages are long lines of houses with gardens behind, wells in front and old men sitting on benches by the gate. In summer the heat on the plain is intense, often well above thirty degrees, and the light is almost white. In winter, the wind from the east, the crivăț, sweeps across the plain and can bring snowdrifts that block the roads.

As a ride, this is not a place for corners. The roads are long and straight, lined with trees in places, with fields on either side and villages every few kilometres. Surfaces vary widely, from new asphalt on main roads to badly patched village streets, and horse carts, tractors and stray dogs are part of the traffic. Use this stretch to cover distance, enjoy the big skies and the sunsets over the fields, and save the twisties for the Carpathians to the north or the Danube cliffs to the west.

Roșiorii de Vede, about eight kilometres away, has fuel, supermarkets and simple restaurants, and the villages along the way have small shops. In summer, stalls by the road sell watermelons from the sandy soils near the Danube, which are sweet and cheap. Drink plenty of water, ride early or late to avoid the midday heat, and watch for farm vehicles pulling out of field tracks.
t.temple and former convent of the assompt:
The Franciscans arrived in Cuernavaca in the 1520s, just a few years after the Spanish conquest, and the fortress like convent they built here, dedicated to the Assumption of the Virgin, is now the city's cathedral. Its massive church, with walls thick enough for defence and an open chapel for preaching to crowds of indigenous converts, is one of the earliest sixteenth century monasteries on the slopes of Popocatépetl listed as a World Heritage Site in 1994. Inside, murals uncovered in the twentieth century show the martyrdom of Christian missionaries in Japan in 1597, a striking reminder of how far the Franciscan world reached; one of the martyrs, Felipe de Jesús, was born in Mexico City.

Cuernavaca, the capital of Morelos, is known as the city of eternal spring for its mild climate, and has long been a weekend escape for people from Mexico City. Hernán Cortés built himself a palace here, now a museum, with murals by Diego Rivera depicting the history of Mexico from the conquest to the revolution. The Jardín Borda, an eighteenth century garden where Emperor Maximilian and Empress Carlota stayed, is a lovely place to rest.

For riders, the road from Mexico City to Cuernavaca is legendary. The old federal road, Route 95, climbs over the mountains south of the capital through pine forest to nearly three thousand metres, then plunges down to Cuernavaca in a long series of curves, including the famous La Pera bend; it is crowded with bikers on weekends. The toll highway alongside is faster. Beyond Cuernavaca, Tepoztlán, a town below dramatic cliffs with a pyramid on the summit, is a short ride east.

Cuernavaca has fuel stations everywhere and a lively restaurant scene. The city's traffic is heavy, and topes, speed bumps, appear everywhere without warning. Security varies, so ride in daylight and keep to main routes. Try the local cecina, thin salted beef, and the many kinds of tamales.
t.temple and former convent of saint james:
Ocuituco claims the first Augustinian convent built in Mexico, begun in the 1530s on the southern slopes of Popocatépetl, and the church of Santiago Apóstol with its cloister belongs to the same World Heritage group of early convents around the volcano as Cuernavaca's cathedral. Its cloister keeps a rare carved stone fountain, and the convent's thick walls and simple lines show the early, almost defensive style of the first missions.

The village of Ocuituco lies in the northeast of Morelos, at around two thousand metres, among orchards of peaches, avocados and plums, with the snowy cone of Popocatépetl looming above. The volcano is active, and puffs of smoke and ash are common; occasionally eruptions close roads and airports. Tetela del Volcán, a few kilometres away, has another Dominican convent from the same period with fine murals.

The roads on the slopes of Popocatépetl are some of the most beautiful in central Mexico, winding through villages, orchards and pine forest, with views of the volcano and the valleys. They can be narrow, steep and potholed, with topes in every village, and traffic is light. The road along the southern slopes links a chain of convents, each with its own character, and makes a superb day's ride.

The convents of this chain were built in a hurry, as the friars raced to convert a huge population after the conquest, and they share a pattern: a large walled atrium where crowds gathered, small chapels at its corners for processions, an open chapel for mass in the open air, and a fortress like church with a cloister beside it. Many of them sit right on top of earlier temples, a deliberate statement of the new faith. Walking through Ocuituco's cloister, with the volcano visible over the walls and village life going on outside, you feel that layering of histories. Local people still use the church for weddings, festivals and Sunday mass, and the feast of its patron, Saint James, falls in late July.

Tetela del Volcán, five kilometres away, offers fuel and something to eat, and Cuautla, further south, is a larger town. Try the local fruit, especially in the markets, and the dishes of Morelos, such as cecina and tlacoyos. Ride in daylight and check volcano alerts before heading up the slopes.
t.church of the virgin of levisa@42.2,20.7:
In the middle of Prizren's old town, behind a wall and a fence, stands a brick-and-stone church whose bell tower rises above the rooftops. This is the Church of the Virgin of Leviša, Bogorodica Ljeviška in Serbian, one of the most important medieval monuments in the Balkans. It was rebuilt in the early fourteenth century under the Serbian king Milutin on the site of an older church, and its interior was covered with frescoes that are among the finest of their time.

Its history has been turbulent. Under the Ottomans it was converted into a mosque, and the frescoes were plastered over, which ironically helped preserve parts of them. In 2004 it was damaged during riots, and it is now part of the World Heritage site of Medieval Monuments in Kosovo, which remains on the List in Danger. Access can be limited, but even from outside the elegant arches, the patterned brickwork and the sense of age are striking.

Prizren itself is one of the most attractive towns in the region. The Bistrica river runs through the centre, crossed by an old Ottoman stone bridge, and around it you will find the Sinan Pasha mosque, hammams, churches and narrow lanes full of cafés and silver filigree shops. Above the town the fortress offers a view over the red roofs to the plain beyond. The League of Prizren, an important Albanian national movement, was founded here in 1878, and its museum tells the story.

The riding around Prizren is excellent. The road south-east into the Šar Mountains climbs steeply past river gorges towards Brezovica and the high pastures, with hairpins and wide views. West and south lie the roads towards Albania and North Macedonia. Surfaces range from smooth new asphalt to rough mountain stretches, and local driving can be spirited, so stay alert. Kosovo uses the euro, and you need valid green card insurance or local cover at the border.

Prizren is a large town with plenty of fuel, food and accommodation. Try qebapa and flija, a layered pancake dish baked slowly under a lid of hot coals, or simply sit by the river with a strong coffee. In August the town fills up for its documentary film festival, which turns the old centre into a lively open-air cinema.
t.temple and former convent of saint john:
Tlayacapan lies in the north of Morelos, among dry hills, with Popocatépetl, the smoking volcano, standing in the distance. Its convent of San Juan Bautista is one of a number of fortress-like monasteries built by Augustinian, Franciscan and Dominican friars in the sixteenth century, within a few decades of the Spanish conquest, and they are among the earliest European buildings in the Americas. UNESCO listed the group in 1994. The church has a plain, heavy front and an open-air chapel, where the friars preached to crowds who were not yet used to indoor services.

The inside of the convent is a good example of how art and religion mixed in the early colonial period. The cloister walls were painted with scenes by indigenous artists working under friars, often in black and white in a style borrowed from European prints, and parts of these murals still survive. Outside, the town itself is known for its potters, who make glazed clay vessels and figures in the local style, and for the chinelos, dancers in tall feathered hats and long embroidered robes who appear at carnival time, each wearing a mask with a pointed beard.

The ride to Tlayacapan is attractive and relaxed. From Cuernavaca or Cuautla, secondary roads climb through dry hills and farmland, with tight bends and views of the valley, and the main hazards are the topes, the speed bumps that guard every village. They are sometimes unmarked, so slow down at the first sign of houses. On clear days the volcano is visible, though it sometimes sends up ash, and the road conditions vary after the summer rains, with potholes and washed-out edges.

Fuel is available in Tlayacapan itself, which has about eight thousand people, and larger stations are in Cuautla, a short ride south, where the cecina of Yecapixtla, thin salty beef cooked over charcoal, is a well-known local dish. Weekends bring visitors from Mexico City, so the town is busiest on Saturday and Sunday, and weekdays are calmer. The elevation is moderate, around sixteen hundred metres, so evenings are mild.
t.pre hispanic city of teotihuacan@19.7,-9:
When the Aztecs came across Teotihuacan, centuries after it had been abandoned, they thought it must have been built by gods and named it the place where the gods were made. The city had reached its peak between about the first and sixth centuries, with perhaps well over a hundred thousand people, a grid of streets, apartment compounds and some of the largest pyramids in the Americas. The Pyramid of the Sun is a huge stepped mass, and the Pyramid of the Moon sits at the far end of the Avenue of the Dead, a long, broad processional road that makes the city feel grand even now.

The people who built Teotihuacan left no readable writing, so much is uncertain, including who they were and why the city declined. What survives are the murals, painted in red and green in the apartment compounds, the Temple of the Feathered Serpent and the obsidian tools, traded across Mesoamerica. The site was listed by UNESCO in 1987, and the neighbouring region has another wonder, the sixteenth-century aqueduct of Padre Tembleque, which ran for more than forty kilometres with tall arches to bring water to the area.

The riding around is easy to reach but not especially exciting, because the highway from Mexico City is a busy toll road, and the area around the pyramids is flat, dry and open. The interest is in the early morning, when you can arrive as the gates open and walk the avenue before crowds and heat build up. The site is at around 2,300 metres and can be cold at dawn and sunny at midday, with thunderstorms common on summer afternoons. A hat and water are essential, as there is almost no shade.

San Martín de las Pirámides, close by, has fuel, cafes and restaurants serving barbacoa, lamb cooked in an underground pit, which is a Sunday tradition in this region. Local shops sell obsidian souvenirs, and some produce pulque, the fermented sap of the maguey plant. Vendors at the site can be persistent but friendly, and a polite no is generally enough.
t.franciscan ensemble of the monastery and:
Tlaxcala has an unusual place in Mexican history, because its people were the main allies of Hernán Cortés in the conquest of the Aztec empire. The Tlaxcalans had resisted Aztec expansion for years, and when the Spanish arrived in 1519 they chose to fight with them rather than against them. In return, they received privileges, and the Franciscan friars who arrived soon after chose Tlaxcala as their first base on the mainland. The monastery and its church, begun in the sixteenth century, still stand above the town, a plain, massive building with a fine wooden ceiling in Moorish style.

The group is part of the early monasteries on the slopes of Popocatépetl that UNESCO listed in 1994, and the old town has the sleepy charm of a provincial capital, with a handsome square and arcades, red-painted buildings and a mix of colonial and modern. Nearby, the hilltop site of Cacaxtla has vivid murals painted more than a thousand years ago, among the best-preserved in the country, and it is worth the short detour.

For a rider, Tlaxcala is a good base, in a small state with quiet roads. To the north-east, the volcano La Malinche rises to over four thousand metres, with a national park and roads that climb through pine forest, and the surrounding plains have roads between fields of maize, barley and maguey. Traffic is light outside the towns, though local drivers can be unpredictable. The altitude, around 2,200 metres, means that mornings and evenings are cool, and in the rainy months, between June and September, afternoons bring heavy showers.

Totolac, a short ride away, and Tlaxcala itself have fuel stations, and the town has many places to eat. Try the local pulque, a mildly alcoholic drink made from maguey, in one of the old pulquerías, and tlacoyos, blue-maize cakes filled with beans. Opening hours of the convent vary, and a small entry fee is charged for the museum.
t.slaveni la cetate necropolis@44.1,24.5:
The Olt river rises in the Carpathians and runs south through Romania to the Danube, and in Roman times it was a boundary. The frontier here, called the Limes Alutanus after the Roman name for the river, ran along the Olt on its journey through the plains of Oltenia, and forts were placed at intervals to watch for raiders. Slăveni stands on that line, and the site on our list, a fort known as La Cetate, is beside a cemetery where the people who served there were buried. The nearby site of Romula, a Roman city that became a provincial capital, was a short distance away.

What you see today is quiet farmland. Roman forts in the lowlands were often built of earth and timber at first and later rebuilt in stone, and the traces of them are usually low banks, ditches and scatters of brick and pottery in ploughed fields. The cemetery has yielded tombstones and grave goods, and their inscriptions show soldiers from many parts of the empire. Local museums in Slatina and Caracal hold some of the finds, and they give a better sense of daily life than the open field can.

The plain of Oltenia is flat and hot, a landscape of maize, sunflowers, wheat and orchards, with villages strung along straight roads, and the riding is gentle rather than exciting. National roads are generally decent but busy with lorries, and smaller roads can be rutted with potholes, especially after winter. In July and August the heat is intense, with shade hard to find, so early starts are wise. Spring is soft and green, and in late summer the sunflower fields turn the horizon yellow. Horse carts, tractors and cyclists are common, often without lights, so be careful at dusk.

Gostavățu and Slăveni are small, so the sensible place for fuel is Drăgănești-Olt, eleven kilometres away, or the larger town of Slatina to the north. Fresh bread, tomatoes and cheese are available in village shops, and in summer there are stalls selling watermelons by the roadside. The people are friendly, and a few words of Romanian are appreciated, even if they are just a greeting.
t.some parts of hahajima and peripheral re:
The Ogasawara Islands lie about a thousand kilometres south of Tokyo, in the Pacific, and getting there takes a full day on a ferry, which is a good start to understanding why they have remained so special. The Bonin Islands, as they are also known, have never been connected to a continent, and as a result the plants and animals that reached them evolved in isolation, giving rise to a wealth of species found nowhere else. UNESCO listed the islands in 2011, and they are often called the Galapagos of the East.

Hahajima, Mother Island, is the southern of the two inhabited islands, reached by a further couple of hours on a smaller boat from the main island of Chichijima. It is a hilly, forested island with a tiny settlement, steep coastal cliffs and a ring of coral reef. The land snails of the Ogasawara are a famous case of rapid evolution, with dozens of species, and the forests shelter endemic trees and a rare fruit bat. In winter, humpback whales visit the surrounding sea to breed, and green turtles nest on the beaches. The reef, which extends around the island, is among the most northerly coral reefs in the world.

Riding here is not a matter of long distances. The islands have a limited network of roads, mostly short and winding between the village and the coves, and visitors rent scooters or small motorbikes or walk. The roads are narrow and steep, with views of the sea at every turn, and traffic is almost nonexistent. Typhoons can cancel boats and strand travellers for days, so allow extra time, and the best season for weather is spring to early summer, though winter is the time for whales.

Fuel is only available in the village, and on a small island it is sensible to start with a full tank and not to count on a second chance. The coastline offers snorkelling, kayaking and hiking, with guides required for some areas to protect the fragile environment. Remember that everything is brought from the mainland by ship, so prices are higher than in Tokyo, and the food is simple, with fresh fish and island lemons.
t.bronze age burial site of sammallahdenma:
In the countryside of Satakunta, west Finland, a low forested ridge hides thirty-odd heaps of stone laid down more than three thousand years ago. Sammallahdenmäki is a Bronze Age burial site, with granite cairns up to several metres across, built by people who lived along what was then the coast. When these cairns were raised, the sea lapped nearby. Since then the land has been rising, still lifting after the weight of the ice sheet, and the shore has retreated kilometres, leaving the graves stranded on the hill among spruce and pine. UNESCO added the site to its list in 1999.

The most unusual structure is known as the Church Floor, Kirkonlaattia, a rectangular pavement of big, flat stones, with no known parallel in Finland. A short, well-marked path loops among the cairns, so you can walk the ridge in an hour, with moss underfoot and the sound of wind in the trees. The cairns are protected, so do not climb on them or move stones. The ridge feels remote, but the road is a few minutes away.

Lappi and Eurajoki are small places nearby, and the nearest real town is Rauma, about fourteen kilometres off, a seaport with a beautifully preserved old wooden quarter, also a UNESCO site, and a tradition of bobbin lace. Rauma has fuel, restaurants and a few small hotels. Eurajoki is known mostly for the Olkiluoto nuclear power plant, whose reactors stand on the coast to the west.

The riding in this part of Finland is flat, smooth and a little monotonous, which is a fair description of most Finnish roads, though that is also their charm. Long straights run through forest and farm, with fine asphalt and strict speed limits enforced by cameras, so keep an eye on the signs. Elk and deer cross at dusk, and a collision can be serious. In June the sun barely sets, and the roads are empty and glowing. Autumn colours in September are superb, and winter is for those with studded tyres only.
t.archaeological site of aigai@40.5,22.3:
In 1977 the Greek archaeologist Manolis Andronikos lifted the stone slab of a vaulted tomb under a huge mound near the village of Vergina and found a gold casket holding the cremated bones of a man in his forties, with a golden wreath beside them. Most scholars now accept that it was Philip II of Macedon, the father of Alexander the Great, murdered in the theatre of the old capital in 336 BC. The mound, the Great Tumulus, is the centrepiece of Aigai, the first capital of Macedon, and today the royal tombs are displayed underground in a museum built inside the tumulus itself, in a half-light that makes the gold glow.

Aigai was a modest place by later standards, a palace on a terrace above the plain with a theatre below, but it was here that the Macedonian kings were buried, and here that the story of Alexander begins. The palace, a large building with an inner courtyard of colonnades, was a vast construction for its time, and the remains of its marble floors and mosaics can still be seen on the hillside. The setting is superb, at the foot of the Pieria mountains, with the broad plain of Imathia opening to the east and the haze of the Thermaic Gulf beyond.

The surrounding country is a land of orchards, especially peaches and cherries, planted in neat rows across the plain, and above them rise the oak and chestnut woods of the lower mountains. Naoussa, a short ride to the west, is known for its red wine, made from the Xinomavro grape, which is dark, tannic and rewarding with lamb. Veria, a pleasant town with a Byzantine quarter, lies a few kilometres to the north.

Riding here is easy and pleasant. Roads cross the plain in long straights between orchards, then climb into the hills with a series of gentle curves and views. Traffic is light, apart from tour buses at the site. The surface is mostly good. Vergina, Melíki and Kouloúra have cafés and small shops, and fuel is available in Veria and in the towns along the main road. The museum is cool even in summer, which is a mercy. Spring, when the orchards flower, and autumn are the best seasons.
t.studenica monastery@43.5,20.5:
The monastery of Studenica lies in a green gorge of the Golija mountains in central Serbia, where a clear river runs down through beech and oak woods toward the Ibar. Stefan Nemanja, the founder of the medieval Serbian state, began building it in the 1190s, and it became the model for all the monasteries that followed. Nemanja himself abdicated in 1196 and later became a monk, dying on Mount Athos in 1199. His son, Saint Sava, brought his father's remains back here, and they rest in the church today.

The central church, dedicated to the Virgin, is built of white marble and surrounded by high stone walls, and it has a Romanesque feel from its carved windows and portals, mixed with Byzantine design in the plan and the domes. Inside, the frescoes are among the finest in the Orthodox world, with a monumental Crucifixion dating to the early thirteenth century and many saints in blues and golds. The monastery was listed by UNESCO in 1986, and it is still an active community, so dress modestly and keep your voice low.

The approach from Kraljevo is a lovely ride. The road follows the Ibar and then turns up the Studenica valley, with smooth asphalt and long, easy corners among forested slopes, with farms and plum orchards in the lower parts. Plums mean rakija, and in many farms you may be offered a glass, which is hospitality rather than a challenge; politely decline if you are riding. Traffic is light, but tractors and trucks are common, so keep a gap on the blind bends. Autumn colours in the beech woods are superb, and spring brings fresh green and flowers.

Kraljevo, about thirty kilometres away, is a town of eighty thousand and the place to fill up and buy supplies. Vrnjačka Banja, a spa town about thirty-three kilometres off, offers more varied lodging and cafes. Near the monastery itself there are a few small places to eat, serving simple Serbian food such as grilled meat, kajmak and fresh bread. If you can, come in the early morning, when the light slants into the courtyard and the bells ring across the valley.
t.temple and former convent of saint domin:
Oaxtepec sits at roughly thirteen hundred metres on the warm southern side of the volcanic highlands of Morelos, where the air is noticeably softer than in Mexico City, an hour or two north. The Dominican convent here is one of the sixteenth-century monasteries on the slopes of Popocatépetl that UNESCO listed in 1994, a group built by the first friars after the conquest, with fortress-like walls, a large atrium for open-air preaching and thick buttresses against the earthquakes that have always visited this region.

The place was important long before the friars. Oaxtepec, once Huaxtepec, was a town the Mexica rulers prized for its mild climate and its gardens, and it is often described as having a botanical garden of medicinal and ornamental plants that served the Aztec court. When the Dominicans arrived in the 1520s they chose a site with an existing ceremonial importance, a habit repeated across New Spain, and the convent later served as a hospital. Today the church and cloister stand quietly at the heart of a town whose modern fame comes from something else entirely: a huge public holiday park with pools, which fills with families on weekends.

For riders, the approach is mostly good tarmac with a mix of fast highway, spirited climbs and hot, lazy village roads. The roads from Mexico City cross the pine-covered ridge south of the capital and drop into Morelos in a long, satisfying descent, with views of the plains and, when the air is clear, the snowy cone of Popocatépetl. Rain arrives in the afternoons from June to September, so mornings are best, and the dry months from November to April are warmer and brighter. Watch for topes, the speed bumps at village entrances, which come without much warning.

Oaxtepec itself is small, with fuel and bakeries, but nearby Cocoyoc, a few kilometres off, has more restaurants and a string of old haciendas that have been turned into hotels. The local specialities lean to fruit: Morelos is known for its sweet red tamales, for sorbets and for the fresh juices on every corner, and the market in the town is a good place for a lunch of tacos and a cold agua fresca. Take a moment inside the cloister, where the shade and silence are a good break from the heat of the road.
t.martesti cetate@44.7,24.8:
South of the Carpathians, where the Wallachian plain starts to lift into hills, there is a quiet stretch of the Argeș county, and this point lies near Lunca Corbului, in a landscape of low ridges, orchards and wide fields. The name Cetate simply means fortress or citadel in Romanian, and the label suggests a place where an old defensive site was recorded, whether Roman or older. This is a case where I would not tell you more than the evidence allows: no great monument stands here, and the pleasure of the place is mostly the country itself.

The region has a long history. Dacian tribes lived in these valleys, the Romans extended their rule over them in the early second century, and the line of the Olt river was one of the key frontiers for the province. A little farther west, near Stolniceni, the Roman fort of Buridava watched over the Olt valley, and that is the other end of this ride. After the Romans left, the area lived through the centuries of Wallachian voivodes, Ottoman suzerainty and the long rural life of a country made up of small villages and large estates.

The roads here are secondary, with decent asphalt and a few potholes, passing through villages whose houses stand behind high gates and neat gardens. Plum and apple orchards are everywhere, and the road verges in summer are lined with sunflowers and maize. Sheep and horse carts appear without warning, and village dogs love motorbikes. The bends are gentle and the speed low, so this is a relaxed day. Spring has blossom, summer is hot, and autumn is rich with fruit, walnuts and the smoke of village fires.

Lunca Corbului is a small town with some shops and a place to fill the tank, and Pitești, the larger city to the north, has fuel, a good selection of restaurants and a pleasant centre. Ask in a village shop for the local bread and cheese, and for the sweet preserves known as dulceață, which are made with every fruit in the garden. Do not expect English to be widely spoken, but a few words of Romanian and a smile go a long way, and people tend to be curious and kind to travellers who come through on motorcycles.
t.nakodojima and peripheral reefs@27.6,142:
No road leads to Nakodojima, and for a good reason: it lies in the Pacific about a thousand kilometres south of Tokyo, in the Mukojima group of the Ogasawara or Bonin Islands, and it is a small uninhabited rock surrounded by reef. The name is a joke the old mariners would have enjoyed. In this group of islands, Mukojima means bridegroom island, Nakodo means matchmaker, and the nearby Yomejima means bride, so the three islets together make a wedding party. Access to the Mukojima group is restricted, and visitors need a permit or must go with a licensed tour.

The Ogasawara islands are oceanic, never connected to any continent, and that isolation has produced a remarkable natural laboratory. Land snails have split into dozens of species on the different islands, and the plants and birds include many species that exist nowhere else. The surrounding waters are clear and warm, with coral, green turtles and, at times, whales and dolphins. UNESCO listed the islands in 2011, in recognition of this evolution in isolation, which is often compared to the Galapagos.

People arrived late. In 1830 a mixed group of settlers, including Westerners and Pacific islanders, settled on Chichijima, and in 1853 Commodore Perry of the United States Navy stopped there on his way to Japan. Japan took control in the 1870s, and the descendants of the first settlers still live on the main island, with surnames that reflect their mixed origins.

The only way to reach the Ogasawara Islands from the mainland is by ferry from Tokyo to Chichijima, a voyage of about a day, and the boat sails roughly once a week. From Chichijima, small boats take visitors on tours to the outer islands, and the sea can be rough. There are small roads on Chichijima and Hahajima, where scooters are a good way to explore, with fuel at the main settlements, but nothing on a rock like this. If you do go, the best season is spring to early summer, before the typhoons of late summer arrive, and in the warm months the water is lovely for snorkelling.

This point is a place to think about, rather than ride to: the coordinates mark a small spot on the map where the sea, the reef and the birds are in charge.
t.natural and cultural heritage of the ohr:
Lake Ohrid is one of the oldest lakes in Europe, perhaps a million years old or more, a deep, clear basin shared between Albania and North Macedonia, and this point lies on the Albanian side, close to Pogradec. The lake is so old and so isolated that it has developed its own species, with dozens of fish, snails and crustaceans found nowhere else. The most famous is the Ohrid trout, locally known as koran, which is protected and appears on menus with some controversy. UNESCO listed the lake and the town of Ohrid together for their natural and cultural heritage, and the Albanian shore is a part of the same landscape.

The shoreline here is quiet and low, with reed beds, small beaches, pebbly coves and rows of willows, and the water is a startling blue in the sun. Behind the lake, the Mokra and Galičica mountains rise steeply, with the snow lingering into May. Near the village of Lin, on a small peninsula, a church of the sixth century contains a splendid early Christian floor mosaic of animals and birds, a reminder that the lake was a Christian centre long before the monasteries of Ohrid.

Pogradec is a relaxed lakeside town of over sixty thousand, with a promenade, cafes and fish restaurants, and it is popular with Albanians and visitors from Kosovo and North Macedonia in summer. A good meal here is grilled trout or carp with a salad and a glass of local raki, and the sunset over the water is a sight worth waiting for. Close to the town, the springs at Drilon, with their clear water and old trees, are a lovely place for a break.

The roads around the lake are generally good, if narrow in places, with the main route running along the shore and a series of climbs into the hills. Traffic can be heavy in summer, and Albanian driving style demands alertness, as overtaking on blind corners is common. Spring and the first weeks of autumn are kindest, with warm water and fewer crowds. Winter is cold, with fog over the lake, and the mountain roads can be icy.

Petrol is easy to find in Pogradec, and smaller places like Përrenjas have stations too. Across the border, Ohrid in North Macedonia is nearby, with its churches, old town and the Byzantine fortress above the lake, but remember to take your vehicle documents and a green card for the border crossing.
t.rrajca@41.2,20.5:
Rrajca is a village in the hills on the western side of Lake Ohrid, in North Macedonia, a short way from the small town of Vevčani, and the point lies in a rolling country of orchards, beech woods and pastures just above the lake. The hills here belong to the Jablanica range, which forms a rugged wall between Macedonia and Albania, and the sound of cowbells and the smell of woodsmoke in the evenings are part of daily life. The village has a mixed population, and the local name in Albanian, Rrajcë, reminds you that this is a border region where Macedonian and Albanian cultures live side by side.

Vevčani, nearby, is a village of stone houses and cobbled lanes known for its springs, which pour out of the mountainside in a cascade of clear water, and for its carnival, held each January around the old New Year, when masked locals parade in satirical costumes in a tradition that goes back many centuries. The village once declared itself an independent republic as a joke in 1987, an act that is still remembered with some pride. Lake Ohrid itself is a few kilometres below, with the city of Struga at the northern end, where the Black Drim river leaves the lake and a poetry festival has been held each August since 1962.

The riding here is gentle and rewarding. The roads wind up from the lakeside through woodland and small villages, with views opening out to the shining lake and the mountains of Albania on the far shore. Traffic is light, apart from the busy road between Struga and Ohrid, and the tarmac is mostly sound, with some potholes in the villages. Spring brings blossom and green hillsides, while autumn is rich with gold and red in the beeches. Summer is warm, but the hills are cooler than the lake. Winter can bring snow to the higher lanes.

Oktisi and Radolista are small villages with a shop or two, and fuel is best taken in Struga or Ohrid, both a short ride away. A meal in a village restaurant will probably include shopska salad, grilled meat, local cheese and fresh bread, and perhaps a glass of rakija. The people are friendly and curious, and a few words of Macedonian go a long way.
t.central balkan tsarichina reserve@42.8,2:
The Balkan range, called Stara Planina in Bulgarian, runs across the whole of the country like a long, wooded wall, and it gave its name to the entire Balkan peninsula. The Tsarichina reserve lies in its central part, within the Central Balkan National Park, in a deep valley that holds some of the oldest and best preserved forests in Bulgaria. The beech and fir trees are huge, and in places have never been cut, so the forest has the tall, silent, shadowy character of ancient woodland. It belongs to the beech forest sites that UNESCO linked together across Europe.

The animals are shy. Brown bears, wolves, lynx, chamois and deer live in the park, and the cliffs of the high ridge are a home for golden eagles and peregrine falcons. Wildflowers, including some endemic to the Balkans, cover the mountain meadows in spring and early summer. The access to the reserve is strictly controlled, since it is a place for conservation and science, so the way to appreciate it is from the edge, or on the marked trails in the national park around it.

The nearby villages have a story of their own. Koprivshtitsa, about sixteen kilometres away, is the town where the April Uprising against Ottoman rule began in 1876, and its hillsides are covered with beautiful nineteenth century houses with colourful wooden balconies, in the style of the Bulgarian National Revival. Klisura, also close, took part in the same uprising and was burned in reprisal, and it has a memorial. The mountains and the villages are bound up together in the Bulgarian idea of national history.

For riders, this is excellent country. The roads cross the Balkan through a series of passes, with the long climbs and descents on good tarmac, bends that follow the contours, and views of forested slopes and distant peaks. The Shipka Pass, with its huge memorial to the Russo-Turkish war of 1877 and 1878, and the Beklemeto pass farther west are among the most famous. Traffic is moderate, with some trucks on the main routes, and weather in the mountains can change quickly, with fog and rain even in summer. Snow closes some of the higher roads in winter.

Koprivshtitsa has a few fuel stations and small restaurants, but the bigger towns of Karlovo and Pirdop, in the valley to the south, are the best places to fill the tank. In the villages, try the local yoghurt, a bowl of bean soup and grilled meat, with a glass of rakia, and look out for the elderly women selling homemade jam by the roadside.
t.stari ras and sopocani@43.1,20.4:
In the hills of southwestern Serbia, near the town of Novi Pazar, lie the ruins of Ras, the first capital of the medieval Serbian state, and the monastery of Sopoćani, which holds some of the finest Byzantine painting in Europe. Stefan Nemanja, founder of the dynasty that ruled for two centuries, was born in this region, and the monuments here were the heart of his realm. Ras was a fortress on a hill above the river, and a short distance away the little church of St Peter, one of the oldest in Serbia, stands on a mound of an earlier cemetery with a round, early plan that suggests Byzantine and local roots.

Sopoćani was founded by King Uroš I in the thirteenth century, and its frescoes, from around 1270, are a high point of Byzantine art. They include a monumental scene of the Dormition of the Virgin, with figures of such solemnity and soft colour that people compare them to the Italian painters who came later. The walls were painted in a blue that you rarely see in older churches. The monastery is quiet, set in a valley with a stream and meadows, and the nuns who live there welcome visitors with a polite reserve. Dress modestly, and expect to be asked to put away cameras inside.

Riding in this part of Serbia is lovely and a bit unruly. The road toward Novi Pazar from Kraljevo or Raška goes through gorges and along rivers with a series of bends, and there are broad uplands of meadows and beech woods. Roads are paved, though often patched, and trucks, tractors and the occasional horse cart share them. Summers are warm and winters can bring heavy snow on the plateaus, so spring and autumn are comfortable choices. The region has a strong Muslim culture alongside the Orthodox heritage, and its mosques and cafés give Novi Pazar its character.

Novi Pazar, about eight kilometres away, is a bustling city of some eighty-six thousand with fuel stations, plenty of cafés, bakeries and grilled meat restaurants where cevapi are served with soft flatbread. A coffee, thick and sweet, in the old bazaar is a nice pause. Carry passport and green card insurance for the nearby borders with Montenegro and Kosovo, and check access conditions if you plan to cross. The churches are open during the day but may close at midday for a rest.
t.paleochristian and byzantine monuments o:
Thessaloniki has the odd distinction of being a Roman city, a Byzantine city, an Ottoman city and a Greek city, all at once, and the churches that UNESCO listed in 1988 tell the earliest part of the story. The Paleochristian and Byzantine monuments include the Rotunda, a huge round brick building put up around AD 300 as a mausoleum for the emperor Galerius, and later converted into a church. Its walls are about six metres thick, and it stands beside the remains of Galerius's palace and triumphal arch. A minaret from the Ottoman period still rises beside it.

The other great monuments are the basilica of Hagios Demetrios, dedicated to the city's patron saint, who is said to have been martyred here in the early fourth century, and the church of Hagia Sophia, with its mosaic of the Ascension in the dome. The early Christian basilica of Acheiropoietos, with its simple columned nave, is among the oldest churches in Greece. In 1917 a huge fire destroyed much of the city, including Hagios Demetrios, which was rebuilt afterwards, and visitors can still see the crypt where the saint is said to have been held.

Ágios Pávlos lies just above the old centre, in the quieter upper town where the streets climb toward the Byzantine walls and the wooded slopes behind. The upper town, called Ano Poli, survived the fire and has retained its crooked lanes, Ottoman houses and little churches. From the walls you can look down over the red roofs of the city to the sea and, on a clear day, to Mount Olympus floating on the far horizon.

Riding in Thessaloniki is a challenge: the traffic is fast and unpredictable, the roads are steep and cobbled in the upper town, and parking is scarce. It makes sense to park near the edge and walk. Beyond the city, the road along the coast toward Halkidiki is a pleasant run, with sea views and light traffic outside high summer.

Thessaloniki is the second city of Greece, with plenty of fuel and food. Try a bougatsa, a pastry filled with custard or cheese, for breakfast, and a koulouri, a sesame ring, from a street seller.
t.sopocani monastery@43.1,20.4:
Sopoćani is one of the quietest and most beautiful monasteries in Serbia, and you may well be the only person in the church. It stands in a green valley a few kilometres west of Novi Pazar, near the springs of the Raška river, in a region that was the heartland of the early Serbian kingdom. King Stefan Uroš I founded it in the 1250s, and he is buried here, and the church was decorated with frescoes between about 1260 and 1270, painted by artists whose name we do not know but whose command of colour and space put them in the first rank of medieval European painting. UNESCO listed Sopoćani together with the nearby Old Ras in 1979.

The great fresco is the Dormition of the Virgin on the west wall, a huge scene in which the apostles gather around the bed while Christ holds the Virgin's soul in the form of a small swaddled child. The blues and whites, preserved remarkably well, were laid on in a way that anticipates the Italian Renaissance by a generation or two, and the faces show a quiet feeling that was rare for the time. Look up and the walls seem to glow.

The monastery was deserted for a long period after the Ottoman conquest, and parts of the structure decayed before being restored in the twentieth century. It is now a working convent, and the sisters ask for modest dress and silence inside the church.

The ride in is a lovely one. From Novi Pazar the road follows a small valley to the village of Sokolovica, with meadows, orchards and plum trees, and the last stretch is a quiet lane that rises gently to the monastery gates. Novi Pazar itself has a mixed Bosniak and Serb history and a distinctly Ottoman feel, with mosques, a bazaar and a fine hammam, and is an easy place to find fuel and a meal of grilled kebabs, ćevapi, with fresh bread and kajmak. The road from here to the monastery of Studenica to the north-west, on the ride list, runs through high farmland and forest, with some beautiful bends.

Spring and early autumn are best, with plum blossom in April and golden light in October. Winters are cold, and snow can close the quieter lanes. Carry a scarf for the church, and leave plenty of time, because the silence is the main thing.
t.monastery of djurdjevi stupovi@43.2,20.5:
Đurđevi stupovi, the Pillars of Saint George, crowns a hill above Novi Pazar, a small church of Saint George with a dome and towers that give the monastery its name. Stefan Nemanja, the founder of the Serbian dynasty that dominated the Balkans for two centuries, built it in the later twelfth century, and it was one of the first great foundations of his rule. The painting inside is Byzantine in style, and the cluster of dome and towers on the hilltop makes a strong silhouette.

Ras itself was the early capital of the Serbian lands, a fortress on a rocky hill with a town below, and its ruins lie in the same area, a short distance away. The valley of the Raška river, which opens out here into a long, fertile basin, was a crossroads between the Adriatic coast and the interior, and it is easy to see why a strong ruler would put his seat on its heights. Nemanja went on to found Studenica, which lies on the ride list and is the grandest of all the Nemanjić monasteries, a white marble church in a forest valley to the north-west.

Riding here is a good experience with some patience. The road from Novi Pazar climbs from the town to the hilltop in a few kilometres, with narrow, steep sections and a gravelly surface, and the monastery car park is small. The roads in the wider Raška region are very varied: wide and fast on the main valley road, then narrow and twisting in the side valleys, with livestock, tractors and old Zastavas to watch for. Weather in the highlands changes quickly, and thunderstorms in summer afternoons are common. Spring and autumn are the best seasons.

Novi Pazar has plenty of fuel, with a population of over eighty thousand, and the villages around have smaller stations. There are small cafes and a few restaurants, and it is worth stopping for Turkish coffee and a sweet pastry in the town, which has a lively street life in the evenings.

Dress modestly for the churches and speak quietly. Photography inside may be limited.
t.st peter s church@43.2,20.5:
On a rocky hill above the town of Novi Pazar stands a small, round church, and it may be the oldest in Serbia. Petrova crkva, the church of St Peter, is a rotunda from the ninth or tenth century, built on the site of earlier foundations, and the medieval ruler Stefan Nemanja, who founded the Serbian state and the dynasty that followed, is said to have been baptised here. Its stone walls are worn, its interior is dim and its setting, with the town spreading out below and the hills behind, makes you feel the age. The surrounding area was the heart of the early Serbian kingdom, called Ras, and the area is protected as a World Heritage site, together with the nearby monastery of Sopocani.

Sopocani is a different kind of marvel. King Uros I founded the monastery in the 1260s, and its church holds frescoes that are counted among the finest of medieval Europe, with a blue so deep and figures so fluid that they stand comparison with the work of the Italian masters who came a generation later. The Dormition of the Virgin, painted on the west wall, is a work that visitors travel far to see. The road on to Studenica, the mother church of the Serbian Orthodox faith, runs through the valley of the Ibar and into the hills, passing forests, small farms and villages with orchards.

The riding is the main reason to come this way. The roads climb and fall through the green hills of the Raska region, with bends that tighten and open, and the surface is mostly decent, though it can be patched and uneven, and trucks use the Ibar valley road. The mountain of Kopaonik rises to the north, with high roads that are quiet and cool in summer, and snow-covered in winter. In spring the orchards bloom, and in autumn the beech woods turn copper.

Novi Pazar is a lively town of about eighty-five thousand people with a mainly Muslim population, quite different from much of Serbia, and its old Ottoman bazaar, mosques and teahouses give it a feel of a market town in another country. There are plenty of fuel stations and cheap places to eat, and the local grilled sausages, kebab-style cevapi, and burek pastry are excellent. Monasteries expect modest dress, with shoulders and knees covered, and a quiet voice.
t.purron@18.2,-97.1:
A wide dry valley, forests of cactus and, hidden among them, one of the oldest dams in the Americas. Purron is the name of a huge earthen embankment in the Tehuacan-Cuicatlan valley of southern Puebla, built perhaps two and a half thousand years ago, and over the centuries it grew to be one of the largest dams of ancient Mesoamerica, holding water for fields in a land that gets little rain. It does not look like much from the road: a long, low ridge of earth and stone, covered in scrub. But it is a testament to the farmers who lived here, in a valley where agriculture was already old when the Egyptians were building pyramids, and where early maize was grown thousands of years ago.

The valley is a biosphere reserve and a World Heritage property, famous for its forests of columnar cactus. Giant tetechos and cardones stand in thick groves like candelabra, with agave, yucca and spiny shrubs between them, and the whole landscape glows green and gold in the late afternoon. Birds such as the cactus wren and a little parrot called the Mexican parakeet use the cactus, and the rocky hills are full of fossils from the time when the area lay beneath a shallow sea. San Juan Raya, the other stop on the ride, is known for its remarkable fossil beds, with sea snails in the rock.

The roads in this valley are not wild, but they have their moods. Highway 135 runs along the valley floor between Tehuacan and Oaxaca, a fast, busy route with trucks, while the side roads to the villages turn to gravel and rough track, where a careful pace and good tyres are needed. Heat is the main challenge. Between April and September it can be fierce, so start at dawn and carry plenty of water. The best months are November to March, with clear skies and warm days, and cold, bright nights.

Coxcatlan, about eight kilometres away, is the nearest village of any size, but for fuel and a proper meal, Tehuacan, the bigger town, is the place to fill up. The town is also known for its mineral water, bottled and sold across Mexico, and for the little salt-works of nearby Zapotitlan, which have produced salt for centuries. Local food is rich in corn and chile, with goat and mole common on the menu. Respect the cactus: it grows slowly, and many species are protected.
t.anejima and peripheral reefs@26.6,142.2:
Anejima is a speck of an island in the Ogasawara group, the Bonin Islands, scattered in the Pacific about a thousand kilometres south of Tokyo. Nobody rides a motorcycle to it. The only practical way to reach the group is the ferry from Tokyo to Chichijima, a trip of roughly a day, and the smaller islands around Chichijima are reached by boat or not at all. So this stop is really about the scenery of a reef and the story of the place, and if you are planning a ride here, plan it around Chichijima's little roads.

The islands have never been joined to any continent, and that shows in the wildlife. Many of the plants, land snails and insects are found nowhere else, which is why people compare the group to the Galapagos. UNESCO listed the Ogasawara Islands in 2011, partly for that evolutionary story. Surrounding the islands are coral reefs of a clear blue, and green turtles nest on the beaches.

The human history is odd and interesting. The islands were uninhabited when Western whalers and sailors started to stop here in the early nineteenth century, and a mixed group of settlers, including people from the Pacific, Europe and America, built a community on Chichijima. Commodore Perry visited in 1853 on his way to Japan. Japan took control in the 1870s. The islands were evacuated during the Second World War and then administered by the United States until they went back to Japan in 1968. The descendants of the first settlers still live there, and you can hear it in some of the family names.

On Chichijima there is a small town, Omura, with a petrol station, shops and places to eat. The roads wind along the coast and up to viewpoints, and traffic is light. Do not expect long rides, but the air is warm and the sea is always close, and the sunsets are famously good.
t.st luke hermitage complex@42.1,23.4:
Above Rila Monastery, in the folds of the Rila Mountains, a path leads to the hermit's cave where it all began. The monastery was founded in the tenth century by Saint Ivan of Rila, a monk who left the world to live as a recluse in these forests, and he gathered followers who built a community. By the coordinates, St Luke's hermitage stands in the same wooded valley, a small chapel and a cluster of buildings that belong to the monastic complex, at the end of a track among spruce and beech.

The setting is lovely. The Rilska river rushes down the valley, the slopes are dense with forest, and above the tree line rise bare granite peaks, the highest in the Balkans. In autumn, the beeches turn gold and copper, and in winter, snow lies thick. The monastery itself, with its striped arcades, domed church and painted frescoes, is the most important in Bulgaria, and was inscribed by UNESCO in 1983. During the centuries of Ottoman rule, it kept the Bulgarian language and faith alive, and is treasured as a symbol of national identity.

The road up to the monastery from the town of Rila is a good, winding mountain road, with long bends, forest on both sides and little traffic outside the tourist season. The valley is a place for a slow ride. Weather is changeable, and clouds can come down fast, bringing rain or fog, and even in summer you will need a warm layer. Snow can close the upper road in winter.

Sapareva Banya, the nearest town in the list, is famous for its geyser, which is said to be the hottest mineral spring in continental Europe, at about a hundred degrees. Fuel is available in Rila town and in larger towns such as Dupnitsa, and you should not count on finding any near the hermitage. Walking shoes are useful for the last part, and a respectful dress code applies at the chapel.
t.old rauma@61.1,21.5:
Rauma smells of tar, sea air and woodsmoke, or at least it does in the old quarter, where over six hundred wooden houses crowd along narrow streets that have changed little in layout since the Middle Ages. Old Rauma is the largest unified wooden town in the Nordic countries, and it was added to the World Heritage list in 1991. The houses are low, painted in ochres, reds and soft greens, with tidy yards, carved doors and little cobbled lanes, and many of them are still lived in, which gives the place a lived-in rather than museum feel.

The town grew up around a Franciscan friary in the fifteenth century, and the roofless ruin of the Church of the Holy Cross still stands among the houses. Rauma was a trading and seafaring town, shipping timber and tar from the forests of Finland across the Baltic, and the sailors' houses of the old quarter have a sturdy, practical character. Today it is also known for bobbin lace, which was made here for generations, and a lace week in July fills the streets with makers and visitors. Locals speak a distinctive dialect, with words that can baffle other Finns, and they are proud of it.

For a rider the old town is a place for walking, as the streets are narrow and the cobbles uneven, so park near the edge and go on foot. The country around is flat, green and watery, on the south-west coast of Finland, and the roads that link Rauma to Pori and Turku are straight and fast, with long views over fields and forests. The corners are few, speed limits are strictly enforced, and at dusk the real danger is elk and deer on the road, so keep an eye on the verges.

Rauma is a town of over thirty-six thousand people, so fuel, supermarkets and restaurants are easy to find. A Finnish lunch of fish soup, or fried Baltic herring with mashed potato, is easy to come by, and the cafés in the old quarter serve coffee and cardamom buns. The best time is summer, when the long evenings give light until late, and the old streets are at their most relaxed.

The ride combines Rauma with Alvar Aalto's sanatorium at Paimio, so you move from medieval timber to twentieth-century modernism in a day.
t.temple and former convent of saint mathh:
In the green valleys south of Mexico City, on the slopes below Popocatépetl, sixteenth-century friars built a chain of fortress-like monasteries, and the church and former convent of San Mateo at Atlatlahucan is one of them. The Augustinians arrived in the 1530s, after the Spanish conquest, and set about converting the local Nahua population, building enormous, thick-walled churches with open-air chapels where crowds could attend mass in the courtyard. The group of fourteen early monasteries on the slopes of the volcano was listed by UNESCO in 1994, and the architecture is a rare sight: plain, defensive on the outside, but inside the cloister are murals painted in black and white by indigenous artists under the friars' direction.

What you see at Atlatlahucan is a massive stone church with a simple facade, buttresses, crenellations and a square bell tower. The cloister, with its arched walkways, has faded frescoes showing saints and Augustinian emblems, and the details reveal a blending of European and Mesoamerican styles. The open chapel in front is a reminder that the first Christians here worshipped in the open air, as they had done for their old gods. The church is still in use, and visitors should be respectful during services.

The town itself, with nearly eight thousand people, is known for its carnival, when dancers called chinelos, in feathered hats and velvet robes with beards, hop through the streets to music. The countryside around is farmland and low hills, with sugarcane, corn, tomatoes and marigolds, and in the distance rises the white cone of Popocatépetl, an active volcano that sometimes puffs steam and ash.

Riding in Morelos is relaxed, with warm weather, light traffic on the quiet roads, and plenty of curves between small towns. The main roads are generally in fair shape, though potholes, speed bumps called topes, and livestock on the road call for attention. Atlatlahucan has fuel and small shops, but for larger supermarkets and services, Cuautla, a short ride south, is the usual place to go. Ash from the volcano can make roads slippery after an eruption.

The best season is November to April, when the air is dry, and the volcano is more often visible. Try a tlacoyo, a stuffed corn cake, from a market stall, and a cold drink of tepache.
t.asenovgrad@42.0,24.9:
Asenovgrad is the last proper town before the Rhodope Mountains, and it sits where the Thracian plain, flat, warm and full of vineyards, runs up against a wall of dark, forested hills. The town is large, with over fifty thousand people, and its streets, churches and markets feel Bulgarian in every detail. It was named after Tsar Ivan Asen II, the medieval ruler who rebuilt the nearby fortress, and the name of that fortress, Asen's Fortress, is what has made the place known to travellers.

The fortress stands on a cliff above the Asenitsa river gorge, a few kilometres south of the centre, and it consists of a ruined wall, a small tower and a surprisingly beautiful church, the Church of the Holy Mother of God of Petrich. The church clings to the rock and is covered with frescoes, and the view down the gorge to the plain is wide. The site has been fortified since ancient times, and Thracians, Romans and Byzantines all held it before the Bulgarians. A steep climb on foot is needed to reach the top, so wear boots you can walk in.

Asenovgrad is also known as a city of churches, and it has so many that it was once nicknamed Little Jerusalem. The old quarter, with its Ottoman-era houses, narrow streets and small chapels, rewards a wander. The area is also wine country, and the Mavrud grape, a dark local variety that produces rich, tannic red wines, is grown around the town. A glass in the evening, once the bike is parked, is a good introduction to Bulgarian wine.

For the rider, Asenovgrad is the gateway to the Rhodope Gorge Route, and the road south toward Bachkovo and Chepelare is a pleasure from the first kilometre. It follows the river through a canyon, with tight bends, rock walls and forest, and the surface is mostly good. Traffic can be heavy within the town, particularly on market days, and trucks use the main road, so be patient. Once you are out of the urban area, the road opens and the riding is delightful.

This is a proper town, with a range of fuel stations, supermarkets, banks, cafes and workshops, and it is the place to stock up before the mountains. Cash is useful in smaller establishments, and prices are low. Take a moment to try a banitsa, the cheese pastry that Bulgarians eat for breakfast, from a bakery near the centre.
t.bachkovo@41.9,24.9:
Bachkovo Monastery stands in a narrow valley on the Chepelare river, a few kilometres into the Rhodope Mountains, and it is the second largest monastery in Bulgaria after Rila. It was founded in 1083 by Gregory Pakourianos, a Georgian-born commander in the service of the Byzantine Empire, who built it as a retreat and a fortress, and for centuries it has been a centre of Orthodox faith and Bulgarian culture. Its stone walls, wooden balconies and courtyard trees have a calm that is quite at odds with the busy road outside.

The monastery's principal treasure is an icon of the Virgin Mary, said to have miraculous powers and to be of Georgian origin, which draws pilgrims throughout the year. The largest gathering comes in August, around the feast of the Assumption, when thousands of people climb the road in procession. The church interior is dark, gilded and richly painted, and in the old refectory there are murals by Zahari Zograf, the nineteenth-century painter, in which the figures stare out with disconcerting energy. Visitors are welcome, but modest dress is expected, with knees and shoulders covered, and photography is restricted inside the church.

The ride from Asenovgrad is the real beginning of the Rhodope Gorge Route. The road follows the river upstream through a gorge, with tight bends, rock walls on one side and the river on the other, and woods of oak and beech climbing the slopes. The surface is generally good but can be patched, and heavy traffic, including pilgrims' coaches and trucks, may slow things at busy times. The air smells of pine and wet stone, and in the early morning there is often mist on the river.

Outside the monastery gates there are restaurants, some built on stilts above the river, serving grilled trout, lamb, shopska salad and a local dish called kavarma, a slow-cooked stew of meat and vegetables. Prices are modest and portions are large, and a long lunch is the best way to spend an hour. A stall sells honey, herbs and tea made from mountain plants, and it is worth buying something to take home.

Fuel is not available at the monastery, but Asenovgrad is only about eight kilometres away and has everything you need. Fill the tank there before heading deeper into the mountains, where the stations become sparse. Spring and early autumn are the best seasons for riding.
t.shiroka laka@41.7,24.6:
Shiroka Laka is what a Rhodope village looks like when someone has decided not to knock it down. Tall stone houses with whitewashed upper floors and overhanging wooden balconies stack up the hillside above a small river, joined by lanes of cobbles that are steep enough to test a pair of motorcycle boots. The roofs are of heavy stone slabs, the walls are thick, and the whole village has been declared an architectural reserve, so the character of the place has been preserved with unusual care.

The village stands about ten kilometres from Chepelare in the central Rhodopes, a region of dark forest, deep valleys and high pasture that has been home to shepherds, charcoal burners and woodcutters for centuries. Shiroka Laka is best known for its music. Folk song and the gadulka and the gaida, the Rhodope bagpipe, have long been part of life here, and the village houses a school of folk arts where young musicians learn the old repertoire. If you walk along the main street on a summer evening, you may hear someone practising, and the sound carries a long way in the stillness.

The village is also famous for its kukeri, the masked dancers who appear at the start of spring to drive away evil spirits. Dressed in shaggy costumes with huge bells at the waist and elaborate masks, they leap and stamp through the streets on the Sunday and Monday before Lent. The Rhodope festival, called Pesponedelnik, has been held here for decades, and draws visitors from all over Bulgaria. It is a loud, colourful and slightly alarming spectacle, and a reminder that pagan customs run deep in the Balkan countryside.

The ride up the Chepelare valley from Bachkovo is one of the finest in Bulgaria, a sequence of flowing bends beside the river, climbing slowly through forest of beech, spruce and pine. The road surface is mostly good, but can be patchy after the winter, and trucks carry timber on the main road, so overtake with care. The air is cool and resinous, and in autumn the leaves turn bright gold and red.

The village is small and does not have fuel. Chepelare, about ten kilometres away, is the nearest sizeable town and has stations, shops and cafes. Locally you can eat well, with a few family restaurants serving bean soup, grilled meat and a thick yoghurt that tastes of the pasture, and prices that will make you wonder what everyone else is charging.
t.lepenski vir@44.6,22.0:
Lepenski Vir sits on a bend of the Danube in the Iron Gates gorge, and it holds the remains of one of the oldest settlements in Europe. People lived on this terrace by the river from roughly the tenth to the sixth millennium before our era, fishing, hunting and gathering, and later farming. They built trapezoid houses with plastered floors, arranged around a central hearth, and carved remarkable sculptures from river boulders: faces with round eyes and open mouths that look something like fish, set beside the hearths. Nothing in the nearby landscape prepares you for how old and strange they are.

The site has a story of its own. When the huge Iron Gates dam was built in the 1960s and 1970s, the rising water would have drowned the terrace, so the whole settlement was carefully moved upslope and rebuilt, with a museum placed over the remains. The original spot lies under the river. There is something poetic about a place that survived ten thousand years by the water and was then saved from it by engineers.

The setting is fine. The Danube here is squeezed into a gorge between the Carpathians and the Balkan mountains, a steep forested canyon that is among the deepest in Europe, with cliffs rising from the water and the opposite Romanian bank close enough to see farmhouses. The road along the Serbian bank runs through the Đerdap National Park, a gentle but constantly changing ribbon of tarmac that rises, falls and bends with the shoreline, with tunnels and rock cuttings and views of the broad, green-brown river. Surfaces are generally good, though occasional rockfall and patched asphalt appear, and trucks and tour buses are common in summer.
