Spring and autumn are the best times, with mist rising from the river in the morning and the forests in colour. Midsummer can be hot, but the river keeps things cooler. In the gorge, sections of the road were rerouted when the reservoir was created, so older maps can be misleading.

Check opening times before you come, as the museum hours can vary seasonally. Facilities are modest, a small café and toilets, so do not expect much more. Donji Milanovac, about fourteen kilometres downstream, is the nearest community with shops and fuel, and it is wise to fill up there before heading into the gorge.

Come with time to look, not just to photograph.
t.thessaloniki@40.6,22.9:
Thessaloniki wears its layers openly. Founded in 315 BC by Cassander, a general of Alexander the Great, who named it after his wife, a half-sister of Alexander, it became a major Roman city and then, for over a thousand years, the second city of the Byzantine Empire. Its seafront is dominated by the White Tower, a sixteenth-century fortification that is the symbol of the city, and the Arch of Galerius and the Rotunda, a Roman building that has been a temple, a church and a mosque, stand in the centre. Mustafa Kemal Atatürk was born here in 1881.

Life in the city is lived outdoors. The waterfront promenade is crowded in the evening, and the old market quarters are full of smells of spice, coffee and baking. A local favourite is bougatsa, a flaky pastry filled with custard or cheese, eaten for breakfast. The Ladadika district, once a market for oil merchants, is now full of tavernas, and the wine bars are lively.

For riders, the city is a gateway to Macedonia and the north. The ring road is quick, though it can be crowded at peak hours. The afternoon ride heads west, across the plain of Imathia, to Vergina, the site of ancient Aegae, where the royal tombs of the Macedonian kings, including that of Philip II, the father of Alexander, are preserved beneath a mound. The road crosses flat farmland, with orchards of peaches and cherries, and the view of the mountains, with Mount Olympus visible on clear days, is magnificent.

Fuel is plentiful, with big stations along the main roads. The wind, the Vardaris, can come down the valley from the north and bring a sharp chill in winter, while summer temperatures climb well into the thirties. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, when the light is clear and the sea breeze is mild. If you eat out, share a plate of mezedes, small dishes, with a glass of tsipouro, and take your time. The Byzantine churches here, with their glittering mosaics, repay a walk.
t.san juan raya@18.3,-97.6:
San Juan Raya is a village in a dry valley in the state of Puebla, and it is famous for two reasons that sit oddly together: a ruined sixteenth-century chapel and the sea. The sea part is ancient. The hills around the village are made of rock laid down in a shallow marine basin more than a hundred million years ago, and they are full of fossil snails and other shells, so many that you can find them on the ground. A small local museum, run by the community, shows the best of them. The valley is part of the Tehuacan-Cuicatlan Biosphere Reserve, listed by UNESCO in 2018, partly because this is one of the places where maize and other crops were first domesticated, thousands of years ago.

The landscape here is startling to people who think of Mexico as simply hot and dusty. The valley is famous for its columnar cacti, forests of tall, branching candelabra species and barrel cactus, mixed with agave, thorn scrub and yucca. In the rainy season, from June to September, the hills turn green and the cacti flower, and in the dry months the colour is grey and dust. Birds are plentiful and lizards bask on every warm rock. Early morning and late afternoon bring the best light and the coolest temperatures.

The old chapel stands on a rise above the village, its walls partly fallen and open to the sky. It dates from the colonial period and was never finished, and the stone has a handsome, weathered look. The people of San Juan Raya are proud of their heritage and manage visits themselves, so ask at the museum before heading to the chapel and hire a guide if you want to walk among the fossils.

The ride from Tehuacan is largely on paved road with a few stretches of gravel near the village. Fuel is best taken in Tehuacan, the nearest large city, since the villages along the way have no stations. Zapotitlan Salinas, nearby, has salt pans worked since pre-Hispanic times and a good botanical garden. Bring water, a hat and sun protection. The best time is autumn or spring, when the temperature is moderate.
t.villa mairea@61.6,21.9:
Villa Mairea stands in a pine wood at Noormarkku, in western Finland, and it is among the masterpieces of Alvar Aalto. He designed it in 1938 and 1939 for Harry and Maire Gullichsen, a wealthy industrial family who owned the Ahlstrom company, a large Finnish timber and engineering business, and who wanted a house that would be a laboratory for modern living. Aalto gave them a house that is white, curved and warm, with materials, wood, stone, brick and cane, mixed in a free and surprising manner. The living room opens through large glass doors to a garden, a sauna and a swimming pool shaped like a kidney, and the interior flows from room to room.

The details are what stay with you. Pine columns inside are wrapped in cane or bound in leather, as if they were tree trunks in a grove, and the stair has a screen of thin vertical posts that echoes the forest outside. A turf-roofed sauna stands on one side of the garden, a nod to Finnish tradition, and the outdoor space is as important as the rooms. The house was meant to show how modernism could be human rather than cold, and it does. Maire Gullichsen, an artist and patron, was the driving force in the commission and also supported Aalto's wider work, including the sanatorium at Paimio.

Visits need planning. The villa is now run by a foundation and it can be seen on guided tours, which must be booked in advance, and the season is limited, so check the dates before you set out. Photography inside may be restricted. The tour lasts about an hour, and the surrounding village of Noormarkku is also worth a walk, with its old ironworks, wooden workers' housing and a few other buildings by Aalto and by other architects.

The riding in Satakunta is flat and calm. Roads cross open farmland, lakes and pine forest, with long, gentle bends and light traffic. Elk are a hazard at dusk, particularly in autumn, and speed limits drop in winter. Pomarkku, thirteen kilometres away, has shops, while Pori, a town of eighty thousand people some twenty kilometres away, has everything. Food in Finland is simple and good: salmon soup, rye bread and cinnamon buns. The best season is from May to September, when the nights are light.
t.kitanoshima and peripheral reefs@27.7,14:
This one is for the map-lovers, because there is no road here at all. Kitanoshima, or North Island, belongs to the Mukojima group, a small cluster of islands in the Ogasawara or Bonin archipelago, about a thousand kilometres south of Tokyo in the Pacific Ocean. The islands were never connected to a continent, which is why their wildlife evolved in isolation, and the whole archipelago was listed as a Natural World Heritage site in 2011.

The only way to reach this part of the ocean is by sea. Regular ferries from Tokyo run to Chichijima, the main inhabited island, and the voyage takes about a day. From there, tour boats and fishing vessels can head out to the nearby island groups, depending on the weather and on rules that restrict landing to protect the fragile ecology. I would not pretend to know the current landing regulations, so check with the Ogasawara village office or a local operator. For a motorcyclist, the closest thing to riding is on Chichijima itself, a small island with a handful of coastal and hill roads, mostly narrow, quiet and winding, with views of green hills and blue bays.

What makes the reefs and islands special is life. The surrounding waters hold coral communities, reef fish, and sea turtles, with green turtles nesting on Ogasawara beaches, and humpback whales visit between about January and April. On land, the archipelago is a laboratory of evolution, with endemic land snails, insects and plants found nowhere else. The Bonin flying fox, a large fruit bat, lives on some islands. Invasive species, including goats and rats, have caused problems in the past, and extensive work has gone into restoring native vegetation.

The history is short but vivid. Polynesian and Micronesian visitors may have come earlier, but the islands were first settled in the nineteenth century by a mix of Westerners and Pacific islanders, and then claimed by Japan. During the Second World War the region saw heavy fighting at nearby Iwo Jima, and the islands came under American administration until 1968. Chichijima has the only services, so everything must be arranged there.
t.finlandia hall@60.2,24.9:
Finlandia Hall stands on the shore of Töölö Bay in the middle of Helsinki, a long white building by Alvar Aalto that opened in 1971. Aalto was Finland's greatest architect, and the hall is typical of his late work, a sculpted block with a sloping roof and a facade of white marble that has a surprisingly soft quality in the Nordic light. The marble has had a hard time with Helsinki's climate, because the thin slabs bowed in the cold and had to be replaced in a restoration. The hall is a concert and congress centre, and it was here in 1975 that European leaders, together with the United States, Canada and the Soviet Union, signed the Helsinki Final Act, a milestone in Cold War diplomacy.

The location is a joy for anyone who likes cities by the water. The bay is a park with paths for walkers and cyclists, the Parliament building and the National Museum are nearby, and the Sibelius monument, a cluster of steel pipes that looks like a giant organ, is a short ride away in Töölö. The city centre is compact, with the grand Neoclassical square and the white Lutheran cathedral on the hill, and the harbour market with its stalls of salmon, berries and coffee.

Riding in Helsinki is straightforward, with good surfaces, courteous drivers and clear signs, but you must watch for trams, cyclists and speed cameras. Speed limits are enforced firmly, and fines in Finland are linked to income, which is a good reason to stay under them. In winter, the roads are icy and motorcycling is out of the question, so the season runs roughly from May to September. Ferries from the harbour take you to Tallinn in about two hours, and the ride to the Estonian capital begins with a boat. For a rider looking for open road, the countryside north and west of Helsinki is lovely, with lakes, forests and low granite hills.

Fuel stations are everywhere in a city of well over half a million, with Kallio and Munkkiniemi having plenty of shops and cafes. Coffee is taken seriously, and Finns drink more of it than almost anyone, so a cup and a cinnamon bun are a proper way to spend a morning. The air near the bay smells of water and pine. In June the light barely fades at night, and a late ride along the shore under a pale sky is something you remember for years.
t.vaasa@63.1,21.6:
Vaasa has the odd distinction of being a city that moved. In 1852 a great fire destroyed the old town, and instead of rebuilding on the same spot, the authorities decided to start again a few kilometres to the north-west on the coast, with a grid of wide streets, a grand esplanade and a new harbour. The old site is now called Korsholm, and you can still find the ruins of the medieval parish church and the old wooden buildings. The newer city is an orderly, airy place, with a long park down the middle, and the sea at its edge.

Vaasa is on Finland's west coast, in Ostrobothnia, where a large Swedish-speaking minority lives alongside Finnish speakers, so signs are in two languages and the town is Vasa as well as Vaasa. The name goes back to the Vasa dynasty of Swedish kings. The city is known for its energy industry, with engine makers and wind-power companies, and for a lively student culture. The harbour area has a seafront promenade, and in summer the terraces fill with people eating ice cream and drinking beer.

The land here is flat. The Ostrobothnian plain is a vast agricultural area with large farms, red wooden barns and long straight roads, and the coast is made of shallow bays and low islands because the land is rising out of the sea after the last ice age. The riding is straight and easy, with little traffic, and it has a calm, almost meditative quality. Enforcement of speed limits is strict in Finland, with fines linked to income, so keep within the limits. Between May and September the days are very long, and in June the sun barely sets. Winter riding is out of the question, with ice and snow from November to March.

Fuel stations are numerous in a city of nearly sixty thousand, with Korsholm next door providing more. Finns drink a great deal of coffee, and a cup with a cinnamon bun is the standard break. The famous local delicacy is the Baltic herring, fried or smoked, and the markets sell it in summer. In the evening, a walk along the shore, with a smell of salt and seaweed, is a fine way to end the day. The islands of the Kvarken, to the west, are a short ride away and worth a visit.
t.high coast kvarken archipelago@63.3,21.3:
The Kvarken is a narrow strait in the Gulf of Bothnia, between Finland and Sweden, and a place where you can watch the land rise. At the end of the last ice age, a sheet of ice more than a kilometre thick pressed down on Scandinavia, and when it melted the crust began to rebound, a process that is still going on. Here the uplift is about eight or nine millimetres a year, one of the fastest rates in the world, so the coastline changes within a human lifetime. New islands emerge, bays turn into lakes and then into meadows, and boat channels need to be redrawn. The Finnish Kvarken Archipelago was listed by UNESCO in 2006 and later joined with Sweden's High Coast, which shares the same story.

The landscape is made of thousands of low islands, skerries and shallow bays, with long ridges of boulders called De Geer moraines, laid down in parallel lines by the retreating ice. They run like corrugations across the land, a pattern you can see from the air. On the ground, you see pine woods, juniper and reeds, with seabirds including eider ducks and terns nesting on the rocks and grey seals hauled out on the skerries. The air is clear and cold, and the smell of salt and tar is strong.

For a rider, the road to the archipelago crosses the flat farmland near Vaasa, then runs over a series of bridges to the islands, with the long Replot bridge the most impressive, a long causeway-like crossing between the mainland and the outer islands. The road surface is good, the bends are gentle, and traffic is light, except in July. Wind can be strong over the open water, so be careful on the bridges, and keep a layer of warm clothing in the pannier even in summer. Daylight in June lasts almost around the clock.

Fuel is available in Vaasa, about twenty-eight kilometres away, and in Korsholm, so fill up before crossing. Replot has a village with a small shop, but it is small. Fishermen's cottages, red with white trim, sit beside little harbours, and you can buy smoked fish and rye bread in season. The best time is June to August, though September can be lovely, with clear light and few people. Stand on the shore for a while, and you may notice how the sea seems to be quietly retreating.
t.the kvarken archipelago zone a@63.3,21.3:
Zone A of the Kvarken is the outer world of islands, where the road gives way to boats. The Kvarken Archipelago is a maze of more than five thousand islands and islets, many of them barely a metre above the water, scattered across the shallow Gulf of Bothnia, and only a few are inhabited. The ones with year-round residents are reached by bridge or ferry, and live by fishing, small farming and, increasingly, by visitors who come for the quiet. The landscape here is slow and subtle, with horizons so low that sky and water seem to be the main features, and trees bent by the wind.

The settlements are tiny and tidy. Replot, the largest island, has a few thousand residents spread out along the roads, with fishing harbours and boathouses, and the sea has always been central to life. Fishing for Baltic herring and perch is still practised, and in the autumn you may see nets hung out to dry. The land is also used for grazing, and in the summer sheep and cows can be seen on the coastal meadows, where wildflowers bloom. Seals bask on the rocks in the sunshine, and white-tailed eagles circle above.

The riding is straightforward. The roads are narrow and quiet, with a good surface, and traffic is very light outside the summer weekends. The bridges and causeways are a pleasure, and the openness gives a feeling of freedom. In the wind, which can be considerable, you will feel the bike pushed about, so ride with a loose grip. The weather can shift quickly, with mist rolling in from the sea or a squall bringing rain, so a waterproof layer is wise. In winter the strait freezes, and ice roads are made for cars, though a motorbike is not suited to them.

Fuel stations and shops are on the mainland, in Vaasa and Korsholm, and there are few on the islands, so start with a full tank and bring food. A small cafe near the harbour may be open in summer, serving coffee, cake and fish soup. The smell of the place is seaweed, pine and diesel from fishing boats, and the sound is gulls and a distant engine. The best light comes late in the day, when the low sun turns the water to copper and the islands to dark shapes.
t.turku@60.5,22.3:
Turku is the oldest city in Finland, and it was the capital until 1812, when the Russian tsar moved the government to Helsinki, closer to St Petersburg. The old name is Åbo, from the Swedish, and the city still has a significant Swedish-speaking community. The heart of the town is the Aura river, which runs through the centre to the sea, lined with restaurants and boats, and the great stone cathedral, Finland's national shrine, stands on a hill above it. The medieval cathedral dates from the late thirteenth century, and its tower, which has burned and been rebuilt several times, is a well-known landmark.

The city was devastated by a great fire in 1827, and most of the old wooden town was lost, but a small part survived on the hill of Luostarinmäki, where a group of old craftsmen's houses is now a museum of handicrafts, with rooms furnished as they would have been in the early nineteenth century. Turku Castle, at the mouth of the river, is an even older structure, begun in the 1280s, and it served as a royal fortress, a prison and a noble residence. The runner Paavo Nurmi, nine times an Olympic champion, was born in the city, and a statue of him stands outside the stadium.

Turku is also the gateway to the Archipelago Sea, a huge scatter of islands between Finland and Sweden, and the ferries to Stockholm leave from the harbour. The road from Turku to Rauma, along the west coast, passes through farmland and forest with gentle bends, and the surface is generally good. Traffic is moderate near the city and light further on. The old town of Rauma, with its wooden houses and cobbled streets, is a World Heritage Site and a good place for lunch. Speed cameras are common, and Finnish traffic fines are high.

Fuel stations are plentiful in a city of about a hundred and seventy-six thousand people, and Raisio and Kaarina, on the outskirts, have more. The riverside cafes serve coffee and sweet pastries, and in summer, boats serve as bars along the quay. The smell of the river on a warm day is a mix of water and cut grass, and the light on the cathedral at dusk is soft and golden. If you arrive in the early morning, the city is still and the river is glassy.
t.mediaeval town of ras@43.1,20.4:
Ras was the cradle of Serbia. In the twelfth century Stefan Nemanja, founder of the Nemanjić dynasty, made it the centre of his state, and its fortress, set on a hill above the Raška river, was the political heart of the Serbian lands for generations. The old town has largely fallen into ruin and lies on a green hill called Gradina, near the modern city of Novi Pazar, with walls, a fortified gate and traces of buildings in the grass.

Below the hill stand two great monuments of Serbian religious life. The Church of Saints Peter and Paul, Petrova Crkva, is among the oldest surviving churches in the country, with a round tower and early Byzantine-influenced architecture, and nearby the Djurdjevi Stupovi monastery, the Pillars of Saint George, was founded by Nemanja himself in the 1170s. A few kilometres away, Sopoćani monastery, built in the thirteenth century by King Uroš I, has frescoes regarded as masterpieces of Byzantine painting. They were painted in a luminous style, with figures that seem to breathe.

Novi Pazar, the nearby city, is quite different in feel: an Ottoman-era town with a large Bosniak Muslim population, mosques, a bustling old bazaar and fine grilled meat. The region is known as Sandžak and sits between Serbia and Montenegro, with a mix of cultures. The Church of the Virgin of Leviša, in Prizren, Kosovo, is the ride's other stop, part of the same heritage listing of medieval monuments.

The roads here wind through green hills and pastures, with orchards and small farms, and are mostly decent, though trucks make the main road busy. Fuel is easy in Novi Pazar. Sunday visits to the monasteries are respectful occasions, and modest dress is expected. Burek and cevapi are everywhere, with yoghurt to drink. Late spring has the best light, and winter brings snow to the hills.
t.gracanica monastery@42.6,21.2:
Gračanica is a monastery of five small domes rising from a Kosovo plain a few kilometres south-east of Pristina, and it is one of the most graceful medieval buildings in the Balkans. King Stefan Milutin of Serbia had it built around 1321 on the site of an older church, and its cross-shaped plan, tall drum-shaped domes and bands of brick and stone make it a masterpiece of the late Byzantine style. UNESCO lists it among the Medieval Monuments in Kosovo.

Inside, the frescoes are what stop people talking. They were painted in the early fourteenth century, in deep blues and reds, and show Milutin with his queen, scenes from the life of Christ and the Virgin, and a Last Judgement. The figures have a calm, elongated elegance. The monastery is an active convent and its nuns tend the garden and run a small shop, so dress modestly, speak quietly and ask before taking photographs inside, as rules vary.

The monastery stands in a village that is predominantly Serbian, within a country whose population is mostly Albanian, and the history of the region is painful and recent. The monument has been under international protection since the war of 1999, and you may see peacekeeping soldiers or police at the gate. Visitors are welcome, but it is a sensitive place, and politely listening and not discussing politics is the safest approach.

Pristina, about ten kilometres away, is a lively, young capital with a grand library of white metal mesh, a huge statue of Skanderbeg and cafes full of students. Lipljan, the nearest town, is small. Roads are decent but traffic can be heavy and drivers impatient. Kosovo uses the euro, and fuel and food are easy, with grilled meat, flija pie and strong coffee on every corner. Check the insurance rules for foreign vehicles at the border, since the green card requirements have varied, and allow time for formalities.
t.prehistoric caves of yagul and mitla in:
Far back in the story of human food, a cave in the Oaxaca valley holds some of the oldest evidence of the domestication of maize. In Guilá Naquitz, one of the caves of Yagul, excavations in the 1960s found small cobs of wild corn and squash seeds dated to around ten thousand years ago, showing how early hunter-gatherers began to cultivate plants. UNESCO inscribed the Prehistoric Caves of Yagul and Mitla in 2010 for that evidence.

The valley is also home to later civilisations. The Zapotecs ruled from Monte Albán for a thousand years, and Yagul was a fortified hilltop city, with a ball court, a labyrinthine palace of connecting rooms and a view over cactus-dotted plains. Mitla, nearby, was a religious centre, famous for its stone mosaics, geometric friezes made of thousands of cut stones fitted without mortar, which are unlike anything else in Mexico. The town is still a living Zapotec community.

The Tlacolula valley is a dry, open country of agave and organ pipe cactus, and mezcal is made here. Santiago Matatlán, a short distance away, calls itself the world capital of mezcal, and small distilleries offer tastings. Tlacolula's Sunday market, one of the oldest and biggest in the region, fills the town with food, livestock, textiles and crafts, so it is crowded but memorable. Hierve el Agua, a petrified waterfall of mineral deposits and natural pools, lies farther east.

The road from Oaxaca is Highway 190, a busy but good road, with trucks and buses and a lot of speed bumps in the villages. Sun and dust are strong in the dry season, from November to April, and the rains from June to September bring storms. Fuel is easy in Tlacolula, and you can eat tlayudas, big crisp tortillas with beans, cheese and meat, and drink hot chocolate with cinnamon. Take water and a hat when you climb to the caves.
t.mexico city@19.4,-99.1:
Mexico City is a lot of things at once: enormous, high, noisy, beautiful, tiring, and endlessly generous. About twenty million people live in its metropolitan area, at an altitude of roughly 2,240 metres, in a basin ringed by volcanoes that rarely show themselves through the haze. It stands on the bed of an old lake, and on that lake the Mexica built Tenochtitlan in the fourteenth century, a city of canals and causeways that astonished the Spanish when they arrived in 1519.

The past lies directly under the present. The ruins of the Templo Mayor, the Aztec main temple, were found in 1978 beside the cathedral on the Zócalo, which is the huge central square, and the cathedral itself, begun in 1573, leans a little as it sinks into the soft ground. The city has been shaken by earthquakes, notably in 1985 and 2017, and many buildings show repairs. Museums are among the world's finest, including the Anthropology Museum in Chapultepec Park, with its Aztec sun stone and the Maya halls.

For a rider, the capital is better entered by plan than by improvisation. Traffic is dense, lanes are fluid, and motorcycles filter through, so stay alert for buses, taxis and potholes, and avoid rush hours. Several roads have driving restrictions based on number plates on days of heavy pollution, so check the rules if you are in a foreign vehicle. Mountain roads in the surrounding highlands, toward Toluca, Cuernavaca or Puebla, climb to cool, pine-covered passes with good curves.

Fuel is abundant, and food is endless: tacos al pastor cut from a spit, tamales for breakfast, mole, and street stalls with fresh fruit. The altitude takes a day to get used to, and a sudden afternoon storm in the rainy season, from June to September, arrives with hail. The old college of San Francisco Javier, at Tepotzotlan, on the northern outskirts, with its golden baroque church, is a treat beyond the city's edge.
t.tehuacan cuicatlan valley originary habi:
The Tehuacán-Cuicatlán valley is a dry trench between the mountains of Puebla and Oaxaca, and it holds one of the richest deserts in the world. Rain falls rarely here, since the high ranges on either side block the moisture, and in that shadow grow forests of columnar cactus, some of the densest anywhere. Candelabra-shaped tetechos and tall organ pipes stand shoulder to shoulder across the hills, with agaves, yuccas and tree-like plants whose bark peels in red papery sheets.

UNESCO inscribed the valley in 2018 as a mixed site, for both its biodiversity and its place in the history of agriculture. People here began to cultivate maize, beans, squash and chilli thousands of years ago, and early farmers built canals and dams to water their fields. Near Purrón, a stone-and-earth dam from about 700 BC is regarded as one of the oldest in the Americas, and at San Juan Raya, fossil shells lie in the hills from a time when this was an ancient sea.

The roads through the valley are hot, curving and often empty. Highway 135 runs through a gorge, past salt works at Zapotitlán Salinas, where villagers have evaporated brine for centuries, and small towns where goat cheese and mole are sold. The landscape is very beautiful in the late afternoon, with the cactus casting long shadows, but the heat in summer can reach forty degrees, and storms in the rainy season cause flash floods in dry riverbeds. Winter is mild and the best season.

The nearest villages, such as San Juan de los Cués and Tecomavaca, are small, with limited services, and Teotitlán has more. Fuel can be sparse, so top up in Tehuacán or Oaxaca before entering. Carry plenty of water and a hat. Local cooks offer goat barbecue and tamales, and the cactus fruit, pitaya, is sold in season. Please do not collect plants or fossils, which are protected, and drive carefully for wandering goats.
t.gamzigrad romuliana@43.9,22.2:
On a low hill in eastern Serbia stand the remains of a palace built for a Roman emperor to retire to, and it never quite worked out that way. Galerius, one of the four rulers of the Roman world under Diocletian's system, was born in this region, and in the late third and early fourth century he had a fortified palace built near his birthplace and named it Felix Romuliana, after his mother, Romula. The walls, with their projecting towers and gates, enclosed temples, halls and baths, and the mosaic floors and carved fragments recovered by archaeologists show how splendid it was. Galerius died in 311, and he was buried here, in a mausoleum on a hill nearby, where two burial mounds still stand. The site is a World Heritage monument and one of the best-preserved late Roman palaces anywhere.

The surrounding country is quiet and open, in the valley of the Timok river between the mountains of the Stara Planina and the hills toward the Danube. It is a region of small farms, orchards and vineyards, with villages of low houses and a thin traffic, and Zaječar, the town about six kilometres away, is the local centre, with a few cafes and a museum. A small spa, Gamzigradska Banja, lies by the ruins, with sulphur water that locals say is good for the joints.

The riding is relaxed. Roads in eastern Serbia are usually quiet, with long gentle curves over low ridges, and the surface is a mixture of good and patched asphalt, where potholes and gravel at the edges require attention. The landscape grows more dramatic toward the Danube and Romania, with gorges and forest, and the route onward here crosses into Romania toward the Domogled and Cerna valley. Check border crossing opening hours and the paperwork needed for your bike and insurance before you set out, as eastern crossings can be slow in summer.

Fuel is easy in Zaječar, a town of about fifty thousand, and in Bor to the west, but smaller villages may have none, so keep the tank topped up. Food is generous, with grilled meat, peppers and cheese, and strong plum brandy offered with hospitality. Late afternoon light on the ruins is warm, and the site is usually quiet enough to be alone with the walls.
t.belgrade@44.8,20.5:
Belgrade sits where the Sava runs into the Danube, a strategic spot that has been fought over for more than two thousand years, by Celts, Romans, Byzantines, Ottomans, Habsburgs and others, and the city has been destroyed and rebuilt dozens of times. The fortress of Kalemegdan, on the ridge above the meeting of the rivers, is where that long story is easiest to see, with its walls, gates and gardens giving a wide view across the water to the flat plain of Vojvodina. The park below is where the city strolls on Sunday afternoons.

The old centre runs from the fortress along the pedestrian Knez Mihailova street, full of shops and cafes, and out to Skadarlija, a cobbled bohemian street of old taverns where musicians play tamburica in the evenings. The great white Church of Saint Sava, one of the biggest Orthodox churches in the world, stands on a hill in the south and took decades to finish. The city is loud, warm and sociable, and nightlife is a local specialty, with bars and clubs on boats along the rivers. In daytime the grilled meat and burek from a bakery are the usual lunch, with a thick coffee to follow.

Leaving Belgrade by motorcycle takes some care, as traffic is dense and drivers are quick, but the countryside opens soon enough. North across the Danube lies the plain of Vojvodina, flat and fertile, and to the north-west the low wooded ridge of Fruška Gora, with monasteries hidden in the hills and vineyards on the slopes, makes a pleasant day. South of the city, the hill of Avala has a tower and a view, and the roads to the east follow the Danube toward the gorge of the Iron Gates. Surfaces are variable, with new motorways and roads in good condition, but also stretches of potholes in towns and villages, and police are strict on speeding.

Fuel is on every approach road and plentiful across Serbia, with the big stations on the motorways open all hours. Remember that foreign registration needs the right paperwork at borders, and the green card for insurance is worth carrying. The river banks at Ada Ciganlija, an island with a lake, are good for a swim in summer, and cafes on the quays are busy until late, which makes a ride back into the city in the evening a lively end to the day.
t.yuzhno sakhalinsk@47.0,142.7:
Yuzhno-Sakhalinsk is the capital of Sakhalin, a long, narrow island off Russia's Pacific coast, and its history has a double layer. Until 1945 the southern half of the island belonged to Japan, and this city was called Toyohara, the administrative centre of a Japanese territory known as Karafuto. After the Soviet forces took control at the end of the Second World War, most of the Japanese population left, the city was renamed, and the Koreans who had been brought to the island as labourers formed a community that remains large today.

You can still see the Japanese past if you look. The regional museum, a handsome building with a pagoda-style roof from the 1930s, was built as the Karafuto Museum, and a few old shrines and stone buildings survive in the city. The streets are laid out on a neat grid in the way Japanese planners favoured, with the mountains behind the city and the broad valley of the Susuya river running toward the sea. The population is about a hundred and seventy-five thousand.

Sakhalin's recent wealth comes from oil and gas, which are produced offshore and piped to the coast, and the city shows signs of it in its new buildings and busy shops. On a hill above the town, the mountain Bolshevik has a ski resort with a cable car, and in summer the view from the top over the valley and the sea is lovely. The nearby Lake Tunaicha is a quieter place for a walk.

For riders, the island's roads offer very different moods. The road to Kholmsk, on the west coast, crosses the mountain range through forests of fir and bamboo, and descends to the Tatar Strait, where the ferries leave for the mainland. The road to Aniva Bay in the south follows the coast through villages and dunes, past old Japanese lighthouses and broad beaches. The climate is damp and foggy, so expect mist and rain even in summer, and the surfaces vary from smooth to broken. The vegetation is rich and strange, with giant butterbur plants growing taller than a person.

Fuel, shops and cafés are plentiful in the city. Seafood is the highlight, including crab, sea urchin and salmon, and Korean-style salads are everywhere. Late summer and early autumn are the best times, though typhoon rain can arrive in September.
t.makarov@48.6,142.8:
Makarov is a small town in the middle of Sakhalin island, and its name carries a history. Until 1945, it belonged to Japan, and was called Shirutoru, one of the settlements of the Japanese territory of Karafuto. After the Soviet occupation, it was renamed for Admiral Stepan Makarov, the Russian naval commander and polar explorer who died in 1904 when his flagship struck a mine off Port Arthur. About six and a half thousand people live here, and the town has a modest, working feel.

Sakhalin is a rich and unusual island, and the landscape around Makarov reflects it. It is covered in dense forest of fir and spruce, with thickets of dwarf bamboo, and in the clearings the plants grow to huge size, including giant butterbur and a towering knotweed that can reach the height of a house. The rivers fill with salmon in late summer and autumn, and the brown bears of the island gather to feed, so anyone walking by a river should be careful and make noise. Fog and rain are frequent, and the weather can change in minutes.

The roads on the island are a patchwork. The main north-south highway links the larger towns and is mostly paved, but the secondary roads can be rough, with potholes and gravel, and bridges over the many rivers may be narrow. Traffic is light, and trucks carry timber and fish. The road toward the east coast leads to quiet bays and long beaches where the Sea of Okhotsk rolls in cold and grey, with driftwood piled on the sand and seabirds overhead.

The island also has old railway lines from the Japanese era, some of which are still used, and the narrow gauge of the local track is a legacy of that time. Look out for old stone and concrete remains of Japanese buildings in the forest, covered in moss.

Fuel is available in Makarov, but stations are few on the island, so fill up whenever you can. The town has a few shops and simple cafés where you can eat fish soup, dumplings and salads. Summers are short, cool and damp, with mosquitoes and midges, and the best period is late July to early September. Winters are long and heavy with snow.
t.berat@40.7,20.0:
Berat is called the town of a thousand windows, and for once the nickname is just. Ottoman-era white houses climb the hillside above the River Osum in tiers, their tall windows stacked like the faces of a theatre. On the north bank, the Mangalem quarter rises to a fortress, the Kala, whose walls still enclose a living neighbourhood, with families, churches and small cafes inside; on the south bank, Gorica faces it across a stone bridge. UNESCO inscribed the old town with Gjirokastër in 2008, and it is among the most attractive in the Balkans.

The valley around is a wide, farmed plain with olive groves, vineyards and the backdrop of Mount Tomorr, which rises beyond to more than 2,400 metres and is sacred to the Bektashi, a Sufi order who make a pilgrimage up the mountain in August. Inside the castle, the museum dedicated to the icon painter Onufri holds some of the finest religious painting in Albania, and the churches have more frescoes than you would guess from the street. The old riverfront has been repaved, and in the evening the whole town goes out for a stroll, called the xhiro.

Riding here asks for attention. Albanian roads have improved enormously, but surfaces can be broken, with potholes, rough patches and gravel at the edges, and drivers pass on blind bends, so give everybody room. Livestock turns up in the middle of the road without warning, and the best defence is to slow down in villages and cut your speed after dusk. The back road toward Tepelenë crosses dry hills and river gorges, and in the Osum canyon region further east the rock walls close in dramatically. Spring, when the hills are green and the rivers run, and early autumn are the best seasons. Summer afternoons are hot.

Berat is a proper town, with almost forty-seven thousand people, so fuel is straightforward and so is food, with byrek, grilled meat, local wine and raki on offer in the old quarters. Nearby Kuçovë, once an oil town renamed Qyteti Stalin in the communist period, shows another side of the country. Park at the bottom of the old town and walk up, because the cobbled lanes were not made for a loaded bike.
t.prizren@42.2,20.7:
Prizren lies where the Lumbardhi river pours out of the Šar Mountains, with the old town packed on both banks and a hilltop fortress, the Kalaja, keeping watch above. It is the most attractive city in Kosovo, and also one of the most layered. Ottoman mosques, an Orthodox church, a Catholic cathedral and a stone bridge crowd close together around the central square, and on summer evenings the whole place is out walking by the river. The population is large, well over a hundred thousand in the municipality, but the old centre feels almost village-sized.

The history is weighty. The Sinan Pasha Mosque, built in the early seventeenth century, dominates the square, and the arched stone bridge across the river is a defining image. In 1878 the League of Prizren met here, a key moment in the Albanian national movement. In the Middle Ages the town was a seat of the Serbian ruler Stefan Dušan, and the medieval Church of Our Lady of Ljeviš, with its frescoes, is part of the UNESCO listing of Kosovo's medieval monuments. For a few days in August, the Dokufest documentary film festival fills the cafes with film people, which gives the place an unusual energy.

The roads out of Prizren head in several directions, and all are interesting. Toward the mountains the valley road climbs through villages and orchards toward Šar Mountains National Park, with forest, rock and mountain pasture ahead. The surface is a mixture, often good on the main routes and poor on minor ones, and you need to watch for potholes, livestock and drivers who overtake generously. Weather in the mountains turns quickly, and snow lasts late. Spring and autumn are good for riding, and summer lunchtimes can be hot.

Practicalities are easy in a city this size. Fuel stations are on all main roads, the euro is the currency, and food is excellent, with grilled meat, flija pastry in some places, peppers, and strong coffee served everywhere. Carry your insurance documents for the border crossings, because they are checked, and check current requirements before travelling. Parking near the old town is limited, so leave the bike at your accommodation and walk the river lanes.
t.debar@41.5,20.5:
Debar sits in the far west of North Macedonia, close to the Albanian border, in a bowl of hills at the northern end of an artificial lake. It is a town of eighteen thousand people with a mixed population, mostly Albanian and Macedonian, a long history of trade and a reputation for craft: woodcarving, silverwork and weaving. Its old bazaar, its mosques and churches and a cluster of small spas on the outskirts give it a layered feel, and the pace of life is easy. The lake was created in the 1960s by the Spilje dam on the Black Drin.

The road north from Debar is where the ride begins. It follows the Radika River up a spectacular gorge into the Mavrovo National Park, one of the largest in the country, and the walls of the canyon are steep and thick with forest. Halfway up, the monastery of St Jovan Bigorski clings to a cliff above the river, with a carved wooden iconostasis from the nineteenth century, so intricately worked that it is considered one of the finest in the Balkans. The monks sell honey and rakija.

Beyond the gorge, the valley opens into the Mavrovo basin, with its lake, ski slopes and mountain villages. The village of Galicnik is perched on a ridge at over fourteen hundred metres, famous for a wedding festival held every July in which traditional dress, music and dance are on display. The roads to it are steep and tight, with sharp bends and few barriers, and the surface is variable. Weather in the mountains changes fast, with cold nights even in summer, and snow closes the high roads in winter.

Debar has fuel stations on the main road, and the nearest large town in the valley is Gostivar, so fill up here before the climb. There is little out in the mountains, but small cafes serve grilled meat, cheese pie and strong coffee. The best months are May to October. Mountain roads have livestock, wandering dogs and the occasional tractor, so keep your speed down. The reward is a landscape of wild forest and high pasture, little visited and very quiet.
t.ohrid@41.1,20.8:
Lake Ohrid is one of the oldest lakes in Europe, perhaps two or three million years old, and it has a character that sets it apart. It lies on the border between North Macedonia and Albania, a deep, clear body of water about thirty kilometres long, ringed by mountains, and it is home to more than two hundred species found nowhere else, including the Ohrid trout and a number of tiny snails and crustaceans. UNESCO listed the lake and the town in 1979 and 1980, for both natural and cultural reasons.

The town of Ohrid, with fifty-five thousand people, climbs a hill above the water, a tumble of red roofs, old houses and cobbled lanes. Samuel's Fortress crowns the top, a medieval castle with long walls and views across the lake, and below, on a rocky point over the water, stands the little church of St John at Kaneo, thirteenth century, one of the most photographed in the Balkans. It was here, in the ninth century, that the disciples of Saints Cyril and Methodius, including Clement, taught Slavic literacy, spreading the Cyrillic alphabet, and Ohrid was once said to have had three hundred and sixty-five churches, one for each day of the year.

The ride goes south around the lake, past Sveti Naum monastery, near the Albanian border, where springs bubble up at the foot of a cliff and peacocks wander in the courtyard. Beyond is the crossing into Albania, where the road continues along the shore. The roads are generally good, with gentle curves, views of the water and the mountains of Galicica National Park rising on one side. In summer, the lake is warm enough for swimming, and the beaches are crowded. Spring and early autumn are calmer. Winds can pick up in the afternoon.

Ohrid has fuel stations on the main roads, shops and many restaurants, so fill up before the border. Try the Ohrid trout, a protected species, so it is not always on the menu, and look for the cultured pearls made by a local workshop with a secret method. Allow time for the border crossing, and carry the vehicle papers and insurance. The old town is best on foot, early in the morning, when the light on the water is soft.
t.zapotitlan cuicatlan@18.0,-97.2:
The Tehuacan-Cuicatlan valley is a basin of dry land in the mountains of southern Mexico, between the states of Puebla and Oaxaca, and it holds something unusual: the greatest density of columnar cacti in the world. Tall candelabra shapes, some of them ten metres high and centuries old, stand in forests across the hillsides, with agaves, yuccas and thorny shrubs around them, and in spring they flower white. UNESCO listed the valley in 2018 as a mixed site, for both its biodiversity and its human history, and it is also a biosphere reserve.

The history is remarkable. Caves in the valley, such as Coxcatlan, hold the oldest known remains of domesticated maize, small cobs dating back thousands of years, and the valley is regarded as one of the cradles of Mesoamerican agriculture. The inhabitants also developed an intricate system of canals and aqueducts to carry water across the dry land, and they harvested salt from springs at Zapotitlan Salinas, where the salt pans are still used. San Juan Raya, nearby, is a village on a hill with a sixteenth-century church and fossil beds with marine shells, evidence that this land was once under a shallow sea.

The ride here crosses dry, hot country. The federal highway between Tehuacan and Oaxaca is a good road, with curves through canyons and views of cacti in all directions, and the side roads to the villages are narrower, with potholes and occasional livestock. It is hot for most of the year, so ride in the morning, and carry water. Thunderstorms between June and September can bring flash floods in the dry riverbeds, so watch the sky. The desert light at dawn and dusk is warm and soft.

Teotitlan, the nearest sizeable town, has about seven and a half thousand people and some services, and Tehuacan, farther north, is bigger and has fuel in abundance. Fill up in one or the other, since the villages may not have stations. Try mole and tlayudas, the large crisp tortillas of Oaxaca, and drink plenty of water. The cactus forest is best seen in the early morning, before the heat builds.
t.plovdiv@42.1,24.7:
Plovdiv is one of the oldest continuously lived-in cities in Europe, and it wears its age with a kind of cheerful disorder. People have lived on these rocky hills beside the Maritsa River for some eight thousand years, and the Romans, who called the city Philippopolis, left a theatre that is still used for concerts, carved into the hillside and facing out across the rooftops. The name comes from Philip II of Macedon, who took the town in the fourth century BC. With about three hundred thousand people, it is Bulgaria's second city, and it has every kind of shop and fuel station you might need.

The old town sits on three of the city's famous hills, with cobbled lanes, painted wooden houses from the Bulgarian National Revival and a huge variety of galleries and cafés. Below it, the Kapana district, a tangle of narrow streets, is the place to find coffee, craft beer and small restaurants, and it was a big part of the city's year as European Capital of Culture in 2019. Bulgarian food here is very good: shopska salad, grilled meats, cold yoghurt soup and rakia, a fruit brandy that arrives at the table whether you ask for it or not.

For the ride, Plovdiv is the flatland start before the mountains. The Thracian plain is warm, fertile and flat, with fruit orchards and roses, and the Rhodope range rises as a blue wall to the south. You head toward Asenovgrad, past the ruined fortress of Asen and the Bachkovo Monastery, founded in the eleventh century and one of the great Orthodox sites of the country. From there the road tightens into the Rhodope gorges, with rock walls, pine forest and the first of the hairpins.

Traffic in Plovdiv is chaotic in the way of southern European cities, with impatient drivers and tram-like confidence, so give yourself room. Fuel is cheaper than in western Europe and widely available, and you should top up before you climb, since the mountain villages are small. Summer is hot, up in the thirties Celsius, so a morning start is wise; spring and autumn are gentler, and the plain is lovely when the roses bloom in late May and June.
t.trigrad gorge@41.6,24.4:
Trigrad Gorge is where the Rhodope Mountains show their teeth. The Trigradska river has cut a deep, narrow canyon through the limestone, with walls that rise some three hundred metres on either side, and the road runs along the bottom of it with the sound of water in your ear. Sunlight arrives late and leaves early, and the air is cool even in summer. The gorge sits close to the village of Trigrad, a small Rhodope settlement, with Devin, a spa town of about seven thousand, some sixteen kilometres away and the best bet for fuel and food.

The famous feature is the Devil's Throat Cave, or Dyavolskoto Garlo, where the river vanishes into a huge cavern with a thunderous roar. Legend says this is the entrance Orpheus took when he went down into the underworld to look for his wife Eurydice, and the Rhodopes are said to be his homeland. A wooden stairway leads you up to the mouth of the cave, and from the top the sight of the river disappearing into the dark is properly dramatic. The cave is a major site for bats and is open for visits at set times, so check before you arrive.

The riding is the sort that makes you slow down, which is the point. The road through the gorge is narrow, with tight bends, rough patches and the occasional rockfall, and the surface in this part of Bulgaria is variable, with potholes that can appear without warning. Cows, goats and sheep cross at will, and so do the occasional tractors. In the mountains, Pomak and Bulgarian villages sit on the slopes, with stone houses, wooden balconies and tiny mosques and churches, and local cooking, such as patatnik, a potato dish, and banitsa, the flaky cheese pie, is hearty and cheap.

Fuel in the high villages is scarce, so fill the tank in Devin or Smolyan. The weather in the Rhodopes can turn quickly, with afternoon storms in summer and early snow in autumn, so keep an eye on the clouds. The best time to come is late spring or early autumn, when the beech forests turn gold and the roads are mostly empty. After a ride through the gorge, a bowl of hot soup tastes better than almost anything.
t.belgrade@44.8,20.4:
Belgrade is a city built on a fault line between worlds, and it announces the fact where the Sava river meets the Danube beneath the old fortress of Kalemegdan. This is where the ride begins, in a capital of well over a million people, noisy, restless, a bit scruffy and constantly alive. It has been fought over by Romans, Byzantines, Hungarians, Ottomans and Austrians, and the fortress walls carry the scars of all of them. Climb up in the early morning, before the day starts, and you can look across the confluence to the flat green plains of Vojvodina.

Getting out is the only part that needs patience. Belgrade traffic is dense, drivers are assertive, tram tracks and cobbles lie in wait, and the ring roads can be slow at rush hour. Once past Zemun, an old Habsburg town on the Danube that still has its own Austro-Hungarian feel, things loosen up and the river road begins. Fuel is on every other corner, so top up before you leave the city and carry some cash for tolls and small shops along the way.

The Danube route east is a real journey. You pass the huge fortress of Smederevo, built in the 1400s by the Serbian despot Đurađ Branković as the last redoubt before the Ottomans overran the country. Then the landscape tightens as the river is squeezed through the Iron Gates, a gorge on the border with Romania, with cliffs on both banks and fortresses like Golubac standing on the shore. Farther on, a carved Roman inscription commemorates the legions who first built a road along this wall of rock.

Before you ride out, eat. The Belgrade bakery breakfast of burek, a flaky cheese or meat pie, with yoghurt, is a local ritual, and later in the day a kafana, the traditional tavern, will serve grilled meat with kajmak, a salty cream spread, and a rakija, the local fruit brandy, that you should treat with respect before getting back on the bike. The spring and autumn light on the water is the best of the year, and the summers are hot and humid, so the early start makes sense.
t.divundu@-18.1,21.5:
Divundu is a crossroads in a place that otherwise barely has roads. It lies where the Okavango River, having come down from Angola and spread out across the sand, squeezes through a rocky step known as Popa Falls before it fans into the great delta far to the south. The settlement, along with neighbouring Bagani, sits inside the western end of the Caprivi Strip, a thin finger of Namibia that Germany acquired from Britain in 1890 in a deal that also traded away Zanzibar. A boundary drawn in distant offices still shapes how this landscape looks on the map.

The riding here is straight and surprisingly alive. The tar passes through the Bwabwata National Park, and animals are not a metaphor. Elephants cross the road at their own pace, and you will want to slow down far before you see them, since a bull in a bad mood is not a thing to meet at speed. Buffalo, kudu and warthogs turn up at the verge. Ride mid-morning or late afternoon, keep your eyes on the tree line, and treat any dark shape in the shadows as a possibility.

Popa Falls is hardly a waterfall in the Victoria Falls sense. It is a long run of low rapids over quartzite ledges, with islands of papyrus and trees in between, and in the dry season it can look more like a staircase of rocks than a cascade. Even so, the sound of the river and the birdlife around it make it a worthwhile half hour. Hippos and crocodiles live in the quieter pools, and the lodges and campsites along the bank have views that make you cancel your plans for the afternoon.

Fuel and food here are modest. A small filling point exists in the area, but supply in remote Namibia can be uneven, so arrive with a full tank from Rundu and take what Divundu offers as a bonus. Small shops, a craft stall or two, and the riverside camps will cover coffee and a meal. Water, sunscreen and a long sleeve are more useful than cleverness. If you want to see a side of Africa where the road is a fine line through living country, this is the stop.
t.katima mulilo@-17.5,24.3:
At the far end of the Caprivi Strip the road finally runs out of Namibia. Katima Mulilo stands on the Zambezi River, a wide, slow, brown stretch of water that here forms the border with Zambia, and the town's name is commonly translated from Lozi as something like putting out the fire, a reference to the rapids upstream. It is the capital of the Zambezi region, with about twenty-five thousand people, and across the river and a short bridge lies Sesheke in Zambia, drawn in on every local conversation.

For a rider who has done the long haul from Rundu, Katima feels like civilisation. There is fuel, supermarkets, banks with machines, a good selection of lodges on the river bank, and a street life that is lively and friendly after the empty bush. It is a border and trade town: trucks bound for Zambia, Botswana and the Copperbelt rumble through, and the market is a good place to understand what ordinary life in this corner of Africa looks like. Expect a heat that sits on you like a hand, and mosquitoes after dark.

The riding in and out is straightforward tar through flat mopane and sand country, with the same animal warnings as the rest of the strip. Elephants wander the river margins and there are national parks in all directions, including Mudumu and Nkasa Rupara in the south and Chobe on the Botswana side. Hippos graze on the banks at night, and locals will tell you where not to walk. A short boat trip at sundown on the Zambezi is better value than most sightseeing, with fish eagles, kingfishers and lazy crocodiles for company.

History here is layered and quite recent. The strip itself is a colonial invention, designed to give Germany access to the Zambezi, and the area saw serious trouble during the war for Namibian independence, when the border was closed to ordinary travel. Today it is quiet and welcoming, and fishing, farming and the tourism trade keep the town moving. If you cross into Zambia, check current border formalities, insurance and bike paperwork well in advance rather than at the barrier. For most riders, Katima is a pleasant end to the trans-Caprivi run, with a cold drink and a river view as the finish.

t.konitsa@40.0,20.7:
A single stone arch, about forty metres wide, crosses the Aoos river just outside Konitsa, and it is one of the finest bridges in the Balkans. It dates from 1823, in the last Ottoman decades of Epirus, and for two centuries it has stood over a green river with high mountains beyond. The bridge looks fragile, but it has survived floods, wars and earthquakes, and in the summer, local youths dive from its parapet into the cool water, a tradition more frightening to watch than to do.

The town stands at the junction of the Aoos and Voidomatis valleys, a few kilometres from the Albanian border, in a green basin ringed by mountains. Above it rises Smolikas, at 2,637 metres the second-highest mountain in Greece after Olympus, and one of the least visited. Its slopes are covered in beech and fir, with an alpine lake, Drakolimni, or Dragon Lake, near the summit, home to a rare species of alpine newt. A second ridge, Gamila, stands to the north-east, with its jagged limestone peaks. This is a landscape of dramatic scale and sharp light.

Konitsa itself is a working town, with a main square, a few cafés and tavernas, and small hotels that cater to rafters, hikers and the occasional motorcyclist. The Aoos is a popular river for rafting and canoeing in spring, when snowmelt swells the flow. Local cuisine features lamb, goat, trout and cheeses, and the pies of Epirus, thin pastry layered with greens, leeks or cheese, are a highlight.

Riding to Konitsa from Ioannina takes you along the Aoos valley, with a good surface and long, flowing curves, and the views of the mountains grow with every kilometre. The road is quiet, though trucks from the border may slow progress. Beyond the town, a narrow road climbs toward the mountain villages of Smolikas, such as Pades and Palaioseli, where the asphalt can be rough and the bends tight. Weather in the Pindus can be unpredictable, with sudden thunderstorms in summer and heavy snow in winter, so check conditions before you set out. Spring and autumn are the best seasons, and the autumn colours are particularly fine.

Konitsa has fuel stations, supermarkets, banks and pharmacies, and is the best place for services before heading into the mountains. Ioannina, about forty kilometres to the south, is the nearest large city. A coffee in the square and a walk to the bridge in the evening, when the stone glows in the last light, is a pleasant way to finish the day.

Plovdiv has been lived in for about six thousand years, which makes it one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in Europe, and it wears the age lightly. The city sits on the plain of the Maritsa river in the middle of southern Bulgaria, built around a cluster of rocky hills that rise out of the flat ground like islands. Locals talk about the seven hills, though one was quarried away long ago. Philip of Macedon took it in the fourth century BC and gave it the name Philippopolis, and the Romans later made it an important city on the road from Belgrade to Constantinople.

The Roman theatre, built under Trajan in the second century AD, is still used for concerts, and it faces out over the plain through a gap between hills. Above it the Old Town climbs in a jumble of cobbled lanes, Ottoman-era houses with overhanging upper floors, painted in strong colours, and tiny galleries. Down in the flat centre, a long pedestrian street leads past the remains of the Roman stadium, which lies partly beneath the shopping street. The Kapana district, a tangle of narrow streets that was rebuilt from a run-down craft quarter, is full of cafes, bars and small workshops. Plovdiv was European Capital of Culture in 2019.

For a motorcyclist, Plovdiv is a useful, easy city. About three hundred and forty thousand people live here, so there is fuel on every approach road, plenty of garages, and wide boulevards. The ride begins when you leave. To the south, the Rhodope Mountains rise quickly above Asenovgrad, with the ruined fortress of Asen in a gorge and lovely, twisting roads through beech forest. To the north, the Rose Valley and the Stara Planina ranges open up towards the Central Balkan, a longer ride with more mountain.

For dinner, order a shopska salad of tomato, cucumber and white cheese, grilled kebapche, a plate of banitsa, and a small glass of rakia to start. Prices are modest by western standards. Summer is hot, with temperatures often in the mid thirties, so start early and be off the plain by midday. Late spring, when the roses bloom, and early autumn offer the best mix of light and cool air. Drivers can be impatient and overtake in interesting places, so keep your eyes on the mirrors.
